52: OAuth access tokens also permit client-side API requests. See Making cross-origin, browser-side API requests in the Zendesk API guide.
53: In your requests, specify the access token in an Authorization header as follows:
54: Authorization: Bearer {access_token}
55: Example:
56: Authorization: Bearer gErypPlm4dOVgGRvA1ZzMH5MQ3nLo8bo
57: If you use curl to test different endpoints, you can use the following format:
58: curl https://obscura.zendesk.com/api/v2/users.json \ -H "Authorization: Bearer gErypPlm4dOVgGRvA1ZzMH5MQ3nLo8bo"
59: Access tokens can be up to 184 characters long.
60: Global OAuth access token
61: If you plan on making an app, integration, or bot available to multiple Zendesk customers, you must use global OAuth access tokens to authenticate Zendesk API requests. You may not use regular API tokens or OAuth tokens because the Zendesk Developer Terms prohibits Zendesk customers from sharing their API credentials with you. For more information, see Set up a global OAuth client.
62: The requirement to use global OAuth tokens doesn't apply if you're developing applications or integrations for internal use.
63: API token (deprecated)
64: API tokens are different from OAuth tokens, which are detailed in the previous section. API tokens are auto-generated passwords in the Zendesk Admin Center.
65: Warning: As passwords, API tokens can be used to impersonate anyone in the account, including admins. Make sure to keep them secure. Delete any unused tokens. Delete a token at once if you suspect it's been compromised and create another one if necessary. For a more secure alternative, use OAuth access tokens as described above.
66: API tokens are managed in the Admin Center interface at Apps and integrations > APIs > Zendesk API. The page lets you view, add, or delete tokens. More than one token can be active at the same time. Deleting a token deactivates it permanently.
67: You can have up to 256 tokens. If you're at the limit, you must delete an existing token to add a new one. Accounts that currently have more than 256 tokens have a limit of 2048 tokens.
68: Basic authentication is used for API tokens. The credentials must be sent with the request in an Authorization header.
69: Use the following format for the credentials:
70: {email_address}/token:{api_token}
71: Example:
72: jdoe@example.com/token:6wiIBWbGkBMo1mRDMuVwkw1EPsNkeUj95PIz2akv
73: After base64-encoding the resulting string, add it to the Authorization header as follows:
74: Authorization: Basic amRvZUBleGFtcGxlLmNvbS90b2tlbjo2d2lJQldiR2tCTW8xbVJETXVWd2t3MUVQc05rZVVqOTVQSXoyYWt2
75: If you use curl to test different endpoints, you can use the following format:
76: curl https://obscura.zendesk.com/api/v2/users.json \ -u [email protected]/token:6wiIBWbGkBMo1mRDMuVwkw1EPsNkeUj95PIz2akv
77: If authenticating over HTTP, url-encode the slash character in {email_address}/token as %2F.
78: SSL requirements
79: The Zendesk v2 API is an SSL-only API, regardless of how your account is configured.
80: All connections to the Zendesk API must support the TLS 1.2 protocol. Support for TLS 1.0 and 1.1 was removed in June 2018.
81: Connections to the API must also support the SNI extension to TLS.
82: If you connect to Zendesk through a client library, make sure it supports both TLS 1.2 and SNI.
83: End user authentication
84: End users can interact with the Zendesk API in two ways: anonymously or authenticated (with email and password).
85: In open instances where users can access the help center without signing in, end users do not require authentication for any API endpoint that lists anonymous permissions. An example is the List Articles endpoint.
86: In a closed Zendesk instance where end users must sign in to view your help center, end users can make authenticated requests to certain API endpoints, such as api/v2/requests, using their email and password if password access for end users is enabled. This allows end users to securely create, view, or update their own requests through the API. For more information on closed Zendesk instances, see Options for end-user access in Zendesk help.
87: A setting in Admin Center lets you explicitly enable or disable password access for end users in closed instances. See Turning on and off API access.

140: This is the reference documentation for the Zendesk Support API, which is also known as the Ticketing API. You can use the Support API with tickets, users, organizations, custom objects, and manage ticket workflows.
141: Any general mechanisms and conventions, such as pagination and authentication, work as described in the Zendesk API introduction and are considered implied in this text.
142: In addition to the reference docs, the following resources are available:
143: Zendesk API quick start
144: Zendesk Ticketing API articles and tutorials
145: Zendesk APIs community
146: Run in Postman
147: If you use Postman, you can import the Support API endpoints as a collection into your Postman app, then try out different requests to learn how the API works. Click the following button to get started:
148: If you don't use Postman, you can sign up for a free account on the Postman website and download the app. For more information about using Postman with Zendesk APIs, see Exploring Zendesk APIs with Postman.
149: Download OpenAPI file
150: Download OpenAPI file
151: Document conventions
152: For information on the syntax and style conventions used in the docs, see Documentation conventions in the general API introduction.
153: Examples
154: For information on the examples in the docs, see Examples in the general API introduction.
155: Security and authentication
156: For information on the authentication required to use the API, see Security and authentication in the general API introduction.
157: Rate limits
158: For information on the number of requests allowed per minute, see Rate limits in the general API introduction.
159: Request format
160: For information on requests, see Requests in the general API introduction.
161: Response format
162: For information on the HTTP status codes returned by the API, see Response format in the general API introduction.
163: Idempotency
164: The Ticketing API lets you specify an idempotency key that allows you to retry a ticket creation request without the risk of creating duplicate records.
165: To specify an idempotency key, provide a Idempotency-Key: {unique_key} header with your request.
166: Example:
167: curl https://{subdomain}.zendesk.com/api/v2/tickets.json \ -d '{"ticket": {"subject": "Printer offline", \ "comment": { "body": "My printer is offline. Restarting doesn’t help." }}}' \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Idempotency-Key: 12345" \ -v -u user:password -X POST
168: This creates the following response, which also includes a x-idempotency-lookup: miss header:
169: Status 201 Created{ "ticket": { "url": "https://{subdomain}.zendesk.com/api/v2/tickets/3.json", "id": 3, "subject": "Printer offline", ... }}
170: If you repeat the same request using the same body and idempotency key, another ticket is not created. Instead, you'll get the same response as before that is cached under the idempotency key. This time the response includes a x-idempotency-lookup: hit header:
171: Status 201 Created{ "ticket": { "url": "https://{subdomain}.zendesk.com/api/v2/tickets/3.json", "id": 3, "subject": "Printer offline", ... }}
172: If you create a request using the same idempotency key but with a different body, you'll receive the following error:
173: 400 Bad Request:{ "error": "IdempotentRequestError", "description": "Request parameters don't match the given idempotency key"}
174: Keys expire after two hours. If a request with a duplicate key is sent two hours after the original request, the request will create a new ticket.
175: The idempotency key is not stored as part of the ticket response. You will not be able to see the key when the ticket is opened.

97: In this 10-minute quick start, you'll use the Zendesk Ticketing API to create a few tickets in Zendesk Support.
98: The tutorial is intended for admins and agents with no developer experience. To make the API requests, the tutorial uses your web browser's built-in JavaScript console.
99: If you're a more experienced developer, check out the API reference. The reference includes curl examples for each endpoint. The API reference also includes links to related Postman collections. See Exploring Zendesk APIs with Postman.
100: What you'll need
101: To complete this tutorial, you'll need the following:
102: A Zendesk Support account with agent or admin access. To get a free account for testing, see Getting a trial or sponsored account for development.
103: API password access is enabled for the account. See Managing password access to the API in Zendesk help.
104: A web browser, such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari, or Microsoft Edge. These browsers include a built-in JavaScript console.
105: Creating tickets
106: To create a ticket, use the JavaScript console to make an HTTP POST request to the Ticketing API's Create Ticket endpoint.
107: Sign in to your Zendesk account as an admin or agent. From the Zendesk Agent Workspace, open your browser's JavaScript console:
108: Chrome: View > Developer > JavaScript Console
109: Firefox: Tools > Browser Tools > Web Developer Tools. Then click the Console tab.
110: Safari: Develop > Show JavaScript Console
111: Microsoft Edge: Tools > Developer > JavaScript Console
112: Paste the following script into your browser's console.
113: for (let i = 1; i < 4; i++) { const subject = `Test ticket ${i}` const body = `This is test ticket ${i}` $.ajax({ url: "/api/v2/tickets.json", contentType: "application/json", type: "POST", data: JSON.stringify({ ticket: { subject: subject, comment: { body: body } } }) }).done(data => { console.log(data.ticket) })}
114: Here's what the code looks like after pasting it into Google Chrome's JavaScript console:
115: The code snippet creates a loop that makes three requests to the Create Ticket endpoint. Each request creates a ticket in Zendesk Support.
116: Press Enter.
117: If successful, the console lists the tickets as JavaScript objects.
118: You can expand each object to see the ticket's properties.
119: To view the tickets in the Agent Workspace, reload the browser tab.
120: Then click Views > Recently updated tickets.
121: When you're done trying out the API, delete the test tickets by selecting them in the list and clicking Delete.
122: Troubleshooting tips
123: If the script returned an error, try the following troubleshooting tips:
124: If you get a 404 (Not Found) response, sign in to your Zendesk account before running the script.
125: If you get a TypeError: $.ajax not a function error, ensure you run the script from the Agent Workspace in Zendesk Support.
126: If you get a JavaScript error indicating that $.ajax is not defined, ensure you don't have any browser settings or plugins that block scripts from loading.
127: Next steps
128: The best way to learn how to use the Zendesk APIs is to try different requests on your own. You can use any of the following resources along the way:
129: To see what's possible using Zendesk APIs, check out the API reference.
130: Use Postman to explore the Zendesk APIs. Postman is a popular application for testing APIs and making API requests. See Exploring Zendesk APIs with Postman.
131: Install curl to run example requests from the API reference documentation. curl is a command-line tool for making HTTP requests without a web browser. See Installing and using curl.
132: Speed up development with an API client. An API client takes care of a lot of the low-level details of making requests and handling responses and lets you focus on the logic of your application.
133: Learn about the most common tasks developers perform with the Ticketing API.
134: Ask questions or look for answers in the Zendesk APIs community.

272: Frequently asked questions, answered.
273: How is Zendesk pricing structured?
274: Zendesk pricing is primarily seat-based (per agent, per month) with plan tiers that include different features. Your total cost typically includes:
275: Base subscription: pricing is determined by your selected plan tier and the number of agent seats needed.
276: Usage-based features: certain features like App Builder, Action Builder and Voice are billed based on consumption exceeding applicable plan allowances.
277: Add-ons: optional products and advanced features are billed in addition to your base plan.
278: Annual vs monthly billing: annual subscriptions often include a discount, compared to paying monthly.
279: Contact Sales to learn more.
280: What’s the difference between Support and Suite service plans?
281: Support plans: if you’re just starting out with email-based customer support, the Support plan is a great place to begin. It covers the essentials with the flexibility to add channels, expand capabilities or upgrade to the full Zendesk Suite as your needs grow.
282: Suite plans: the Zendesk Suite is your all-in-one customer service solution. Equipped with ticketing, messaging, live chat, help centre and voice support, it’s ideal for businesses providing multi-channel customer support. All Suite plans include powerful automations and AI agents available 24/7 to resolve customer issues quickly and effectively.
283: Learn more about Support plans and Suite plans as the different service plan levels available, or contact Sales if you’re evaluating enterprise requirements.
284: How does pricing for AI agents work?
285: Zendesk AI agents are included in every Suite and Support plan, with pricing based on the successful outcomes they deliver.
286: Automated resolutions: the unit of measurement used for calculating and billing your account for AI agent usage. Paying per automated resolution means that you pay only for customer requests that were successfully resolved by the AI agent, without any escalation to a human agent.
287: Learn more
288: What are Forethought AI agents?
289: Forethought AI agents by Zendesk are self-improving AI agents that can understand customer requests, take action and continuously improve outcomes over time. These agents bring specialised AI into the Zendesk AI ecosystem and can handle more complex workflows across all channels and environments.
290: They’re built to work seamlessly within Zendesk for those looking to elevate their service experience – and, just as importantly, they work on any platform, making it easy to bring best-in-class AI agents to an existing stack.
291: Contact Sales to learn more.
292: What add-ons are available and how are they priced?
293: Zendesk offers add-ons that extend your service plan with additional functionality such as advanced capabilities, additional channels or specialised products.
294: How add-ons are priced: add-ons are typically priced separately from your base plan and may be billed by seats, usage or the specific add-on.
295: Availability: add-ons can vary by plan tier and by purchase path (self-serve vs sales-assisted).
296: Explore options: view all available add-ons here.
297: How can I purchase Zendesk?
298: There are two main ways to buy Zendesk:
299: Online purchase: best for individuals and teams who want to get started quickly. Typically paid by card during checkout.
300: Sales-assisted: best for larger organisations, complex requirements or enterprise plans. Typically involves working with our sales team and may support invoice-based billing depending on eligibility and terms.
301: Payment methods: bank account (direct debit), credit or debit card or PayPal. For all other types of payments, contact your account representative.
302: Supported currency: currently, Zendesk supports USD, EUR, GBP and BRL.
303: Unsure? Contact Sales to confirm the right service plan and purchasing method.
304: Can I purchase enterprise plans online?
305: Enterprise service plans generally require sales engagement. If you’re looking for an enterprise plan, the best next step is to contact Sales so we can help you evaluate the right package, confirm requirements and set up purchasing (often including invoice options where applicable).

309: Monthly billing: more flexibility, typically a higher effective monthly rate.
310: Annual billing: usually discounted compared to paying monthly.
311: Upgrades/downgrades: service plan changes can affect billing and may apply immediately or at renewal, depending on your subscription terms.

320: To estimate your total Zendesk cost, consider these main components:

322: Add-ons: include any add-ons you need.

41: Overview
42: Copy
43: The Intercom Developer Platform is a suite of SDKs and APIs for building apps that connect with Intercom. You can use these apps to extend the functionality of Intercom or to integrate Intercom with other services.
44: New to Intercom?
45: For more information about Intercom products, visit our main website or read our user documentation.
46: Install Intercom
47: Install the Messenger into your product for web or mobile. This will allow your customers to send messages to your Intercom Inbox and provide a way for you to test Messenger integrations.
48: You can also:
49: Make customizations to the Messenger
50: Set up identity verification
51: Enable push notifications for iOS, Android, and React Native.
52: For Public App Developers
53: Public apps (sometimes referred to as integrations) are apps that are available for any customer to install. These apps have access to other peoples' Intercom data, which means there are specific requirements in order to publish them, such as setting up OAuth and submitting to the Intercom team for review.
54: Set up a development workspace
55: To develop a public app you will need to use a development workspace: sign up here to create your free account.
56: This will give you access to your Developer Hub, where you can configure webhooks, define your endpoints for Messenger and Inbox apps, set up OAuth, and submit your app for review.
57: Development Workspaces vs. Paid Workspaces
58: Development workspaces have limitations listed here and do not have the full functionality of a paid Intercom workspace. Development workspaces are only available for the US region.
59: Build your app
60: Here's the fun part! Build your app using any stack you'd like. For apps that are sent via the Messenger or available for the teammates in the Inbox, you'll need to use our Canvas Kit framework.
61: To see how it works, try building an app for Inbox or building an app for Messenger.
62: You are also required to set up OAuth so that your app has permission to access and interact with customers' data.
63: We recommend creating a [Staging] or [Dev] app and a [Production] app to assist in the development process.
64: Submit for review
65: Once development is done and OAuth is configured, in the Developer Hub of your [Production] app you can choose the listing type, provide installation URLs, and follow the steps outlined in this guide to submit it for review.
66: Make sure that your app follows our developer terms and platform guidelines. Once it's approved, your app is ready to be used by any of Intercom's 25K+ customers.
67: For Private App Developers
68: Private apps are apps that you can build specifically for your Intercom workspace that only access your own data. You can build a private app using your Access Token and it does not require a review.
69: Install apps from the App Store
70: Your team probably needs to integrate with other tools; we might have an app for it. Install connectors to tools you already use, like:
71: Slack
72: Stripe
73: WhatsApp
74: Salesforce
75: Available apps can be discovered and installed in the Intercom App Store, including apps built by Intercom, and apps built by other companies.
76: Build your own integration
77: If you aren't able to find an existing app that solves the problem you're facing, you can build your own using our REST APIs and Canvas Kit framework.
78: Go to the Developer Hub and create a new app. Make sure it's associated with your main Intercom workspace from the dropdown. Then you can use the Access Token from that app to start building.
79: Your app can be whatever you want — to see how it works, try building an app for Inbox or creating your own reports using the API. You can find more guides to help you build under the Guides section in the sidebar.
80: Configure your app
81: Your app should already be installed on the workspace where you created it. To uninstall the app, add it to another workspace, or regenerate the token, go to Your Workspaces in your Developer Hub — this guide will show you how. You can start using your app right away, and no review is required for a private app.
82: Getting help
83: Let us know
84: If you have any feedback on our developer documentation, please let us know what you think in the forms at the bottom of each page. Report issues with code blocks by clicking the feedback icon in the top right of the block.
85: Join our Intercom Community to get help, chat to Intercom experts, and connect to other developers building with Intercom. If you need immediate assistance, contact Intercom customer support directly using the Messenger in the bottom right of this page.

41: Authentication
42: Copy
43: To access the Intercom API, you have two authentication options depending on whether you app is public or private.
44: An Access Token is for if you're using the API to access data in your own Intercom workspace, in other words, building a private app.
45: OAuth is for if you're building a public app that accesses other people's Intercom data.
46: Access Tokens
47: Access Tokens can be used for the following cases:
48: You want to use the API to build a private Intercom app
49: You want to run scripts to create or get data from your Intercom workspace
50: You want to use the API to programmatically automate certain actions in your Intercom workspace
51: In all of these cases, the data you are accessing is your own team's customer data.
52: How to get your Access Token
53: We provide you with an Access Token as soon as you create an app on your workspace.
54: You can find your Access Token in the Configure > Authentication section in your app within the Developer Hub.
55: It is also visible on the Test & Publish > Your Workspaces page. This displays workspaces that have the app installed. More about how this works can be found in the Installing & Uninstalling Apps guide.
56: Access Tokens are issued to a teammate
57: An Access Token is issued to the teammate who installed the app on the workspace, or who last regenerated the token. Its access to conversations is limited by that teammate's conversation access, in addition to the app's scopes. See Conversation access is limited by the installing teammate.
58: Never give your Access Token to a third-party
59: Your Access Token can give access to your private Intercom data and should be treated like a password. If an app provider asks you for your Access Token, please do not provide it. Instead, let us know - apps are required to use OAuth rather than asking users for Access Tokens.
60: OAuth
61: You should use OAuth if:
62: You are requesting access to other people's Intercom accounts/data (for example, through an integration you've built)
63: You currently ask people for their API Keys to request resources on their behalf
64: You want to make it easier for your customers to share their customers' data with you
65: OAuth Flow
66: Getting Started with OAuth
67: To set up and test the OAuth installation flow in your development workspace by following this tutorial.
68: Never ask users for their Access Token
69: Asking your users for their Access Tokens rather than implementing OAuth is against our terms of service and may result in your API access being revoked.
70: How to use the token
71: Once you have a token, whether an access token or a token via the OAuth process, simply provide it as an Authorization:Bearer header in your requests, as shown below. If you want to go deeper on how the Authorization:Bearer header works please check out the full spec here.
72: $ curl \
73: -s https://api.intercom.io/users/5321a20f72cdbb4192000013 \
74: -H 'Authorization:Bearer <access_token>' \
75: -H 'Accept:application/json'
76: Alternatively, helper functions are provided in some of our SDKs to authorize via Access Tokens. This means you don't need to specify the header explicitly - it's all done under the hood.
77: intercom = Intercom::Client.new(token: '<access_token>');
78: {"token": '<access_token>'}
79: var client = new Intercom.Client({ token: '<access_token>' });

41: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
42: Copy
43: Learn how to use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to enable AI agents to securely access and interact with your Intercom data whenever helpful.
44: Region availability
45: The Intercom MCP server is available for US and EU hosted workspaces. AU hosted workspaces are not yet supported. Connect using the endpoint that matches your workspace's hosted region — see the connection URLs below.
46: What is Model Context Protocol?
47: MCP is a protocol that enables AI tools and applications to connect with Intercom's data and services in a secure, standardized way. It provides a structured method for AI models to:
48: Find and retrieve Intercom data (conversations, contacts, etc.)
49: Access specific tools and functionality provided by Intercom
50: Maintain context about your Intercom workspace when working with AI assistants
51: How MCP Works
52: Intercom hosts a remote MCP server that follows the authenticated remote MCP specification (docs). This server handles requests from AI tools and provides access to Intercom data through a secure interface.
53: Connection URLs:
54: Use the endpoint for your workspace's hosted region. You can tell your region from your workspace URL: app.intercom.com is US hosted and app.eu.intercom.com is EU hosted.
55: RegionStreamable HTTP (Recommended)Legacy SSE (deprecated)
56: UShttps://mcp.intercom.com/mcphttps://mcp.intercom.com/sse
57: EUhttps://mcp.eu.intercom.com/mcphttps://mcp.eu.intercom.com/sse
58: Requests to the EU endpoint are processed within the EU, in line with Intercom's Regional Data Hosting commitments.
59: When an AI tool or application needs to access Intercom data:
60: The tool connects to Intercom's MCP server
61: Authentication verifies the user's permissions
62: The tool can then access relevant Intercom data and functionality
63: The connection remains live to receive updates as needed
64: Benefits of Using MCP
65: Secure Access: All data access is authenticated and authorized
66: Standardized Interface: Consistent interaction pattern across different AI tools
67: Contextual Understanding: AI assistants maintain awareness of your Intercom environment
68: Increased Development Efficiency: Retrieve and interpret customer data from Intercom via your internal AI tools to be more efficient in your work
69: Available Tools
70: The Intercom MCP Server provides 16 tools for interacting with the Intercom API. OAuth connections can also get the Fin Operator tools.
71: Universal Tools
72: search
73: Universal search tool for finding conversations and contacts using a query DSL approach.
74: Key Features:
75: Must specify object_type:conversations or object_type:contacts to indicate which API to call
76: Supports complex field-based queries with operators (eq, neq, gt, lt, contains, etc.)
77: Returns summary results with IDs prefixed by type (conversation_* or contact_*)
78: Built-in pagination support with starting_after parameter
79: Free-text search capability with q: parameter
80: Example Queries:
81: object_type:conversations state:open source_type:email
82: object_type:contacts email_domain:"example.com"
83: object_type:conversations source_body:contains:"refund" limit:20
84: object_type:conversations team_assignee_id:15
85: object_type:conversations admin_assignee_id:6
86: Pagination:
87: Results are paginated with up to 150 items per page (default 5, set with limit: parameter)
88: When more results exist, the response includes a _note with the cursor to use
89: To fetch the next page, add starting_after:cursor_value to your query
90: Example: object_type:conversations state:open starting_after:cursor_abc123
91: Response includes:
92: total_in_page: Count of results in current page
93: results: Array of result objects with IDs prefixed by type
94: pages: Pagination metadata (when available)
95: _note: Helpful hint when more pages exist (e.g., "More results available. To get the next page, add to your query: starting_after:cursor_abc123")
96: fetch
97: Retrieve complete detailed information for specific resources.
98: Key Features:
99: Use IDs returned from search results (prefixed with conversation_, contact_, or company_)
100: Returns full resource details including metadata, conversation parts, custom attributes
101: Includes direct links to Intercom app for easy navigation
102: Direct API Tools
103: search_conversations
104: Search conversations by specific IDs with advanced filtering options including source type, author details, state, assignment fields (team_assignee_id, admin_assignee_id), and timing statistics.
105: Key Filter Parameters:
106: ids: Array of conversation IDs
107: source_type: Filter by source type (email, chat, etc.)
108: source_author_name, source_author_email: Filter by author details
109: state: Filter by conversation state (open, closed, snoozed)
110: team_assignee_id: Filter by team assignee ID (string)
111: admin_assignee_id: Filter by admin assignee ID (number)
112: statistics_time_to_assignment, statistics_time_to_admin_reply, statistics_time_to_first_close: Filter by timing statistics with operators (<, >, =, !=, <=, >=)
113: Pagination Support:
114: Results are paginated with up to 150 items per page (default 5)
115: If more results exist, the response includes a pages object with pages.next.starting_after cursor
116: To fetch the next page, make another request with the SAME search parameters plus the starting_after value from the previous response
117: Continue until pages.next is not present in the response
118: Response includes:
119: total_in_page: Count of results in current page
120: conversations: Array of conversation objects
121: pages: Pagination metadata (when available)
122: _note: Helpful hint when more pages exist
123: get_conversation
124: Retrieve a single conversation by ID with complete details including all conversation parts and metadata.
125: Required Parameters:
126: id: A raw numeric ID (e.g., 12345), the prefixed conversation_12345 form, or an Intercom Inbox URL. Normalized automatically, and must resolve to a numeric conversation ID. Also works for tickets: pass the ticket's id (the number at the end of its Inbox URL) or the Inbox URL itself. A ticket comes back as a conversation with its ticket details: state, type, title and other ticket attributes. The ticket number shown in the Inbox (such as #123) is not an id and doesn't find the ticket
127: search_contacts
128: Search contacts by IDs, name, email, phone, custom attributes, or email domain with flexible matching options.
129: Pagination Support:
130: Results are paginated with up to 150 items per page (default 5)
131: If more results exist, the response includes a pages object with pages.next.starting_after cursor
132: To fetch the next page, make another request with the SAME search parameters plus the starting_after value from the previous response
133: Continue until pages.next is not present in the response
134: Response includes:
135: total_in_page: Count of results in current page
136: data: Array of contact objects
137: pages: Pagination metadata (when available)
138: _note: Helpful hint when more pages exist
139: get_contact
140: Get complete contact information including custom attributes, location data, and activity timestamps.
141: list_companies
142: List companies with optional filters.
143: Key Filter Parameters:
144: name: Find a company by exact name match (returns single company)
145: company_id: Find a company by external company_id (returns single company)
146: tag_id: Filter companies by tag ID
147: segment_id: Filter companies by segment ID
148: per_page: Results per page (default 15, max 60)
149: page: Page number (default 1)
150: Uses page-based pagination. Response includes total_count and pages with total_pages.
151: get_company
152: Retrieve complete details for a specific company including all custom attributes, segments, and tags.
153: list_articles
154: List all articles in the Intercom Help Center.
155: Key Parameters:
156: page: Page number to retrieve (default 1)
157: per_page: Articles per page (1-150, default 25)
158: Uses page-based pagination. Response includes pages with total_pages.
159: search_articles
160: Search for articles in the Intercom Help Center. At least one search parameter must be provided.
161: Key Parameters:
162: phrase: Free-text search across article title and body
163: state: Filter by published or draft
164: help_center_id: Filter by Help Center ID (numeric)
165: highlight: When true, returns highlighted matching snippets
166: get_article
167: Retrieve complete details for a specific article including full HTML body, metadata, and parent collection information.
168: Required Parameters:
169: id: The article ID to retrieve
170: Optional Parameters:
171: locale: Locale code of the translation to return, for example fr or pt-BR. Omit it for the article's default-locale content. The response lists the article's available_locales, and an unknown locale is rejected with that list
172: create_article
173: Create a new article in the Intercom Help Center.
174: Required Parameters:
175: title: The article title
176: Optional Parameters:
177: description: A short summary
178: body: Article content in HTML format
179: state: published or draft (defaults to draft)
180: parent_id: Numeric ID of the collection or section to place the article in
181: parent_type: collection or section. Ignored by the Intercom API, which places the article by parent_id alone
182: ai_chatbot_availability: Whether Fin AI Agent can use the article. Omit it to keep Intercom's default
183: ai_copilot_availability: Whether Copilot can use the article. Omit it to keep Intercom's default
184: ai_sales_agent_availability: Whether the AI Sales Agent can use the article. Omit it to keep Intercom's default
185: audience_ids: IDs of the Fin audiences to target the article to, as integers or digit-only strings. Get them from list_audiences. An unknown ID is rejected with a 404 and nothing is saved. This sets Fin AI Agent targeting only and doesn't change who can see the article in the Help Center
186: The content is written in the article's default locale. To add translations, create the article first, then call update_article with its ID and locale once per translation.
187: The article is attributed to the teammate the connection acts as: the admin who authorized an OAuth connection, or the teammate a Bearer token belongs to. The author can't be set per call.
188: update_article
189: Update an existing article. At least one field to update must be provided.
190: Required Parameters:
191: id: The article ID to update
192: Optional Parameters:
193: locale: Locale code of the translation to write, for example fr or pt-BR. With locale, the title, description, body, state, the three ai_*_availability flags and audience_ids apply to that translation only, and at least one of them is required. parent_id and parent_type still apply to the whole article. Omit it to write the article's default-locale content, which may not be English. Writing to a locale the article doesn't have yet creates that translation and needs a title. Without one, Intercom rejects the write with a 400 and nothing is saved. Intercom rejects unsupported locale codes, and get_article lists the article's available_locales
194: title: Update the article title
195: description: Update the short summary
196: body: Update the article content (HTML format)
197: state: Change to published or draft. Omit it to leave the publish state unchanged
198: parent_id: Move the article to a different collection or section (numeric ID)
199: parent_type: collection or section. Ignored by the Intercom API, which places the article by parent_id alone
200: ai_chatbot_availability, ai_copilot_availability, ai_sales_agent_availability: Whether Fin AI Agent, Copilot and the AI Sales Agent can use the article. Without locale each one sets the default language's availability, and with locale that translation's. Omit them to leave availability unchanged
201: audience_ids: IDs of the Fin audiences to target the article to, as integers or digit-only strings. Get them from list_audiences. Without locale this sets the targeting of every translation, so [] clears it everywhere. With locale it sets that translation's targeting only. An unknown ID is rejected with a 404 and nothing is saved. This sets Fin AI Agent targeting only and doesn't change who can see the article in the Help Center
202: Each update also sets the author of the content it writes to the teammate the connection acts as: the default-locale content without locale, or that translation with it. The author can't be set per call.
203: list_audiences
204: List the workspace's Fin audiences: the groups of contacts that Fin content can be targeted to. Use an audience's id in audience_ids on create_article or update_article. These aren't Help Center audiences, and they aren't contact or company segments.
205: Key Parameters:
206: page: Page number to retrieve (default 1)
207: per_page: Audiences per page (1-50, default 50)
208: Uses page-based pagination. Response includes total_count, page, per_page and total_pages, plus a hint naming the next page while more pages exist.
209: Each audience has a string id, a name, and the predicates and role_predicates rules that define it. audience_ids accepts the string id as it is. Names come back HTML-escaped, for example & as &. There's no name or type filter, so page through the list to find an audience by name.
210: Requires the Read audiences permission. If your OAuth connection was made before the Intercom MCP integration had this permission, calls to this tool return an error asking you to reconnect. Disconnect and reconnect the Intercom MCP server to grant it. A Bearer token's app needs it too; without it, calls return Intercom's own 401 error.
211: add_internal_note
212: Add an internal note to a conversation. Notes are visible to teammates only — nothing is sent to the customer, and this tool cannot send customer-visible replies. Adding a note never changes the assignee, but a note on a conversation that is snoozed and assigned to someone other than the teammate the connection acts as will unsnooze (reopen) it.
213: Required Parameters:
214: conversation_id: A raw numeric ID (e.g., 12345), the prefixed conversation_12345 form, or an Intercom Inbox URL. Normalized automatically, and must resolve to a numeric conversation ID. Also works for tickets: pass the ticket's id (the number at the end of its Inbox URL) or the Inbox URL itself. The ticket number shown in the Inbox (such as #123) is not an id and doesn't find the ticket. A note on a ticket doesn't change its state or assignee
215: body: The note content in HTML format (plain text is also accepted). Whitespace between block-level tags becomes empty paragraphs and renders as blank space, so emit tags without newlines or indentation between them
216: The note is attributed to the teammate the connection acts as: the admin who authorized an OAuth connection, or the teammate a Bearer token belongs to. Authorship cannot be set per call.
217: Response includes:
218: The conversation ID and the created note part (id, part_type, created_at, author) — not the full conversation. A part_type of note_and_unsnooze means the note reopened the conversation. Use get_conversation to read the updated thread
219: Requires the Write conversations permission in addition to read access. If your OAuth connection was made before the Intercom MCP integration had this permission, calls to this tool return an error asking you to reconnect. Disconnect and reconnect the Intercom MCP server to grant it.
220: A Bearer token also needs the Read admins permission to attribute the note. Without it, or without Write conversations, calls to this tool return an error asking you to add the missing permission to the app the token belongs to.
221: submit_mcp_feedback
222: Send feedback about the Intercom MCP server to Intercom: a tool that's missing, a result that's wrong or confusing, or a flow that takes more calls than it should. Intercom uses it to improve the MCP server. Nothing is written to your workspace: no ticket or conversation is opened, and nobody replies. Don't use it for support requests, for the Intercom product itself, or for other MCP servers.
223: Required Parameters:
224: summary: A one-sentence headline for the problem or request, in plain English (15-150 characters). A summary that contains a URL, markup, a UUID, a snake_case name or seven or more digits in a row is rejected
225: category: missing_capability, bug, workflow_friction or other
226: feedback: The full detail: what was missing, what went wrong, or what was harder than it should be (10-4000 characters)
227: task_context: The wider task the user was working on (up to 1000 characters)
228: source: user when the user asked to send the feedback or raised the problem, or agent when the AI client noticed it
229: Optional Parameters:
230: tool_name: The tool the feedback is about. Only tools listed on your connection are accepted
231: requested_capability: The operation that was missing, named as the Intercom REST API operation where possible (up to 200 characters)
232: The server adds the workspace, the teammate, the region and the connection type to each record. These come from your connection, not from the AI client. Don't include customer personal data, conversation contents or secrets.
233: Response includes:
234: A receipt with status set to received, the submission's id, and a note saying that no reply will be sent
235: A Bearer token needs the Read admins permission to submit feedback. Without it, the response has status set to rejected and nothing is stored.
236: Fin Operator tools
237: Operator is Fin's internal AI agent. If your workspace has Fin Operator, the Intercom MCP server also lets your AI client ask Operator to do work inside your workspace, read the answers back, and review and apply the changes Operator proposes.
238: The Fin Operator tools work only when all of the following are true:
239: Your workspace has Fin Operator.
240: You connected with OAuth. Bearer token connections do not get the Fin Operator tools.
241: You can use Operator in Intercom. The tools are authorized as you, so you need the same permission over MCP that you need in the Intercom app.
242: If you connected with OAuth but your workspace doesn't have Fin Operator, or you don't have permission to use it, the tools can still be listed. Calls to them don't run Operator. Instead, send_operator_message returns a short message from Intercom on how to get access, for example by starting a trial, asking an admin, or buying the add-on, and the other four tools say that Operator isn't available yet. The tools start working once you have access.
243: Connected before the Fin Operator tools were added?
244: If your OAuth connection was made before the Use Fin Operator permission existed, the tools are listed but calls to them return an error asking you to reconnect. Disconnect and reconnect the Intercom MCP server to grant it. Reconnecting also keeps every existing tool working.
245: There are five Fin Operator tools:
246: send_operator_message: send Operator a message; collect the answer later
247: get_operator_response: read the latest response from an Operator chat
248: get_proposal_details: show what each pending proposal would change. Read-only
249: apply_proposals: apply proposals to your workspace's live configuration
250: reject_proposals: discard proposals
251: Only send_operator_message uses Operator credits, in the same way as a turn started in Intercom; the other four tools are free.
252: For parameters, response statuses, tool annotations, a typical workflow, rate limits and troubleshooting, see the Fin Operator tools guide.
253: Setting things up
254: Authentication Methods
255: The MCP server supports two authentication approaches:
256: OAuth Flow (Recommended): Browser-based authentication with a consent step, described below
257: Bearer Token: Direct API token authentication
258: What to expect during OAuth
259: When you connect a client with OAuth, your browser shows two screens in order:
260: The Intercom MCP consent page. This names the application asking to connect, lists what it will be able to do in your workspace, and shows its Client ID and the address it redirects to after you approve. Choose Allow to continue or Cancel to stop. Cancel grants nothing.
261: Intercom's authorization screen. This asks you to authorize access for Intercom MCP, the server, rather than for the application. After you authorize, you are returned to the application.
262: Intercom's authorization screen can only name the Intercom MCP server, so the consent page is where you see and confirm which application receives access. The application name is supplied by the application itself and is not verified by Intercom.
263: Check the redirect address
264: Before you choose Allow, check that the Redirects to address belongs to the application you expect. If you did not start the connection yourself, or you do not recognize the application or the redirect address, choose Cancel.

307: Connecting your own MCP client
308: The providers listed above are already on the allowlist. If you're building your own MCP client, OAuth client registration is automatic — the server supports Dynamic Client Registration — but every redirect URI a client registers is checked against an allowlist, which controls where the server will send authorization responses.
309: What this means for your client:
310: Bearer token authentication doesn't use a redirect URI, so there's nothing to request.
311: OAuth with a callback on localhost or 127.0.0.1 is already allowed on any port, so you can develop and test locally right away.
312: OAuth with any other callback needs an allowlist entry before the flow will complete.
313: Until we've added your redirect URI, registration and authorization fail with one of these errors:
314: Redirect URI https://your-app.example.com/callback is not in the allowlist, reach out to Intercom Customer Support if you believe we should support it
315: Invalid request: Redirect URI is not allowed
316: App Store review is a separate approval
317: Submitting your app for review in the Developer Hub doesn't add its redirect URI to the MCP server allowlist, even though you register the URI there. If your app connects to the MCP server with OAuth, request an allowlist entry as well.
318: Requesting an allowlist entry
319: Contact Intercom Customer Support through the Messenger in the bottom right of this page, and include:
320: The name of your client and what it does with Intercom data
321: Each redirect URI in full, exactly as your client sends it
322: The environment each URI serves: development, staging, or production
323: Your workspace ID
324: Whether you need a wildcard entry like https://*.example.com, and what it needs to cover
325: We add the narrowest entry that covers your callbacks. For a host you own, that's usually the origin — an entry for https://app.example.com covers every path on that host. If your callback runs on a platform shared with other companies, we add the exact path instead, so list every path you use. Wildcards are granted only for domains where you control every subdomain.
326: One entry covers both mcp.intercom.com and mcp.eu.intercom.com, so a single request is enough for both regions.
327: Working with Pagination
328: All search and list tools support pagination to handle large result sets efficiently.
329: Cursor-based pagination is used by search, search_conversations, and search_contacts — use the starting_after parameter.
330: Page-based pagination is used by list_articles, list_companies and list_audiences — use the page parameter.
331: Example Pagination Workflow
332: 1. Initial Search Request
333: Using the search tool:
334: object_type:conversations state:open limit:50
335: 2. Response with More Results
336: If more results exist, you'll receive:
337: {
338: "total_in_page": 50,
339: "results": [...],
340: "pages": {
341: "type": "pages",
342: "page": 1,
343: "per_page": 50,
344: "total_pages": 5,
345: "next": {
346: "page": 2,
347: "starting_after": "cursor_abc123"
348: }
349: },
350: "_note": "More results available. To get the next page, add to your query: starting_after:cursor_abc123"
351: }
352: 3. Fetch Next Page
353: Use the cursor from the response:
354: object_type:conversations state:open limit:50 starting_after:cursor_abc123
355: 4. Continue Until Complete
356: Keep paginating until the response no longer includes pages.next or _note, indicating you've reached the last page.
357: Tool-Specific Pagination
358: For search_conversations and search_contacts, use the starting_after parameter:
359: {
360: "state": "open",
361: "per_page": 50,
362: "starting_after": "cursor_abc123"
363: }
364: The response will include the same pagination metadata to guide you through the result set.
365: Required Scopes
366: The Intercom MCP server requires the following permissions to access your workspace data. When using Bearer token authentication, ensure your access token includes these scopes. Learn more about OAuth permissions.
367: Read and list users and companies: Required for contact and company data access
368: Read conversations: Required for conversation data access
369: Write conversations: Required for adding internal notes to conversations (add_internal_note)
370: Read and write articles: Required for Help Center article access (list, search, get, create, update)
371: Read audiences: Required for listing Fin audiences (list_audiences). An OAuth connection authorized before the Intercom MCP integration had this permission must be disconnected and reconnected to get it
372: Read admins: Required for Bearer tokens on the tools that act as you: adding internal notes, creating and updating articles, and submitting feedback (add_internal_note, create_article, update_article, submit_mcp_feedback). OAuth connections need nothing extra for it
373: Use Fin Operator: Required for the Fin Operator tools. Granted through OAuth only; it cannot be added to a Bearer token.
374: During OAuth, the consent page summarizes these permissions as: view conversations and add internal notes to them, view contacts and companies, view, create and update articles, view Fin audiences, and use Fin Operator. The Use Fin Operator permission is requested for every connection, but the tools only work for workspaces that have Fin Operator.

385: # Clear MCP auth cache

394: ps aux | grep mcp-remote | grep -v grep
395: Error Handling
396: Invalid queries: The search tool validates field names and operators, returning specific error messages
397: Authentication failures: Check token validity or restart OAuth flow
398: Rate limiting: Intercom API limits apply - reduce request frequency if needed
399: Troubleshooting Tips
400: Restart AI Agent after configuration changes
401: Use the MCP Inspector to verify tool availability
402: Check browser console for OAuth-related errors
403: Verify Intercom API token permissions for bearer auth
404: The consent page expires after 15 minutes. If Allow shows "Authorization could not be completed", start the connection again from your client
405: Only one connection can be pending per browser. Starting a second connection in another tab before finishing the first makes the first tab's Allow fail with the same message. Start the connection again
406: An "Invalid redirect URI" error that says the URI does not match any registered URI for this client, shown before the consent page, means the client opened its callback on a port it did not register. Clear the client's saved authentication for the Intercom server (see Authentication Problems above) and connect again, so the client registers its current callback address
407: The consent page only appears in the OAuth flow. Bearer token authentication is unchanged
408: If you choose Allow and Intercom then shows "We're having technical difficulties", you most likely connected using another region's endpoint, for example the US endpoint for an EU hosted workspace. Remove the connection from your client and connect again using the endpoint for your workspace's region (see How MCP Works). The MCP server isn't available for AU hosted workspaces.

192: FAQs
193: How does Intercom pricing work?
194: Intercom pricing has two components:
195: Seats: You pay per teammate based on your plan (Essential, Advanced, Expert)
196: Usage: You pay for what you use (e.g. Fin outcomes, messaging channels)
197: All plans include access to Intercom and Fin AI Agent. Want a tailored estimate? Use the pricing calculator.
198: How is Fin AI Agent priced?
199: Fin is priced at $0.99 per outcome.
200: An outcome is counted when:
201: A customer confirms their issue is resolved, or
202: They don’t ask for more help after Fin responds, or
203: Fin completes a workflow (Procedure), including handoffs
204: You’re only charged once per conversation, even if multiple questions are answered.
205: Can I use Fin with my existing helpdesk?
206: Yes. Fin can be used with tools like Salesforce and others.
207: Pricing:
208: $0.99 per outcome
209: Minimum monthly commitment applies (e.g. 50 outcomes)
210: No seat costs
211: No setup, integration, or platform fees
212: What plans does Intercom offer?
213: Intercom offers three plans:
214: Essential
215: Advanced
216: Expert
217: Your plan determines:
218: Seat price
219: Feature access
220: Included capabilities (e.g. Lite seats on higher tiers)
221: What is a seat (Full vs Lite)?
222: Full seat: Paid. Required for teammates who interact with customers and use core features.
223: Lite seat: Free (on Advanced/Expert). Limited access for internal collaboration.
224: Only Full seats can send messages or fully use features like outbound content.
225: Are there additional usage charges?
226: Yes. Beyond seats, pricing is usage-based for certain features:
227: Fin AI Agent: $0.99 per outcome
228: WhatsApp: Charged per message sent
229: SMS: Charged per message (varies by region)
230: Email campaigns: Charged per bulk email sent
231: Phone: Usage-based (varies)
232: Inbound support (e.g. responding to customer emails) is included.
233: What is Proactive Support Plus?
234: An optional add-on for outbound engagement.
235: $99/month includes 500 messages
236: Covers: Product Tours, Surveys, In-app messages, Mobile Push, Carousels
237: Additional messages are charged per unit
238: How much is Copilot?
239: Copilot is an optional add-on at $29 per agent/month billed annually, or $35 per agent/month billed monthly, for unlimited usage.
240: Copilot is a personal AI assistant in the Inbox that helps your team resolve conversations faster. Every agent also gets 10 Copilot and 10 AI Auto-translation conversations free each month.
241: What is the Pro add-on?
242: Pro is an optional add-on at $100/month, which includes analysis of 500 conversations/month and 6,000 credits per month.
243: Pro is a set of advanced AI features for managing and improving your support operation. It includes Operator, an agent for customer operations, plus features that help you analyze performance, monitor quality, identify trends, and continuously improve Fin.
244: Credits are the unit used to measure and charge for Operator usage. Every Pro workspace receives monthly credits, and on contracted plans the number of credits included scales with conversation volume. If you use more credits than what’s included in Pro, you can buy additional credits at $0.01 per credit. Simple actions use fewer credits, while more complex work, like analyzing large sets of conversations, building automation, or testing changes, uses more. You can track usage, set alerts, and use hard limits to control spend.
245: Do I need a contract?
246: No.
247: Monthly or annual self-serve plans are available (Essential, Advanced)
248: Contracts are optional and required for:
249: Enterprise needs
250: Premier Support / onboarding
251: Custom terms
252: What’s the minimum to get started?
253: 1 Full seat minimum
254: No required platform fees beyond that
255: Usage (e.g. Fin, messaging) is pay-as-you-go
256: This makes it easy to start small and scale.
257: Is there a free trial?
258: Yes.
259: 14-day free trial
260: No credit card required
261: Includes all features, Fin, and add-ons
262: You only pay once you choose a plan and add payment details.
263: How do I change my plan or seats?
264: You can:
265: Upgrade/downgrade plans
266: Add/remove seats
267: Add or remove add-ons
268: Handled directly in your workspace (or via Sales if under contract). Downgrades typically take effect at renewal.
269: Are there discounts available?
270: Yes.
271: Startups: Up to 93% off + 1 year of Fin free (via Early Stage program)
272: Enterprise discounts may be available via Sales

494: Overview
495: Freshdesk is a cloud-based customer support platform that was founded with the mission of enabling companies of all sizes to provide great customer service. Our goal is simple: make it easy for brands to talk to their customers and make it easy for users to get in touch with businesses.
496: Freshdesk's APIs belong to the Representational State Transfer (REST) category. They allow you to perform 'RESTful' operations such as reading, modifying, adding or deleting data from your helpdesk. The APIs also support Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS).
497: What API commands are used by Freshdesk?
498: Freshdesk APIs are plain JSON over HTTP and use the following HTTP verbs:
499: Command
500: Purpose
501: POST
502: Create an object
503: GET
504: Fetch one or more objects
505: PUT
506: Update an object
507: DELETE
508: Remove an object
509: Note:
510: All API requests should hit the secured endpoint, that is, only HTTPS
511: What's New
512: Version 2 of the API brings several new features as well as changes to the previous APIs. This section highlights some of the new features introduced in v2.
513: Higher rate limits as a result of significant performance enhancements
514: Improved error handling - errors will return appropriate HTTP status codes and an error body
515: Four new API categories - Business Hours, Products, Email Configs, and SLAs
516: New APIs that enable you to Reply to a ticket and enhancements to existing APIs that enable you to Update a ticket's description, Update a ticket's notes, and Retrieve a list of tickets that have been recently modified
517: XML Support has been deprecated, only JSON is supported
518: Only SSL calls (HTTPS) will be allowed
519: Works only via Freshdesk domains and not via custom CNAMEs
520: Support for page sizes up to 100 has been added
521: New API deprecation and breaking change policies
522: Some categories have been renamed for consistency with the web application. For example, Forums are now Discussions and Users are now Contacts

670: Policies
671: Freshdesk APIs are classified into either production or beta APIs. A production API is one that has been made generally available for public use and is stable. A beta API is one that is still in development or is for internal or limited use and whose stability cannot be guaranteed. Beta APIs may be removed or modified at any time without advance notice. The following policies apply to production APIs only.
672: Deprecation Policy
673: The current version of production level APIs is v2. The legacy v1 API is fully deprecated and restricted for new users. For active versions, when a new major update is made generally available (not beta), the older version will be deprecated and will cease to function after six months. Once an API is removed, any request to it will result in a 404 error.
674: Breaking Change Policy
675: Changes that do not break an API, such as adding a new attribute can be made at any time. Changes that break a production level API such as removing attributes or making major changes to the API’s behavior will only be done with an advance notice of 60 days. However, there may be rare occasions where due to legal, performance, or security reasons, we are forced to make breaking changes without advance notice.

779: Authentication
780: How does it work? Who can access my helpdesk? Can everybody see my data?
781: Before you can set the priority of a ticket or change a customer's name or use any of the APIs listed above, you need to "authenticate your ID" or "log in" in the same way as you log in to your helpdesk's web portal.
782: You can use your personal API key to authenticate the request. If you use the API key, there is no need for a password. You can use any set of characters as a dummy password.
783: curl -v -u apikey:X -H "Content-Type: application/json" -X GET 'https://domain.freshdesk.com/api/v2/tickets'
784: For example, if your API key is abcdefghij1234567890, the curl command to use is:
785: curl -v -u abcdefghij1234567890:X -H "Content-Type: application/json" -X GET 'https://domain.freshdesk.com/api/v2/tickets'
786: Where can I find my API key?
787: Log in to your Support Portal
788: Click on your profile picture on the top right corner of your portal
789: Go to Profile settings Page
790: Your API key will be available below the change password section to your right
791: For more information, please refer to this solution article
792: Note:
793: If you are sure that your credentials are correct, but are still unable to access your helpdesk, make sure that the "APIkey:X" is Base64-encoded before passing it as an "Authorization" header.
794: What are the resources available via the API?
795: Every single piece of information - be it a customer's ID or the priority of a specific ticket - can be identified by its own unique identifier or "URI". If you want your data from the helpdesk, whether via your smartphone app or via a third party service, you need this identifier. All URIs follow a specific format and that format is:
796: https://your_helpdesk_domain_name/api/v2/resource_name
797: For example, if you are Davy Jones and you are managing problems of drowned souls via your Freshdesk portal "thelocker.freshdesk.com", then to access the contacts in your helpdesk, the syntax would be
798: https://thelocker.freshdesk.com/api/v2/contacts
799: For tickets, it would be
800: https://thelocker.freshdesk.com/api/v2/tickets
801: Note:
802: We have shortened API resource URLs throughout this document by omitting the domain name. For example, /api/v2/tickets is actually https://domain.freshdesk.com/api/v2/tickets
803: Will everyone have the same access rights?
804: No, your ability to access data depends on the permissions available to your Freshdesk user profile. For example, if your Freshdesk Agent Role is "Newbie Agent" who is only allowed to view tickets but not reply to them, then you will not be able to use the APIs to reply to a ticket.

830: Embedding
831: Our previous version of APIs returned a large number of fields by default. In order to increase performance and reduce data usage, we have removed several of these fields in our v2.0 APIs. For example, when you view a ticket, we no longer return the requester's name or the company name. However, there may be situations where these fields are required and hence, we have included a mechanism to embed additional resources into an API call in order to minimise the number of required API calls.
832: Note:
833: Embedding resources into an API will consume an additional API call credit per embedded resource.
834: You can request for additional resources using the "include" keyword. For example you can embed the requester's details within the ticket view API by using the following command

836: curl -v -u 'abcdefgh12345678:X' -X GET 'https://domain.freshdesk.com/api/v2/tickets/20?include=requester'

932: Errors
933: I have encountered an error. How do I debug it?
934: API requests that result in errors will return an appropriate HTTP status code to help you identify the type of error. You can use the table below to understand what each code means.
935: HTTP Status Code
936: Text
937: Description
938: 400
939: Client or Validation Error
940: The request body/query string is not in the correct format. For example, the Create a ticket API requires the requester_id field to be sent as part of the request and if it is missing, this status code is returned.
941: 401
942: Authentication Failure
943: Indicates that the Authorization header is either missing or incorrect. You can learn more about the Authorization header here.
944: 403
945: Access Denied
946: This indicates that the agent whose credentials were used in making this request was not authorized to perform this API call. It could be that this API call requires admin level credentials or perhaps the Freshdesk portal doesn't have the corresponding feature enabled. It could also indicate that the user has reached the maximum number of failed login attempts or that the account has reached the maximum number of agents
947: 404
948: Requested Resource not Found
949: This status code is returned when the request contains invalid ID/Freshdesk domain in the URL or an invalid URL itself. For example, an API call to retrieve a ticket with an invalid ID will return a HTTP 404 status code to let you know that no such ticket exists.
950: 405
951: Method not allowed
952: This API request used the wrong HTTP verb/method. For example an API PUT request on /api/v2/tickets endpoint will return a HTTP 405 as /api/v2/tickets allows only GET and POST requests.
953: 406
954: Unsupported Accept Header
955: Only application/json and */* are supported.
956: When uploading files multipart/form-data is supported.
957: 409
958: Inconsistent/Conflicting State
959: The resource that is being created/updated is in an inconsistent or conflicting state. For example, if you attempt to Create a Contact with an email that is already associated with an existing user, this code will be returned.
960: 415
961: Unsupported Content-type
962: Content type application/xml is not supported. Only application/json is supported.
963: 429
964: Rate Limit Exceeded
965: The API rate limit allotted for your Freshdesk domain has been exhausted.
966: 500
967: Unexpected Server Error
968: Phew!! You can't do anything more here. This indicates an error at Freshdesk's side. Please email us your API script along with the response headers. We will reach you out to you and fix this ASAP.

1044: Pagination
1045: API responses that return a list of objects, such as View List of Tickets and View List of Contacts are paginated. To scroll through the pages, add the parameter page to the query string. The page number starts with 1.
1046: https://domain.freshdesk.com/api/v2/contacts?page=2
1047: By default, the number of objects returned per page is 30. This can be adjusted by adding the per_page parameter to the query string. The maximum number of objects that can be retrieved per page is 100. Invalid values and values greater than 100 will result in an error.
1048: https://domain.freshdesk.com/api/v2/contacts?per_page=10
1049: The per_page and page parameters can also be used together. The following example will retrieve the contacts from 11 to 20.
1050: https://domain.freshdesk.com/api/v2/contacts?per_page=10&page=2
1051: The 'link' header in the response will hold the next page url if exists. If you have reached the last page of objects, then the link header will not be set.
1052: Headers:
1053: "link":< https://domain.freshdesk.com/api/v2/tickets?filter=all_tickets&page=2>;rel="next"
1054: Best Practices
1055: Rate Limit
1056: Whenever possible, please queue API calls at your end. This ensures that you can buffer calls on your end to avoid hitting the rate limit and retry API calls when you hit the rate limit after the retry-after time.
1057: Cache non-volatile data on your end whenever it is feasible. For e.g. the mapping between agent name and ID is extremely unlikely to change. Hence, by caching it on the client side, you will be able to avoid API calls.
1058: As soon as you recognise that a rate limit increase will be required in the future, contact us. This will make it possible for us to ensure that we are prepared to increase the limit as and when as it is needed.
1059: Other
1060: Avoid making API calls directly from a mobile app, rather send the request to your servers and make the API calls from there. This ensures that in the event of an API endpoint being modified, you will be able to make and deploy the change to your server rather than updating your app and forcing your users to the latest version.
1061: Always use HTTP connection/multiplexing when making the API request. This will save some time while opening TCP connection to Freshdesk.
1062: When retrieving a list of objects, avoid making calls referencing page numbers over 500 (deep pagination). These are performance intensive calls and you may suffer from extremely long response times.

2567: Use filters to view only specific tickets (those which match the criteria that you choose). By default, only tickets that have not been deleted or marked as spam will be returned, unless you use the 'deleted' filter.

2569: 1. By default, only tickets that have been created within the past 30 days will be returned. For older tickets, use the updated_since filter

2571: 3. When using filters, the query string must be URL encoded - see example
2572: 4. Use 'include' to embed additional details in the response. Each include will consume an additional 2 credits. For example if you embed the stats information you will be charged a total of 3 API credits for the call.

2818: Filter Tickets
2819: get
2820: /api/v2/search/tickets?query=[query]
2821: OAuth 2.0 Scope
2822: 1
2823: freshdesk.tickets.search
2824: Use custom ticket fields that you have created in your account to filter through the tickets and get a list of tickets matching the specified ticket fields.
2825: Format - "(ticket_field:integer OR ticket_field:'string') AND ticket_field:boolean"
2826: Note:
2827: 1. Archived tickets will not be included in the results
2828: 2. The query must be URL encoded
2829: 3. Query can be framed using the name of the ticket fields, which can be obtained from Ticket Fields endpoint. Ticket Fields are case sensitive
2830: 4. Query string must be enclosed between a pair of double quotes and can have up to 512 characters
2831: 5. Logical operators AND, OR along with parentheses () can be used to group conditions
2832: 6. Relational operators greater than or equal to :> and less than or equal to :< can be used along with date fields and numeric fields
2833: 7. Input for date fields should be in UTC Format
2834: 8. The number of objects returned per page is 30 also the total count of the results will be returned along with the result
2835: 9. To scroll through the pages add page parameter to the url. The page number starts with 1 and should not exceed 10
2836: 10. To filter for fields with no values assigned, use the null keyword
2837: 11. Please note that the updates will take a few minutes to get indexed, after which it will be available through API

5526: Ticket Fields
5527: Note:
5528: Only users with admin privileges can access the following APIs.
5529: The custom and default ticket fields in Freshdesk have the following properties.
5530: JSON Parameters
5531: Ticket Field
5532: Description
5533: id
5534: ID of the ticket field
5535: default
5536: Set to true if the field is not a custom field
5537: description
5538: Description of the ticket field
5539: label
5540: Display name for the field (as seen by agents)
5541: name
5542: Name of the ticket field
5543: position
5544: Position in which the ticket field is displayed in the form
5545: required_for_closure
5546: Set to true if the field is mandatory for closing the ticket
5547: type
5548: For custom ticket fields, The type of value associated with the field will be given (Examples custom_date, custom_text...)
5549: required_for_agents
5550: Set to true if the field is mandatory for Agents
5551: required_for_customers
5552: Set to true if the field is mandatory in the customer portal
5553: label_for_customers
5554: Display name for the field (as seen in the customer portal)
5555: customers_can_edit
5556: Set to true if the field can be updated by customers
5557: displayed_to_customers
5558: Set to true if the field is displayed in the customer portal
5559: portal_cc
5560: Applicable only for the requester field. Set to true if customer can add additional requesters to a ticket
5561: portal_cc_to
5562: Applicable only if portal_cc is set to true. Value will be all when a customer can add any requester to the CC list and company when a customer can add only company contacts to the CC list
5563: choices
5564: List of values supported by the field
5565: is_fsm
5566: True if the Ticket field is inside FSM section (Applicable only if FSM is enabled)
5567: field_update_in_progress
5568: True if the choice update is in progress (Applicable for the fields which has 100+ choices)
5569: dependent_fields
5570: Applicable only for dependent fields, this contains details of nested fields (see the sample response given below)
5571: section_mappings
5572: Applicable only if the field is part of a section. This contains section ID and position of the ticket field in the section

7910: Ticket Form Fields
7911: Note:
7912: Only users with admin privileges can access the following APIs.
7913: The ticket form fields in Freshdesk have the following properties.
7914: JSON Parameters
7915: Form Fields
7916: Description
7917: id
7918: ID of the form field
7919: name
7920: Name of the form field
7921: label
7922: Display name for the form field (as seen by agents)
7923: label_for_customers Mandatory
7924: Display name for the form field (as seen in the customer portal)
7925: position
7926: Position in which the form field is displayed in the form
7927: type
7928: Details on whether the form field is a custom or a default field. If it is a custom field, details on the field type (dropdown, decimal, date, etc.)
7929: default
7930: True if the form field is a default form field
7931: customers_can_edit Mandatory
7932: Set to true if the form field can be updated by customers
7933: required_for_closure
7934: Set to true if the form field is mandatory for closing the ticket
7935: required_for_agents
7936: Set to true if the form field is mandatory for Agents
7937: required_for_customers Mandatory
7938: Set to true if the form field is displayed in the portal
7939: displayed_to_customers
7940: Set to true if the form field is displayed in the portal
7941: portal_cc
7942: Applicable only for the requester field. Set to true if customer can add additional requesters to a ticket
7943: portal_cc_to
7944: Applicable only if portal_cc is set to true. Value will be all when a customer can add any requester to the CC list and company when a customer can add only company contacts to the CC list
7945: hint_for_customes Mandatory
7946: Can see the tooltip for the form field in the form
7947: placeholder_for_customers Mandatory
7948: Can see the placeholder for the form field in the form

8116: Conversations consist of replies as well as public and private notes added to a ticket. Notes are non-invasive ways of sharing updates about a ticket amongst agents and customers. Private notes are for collaboration between agents and are not visible to the customer. Public notes are visible to, and can be created by, both customers and agents.

8758: Outbound Messages
8759: Freshdesk leverages the WhatsApp Business Platform to enable businesses to send proactive, templated notifications to clients who have explicitly opted-in for updates like order confirmations, shipping alerts, appointment reminders, and payment notifications.
8760: The API rate limits for outbound messages cover both send and retrieve endpoints. These limits are set at 1,000 calls per minute for the Pro plan and 2,000 calls per minute for the Enterprise plan.
8761: To comply with WhatsApp's policies, these outbound messages must use structured templates, which are:
8762: Pre-Approved: Each template must be defined by the business and submitted to Meta for review and approval before it can be used. This ensures the content is non-promotional (for Utility and Authentication categories) or compliant (for Marketing categories).
8763: Customizable: Templates are comprised of three main components:
8764: Body (Mandatory): Plain text with placeholders (variables) for dynamic content.
8765: Header (Optional): Can contain text, an image, video, or document attachment, or a title with variables.
8766: Footer (Optional): Short, static text.
8767: Buttons (Optional/Interactive): Can include Call-to-Action (e.g., website URL, phone call) or Quick Reply buttons for immediate user interaction.
8768: Note: Template message delivery on WhatsApp Business Platform via public API is only available to customers on Pro and Enterprise tiers of our paid plans.

8925: Send Proactive Message
8926: post

8931: This API allows you to send proactive WhatsApp messages to customers using pre-approved templates. The message will be queued and sent asynchronously through the WhatsApp Business API.
8932: Note:
8933: Templates must be created in WhatsApp Business Account (WABA) and approved by Meta before they can be used. Only approved template names can be used in the API request.

8981: Note:
8982: The components array injects dynamic data into pre-approved WhatsApp template placeholders.
8983: Construction Guidelines:
8984: Conditional Inclusion: Only include a component (header, body, or button) if its corresponding template section contains dynamic placeholders ({{1}}, {{2}}, ...). Omit the component object if the section is static.
8985: Parameter Specification: The parameters array within each component must populate the placeholders in their exact order as they appear in the template.
8986: Media Links: For image, document, or video parameters, provide a publicly accessible URL inside the component's link object.
