150: New APIs 151: Documentation Powered by ReDoc 152: Gladly API (1.0) 153: Download OpenAPI specification:Download 154: Introducing the Gladly API 155: At Gladly, we believe that customer service is best when it's a conversation. 156: That means more than just helping customers with one-off questions or issues: it's about making them feel known, valued, and respected for the individuals they are. 157: The Gladly API was built to help facilitate those relationships, providing agents with the rich customer context 158: they need to deliver seamless experiences that make customers feel like they're more than just a number in a sea of others. 159: Overview 160: You can integrate easily with Gladly by calling Gladly's REST API 161: and implementing the Lookup API to provide data from your own services. 162: Some examples of what you do through Gladly APIs include managing customer profile data, interacting with a customer's timeline, 163: providing the latest information about a customer's orders, and more. 164: REST API 165: Clients can access the REST API via HTTPS at your organization's Gladly domain (e.g. https://{organization}.gladly.com). 166: Resources follow REST semantics and utilize industry-standard HTTP verbs, response codes, and authentication schemes. 167: In addition, all responses and payloads are in JSON with consistent error codes and formats. 168: Lookup API 169: The Gladly Lookup API allows your organization to provide data services to power the agent's experience with a complete view of your customers' 170: information, transactions, and activity. You can provide a web service that implements the Lookup API and Gladly will call it when that data is needed. 171: Like the REST API, the Lookup API is specified using REST semantics, and exchanges JSON requests and responses authenticated and signed with secure keys. 172: Gladly will perform lookups when certain activities occur within Gladly, such as when a customer's profile is loaded. 173: A detailed overview of Lookup Adaptor architecture, requests, resposnes and more can be found here. 174: Testing 175: Test the myriad possibilities of the Gladly API in a safe, secure space. We'll enable the Gladly API in a separate sandbox environment, so you can experiment freely without impacting your production environment (or vice versa). 176: Your sandbox environment is accessible at https://{organization}.gladly.qa, where organization is your company name. For specific API endpoints, see documentation below. 177: Getting Started 178: Think of this section as getting the keys to unlocking your access to the Gladly APIs. 179: First, you'll need to set up an account with the necessary API permissions. 180: With these permissions, you can then go on to create the API Token(s) you need to access Gladly's API resources. 181: Permissions 182: Gladly Administrators can set API permissions on an agent-by-agent basis. 183: We'll discuss how this maps to API access in the section on authentication below. 184: To allow a user to create API tokens and access the API: 185: Log in to your Gladly instance. 186: Open the menu on the top left-hand corner of the page. 187: Navigate to Settings > *Users 188: Search and click the user profile you wish to give access to. 189: You'll see a permission called API User. Select it, while making sure to keep the user's Agent role intact. 190: Hit Save to give access. 191: We recommend creating a dedicated user to make API calls, whose account won't be used for agent and organization management. 192: This will help you with any future audits of API activity vs. agent activity. 193: Creating API Tokens 194: You must create an API token to access Gladly API resources (see above Permissions). 195: If your profile already has access to the API User permission, you'll see a menu item titled More settings. Click More settings: 196: Click API Tokens, then the Create Token button on the upper right-hand corner of the page: 197: A token will be generated and named, by default, New Token (though depending on whether you have existing tokens, it may be named New Token 2, or New Token 3, etc.). 198: You can rename the token to something more easily referenceable by clicking the name to edit. 199: This token will be associated with your agent profile, which we refer to as the API User in this document. 200: For security purposes, you'll only see a new token once before you navigate away from the page. 201: Replacing/Rotating API Tokens 202: Should you lose this token, or wish to rotate your application keys, you can do the following: 203: Generate a new token. 204: Store the new token in a secure location. 205: Delete the old token. 206: Update your applications/scripts with the new token. 207: Authentication 208: BasicAuth 209: Gladly API uses token-based Basic Authentication. API tokens are associated with designated Gladly users. 210: To create and use an API token, your user must have the API User permission. An API token can be used to perform any API request without restriction. 211: user name 212: password 213: agent email 214: API token 215: The credentials must be passed via an Authorization HTTP header. All requests must be made over HTTPS. 216: curl -u user@organization.com:$GLADLY_API_TOKEN \ 217: https://organization.gladly.com/api/v1/organization 218: Security Scheme Type HTTP 219: HTTP Authorization Scheme basic 220: Agents 221: An Agent represents the user profile of a person who helps customers in Gladly. 222: The API allows you to lookup Agents who participated in conversations with customers. 223: List Agents 224: Returns a list of agents. 225: Responses 226: 200 227: Agents 228: get /api/v1/agents 229: https://organization.gladly.com/api/v1/agents 230: Response samples 231: 200 232: Content type 233: application/json 234: Copy 235: Expand all Collapse all 236: [ 237: { 238: "id": "WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA", 239: "name": "Amy Agent", 240: "emailAddress": "amy.agent@company.com" 241: } 242: ] 243: Get Agent 244: Get an agent profile by their unique id. 245: path Parameters 246: agentId 247: required 248: string 249: Example: WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA 250: id of the agent 251: Responses 252: 200 253: Agent 254: get /api/v1/agents/{agentId} 255: https://organization.gladly.com/api/v1/agents/{agentId} 256: Response samples 257: 200 258: Content type 259: application/json 260: Copy 261: Expand all Collapse all 262: { 263: "id": "WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA", 264: "name": "Amy Agent", 265: "emailAddress": "amy.agent@company.com" 266: } 267: Get Agent Availability 268: Get an agent's availability. An agent who has never logged in is OFFLINE. 269: path Parameters 270: agentId 271: required 272: string 273: Example: WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA 274: id of the agent 275: Responses 276: 200 277: AgentAvailability 278: 404 279: Agent not found 280: get /api/v1/agents/{agentId}/availability 281: https://organization.gladly.com/api/v1/agents/{agentId}/availability 282: Response samples 283: 200 284: 404 285: Content type 286: application/json 287: Copy 288: Expand all Collapse all 289: { 290: "agentId": "WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA", 291: "status": "AWAY", 292: "reason": 293: { 294: "id": "eRaHXjD4li-moMR8LbULXc", 295: "name": "Lunch" 296: }, 297: "channels": 298: [ 299: "MAIL", 300: "MESSAGING" 301: ], 302: "updatedAt": "2026-06-22T09:00:00.000Z" 303: } 304: Get Agent CallRecorder 305: Get an agent call recording status. 306: path Parameters 307: agentId 308: required 309: string 310: Example: WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA OR agent@customer.com 311: Gladly ID or Gladly email address of the agent 312: Responses 313: 200 314: CallRecorder 315: 404 316: Agent not found 317: get /api/v1/agents/{agentId}/call-recorder 318: https://organization.gladly.com/api/v1/agents/{agentId}/call-recorder 319: Response samples 320: 200 321: 404 322: Content type 323: application/json 324: Copy 325: Expand all Collapse all 326: { 327: "agentId": "WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA", 328: "customerId": "ZcyobierQhucTS5GV1R2Fw", 329: "conversationItemId": "g6UatsvAQC69AcDpOKF-yQ", 330: "recording": true 331: } 332: Update Agent CallRecorder 333: Update an agent's active call recording status. Please note that if one Customer Lookup integration times out / responds with an error that Gladly will consider this an error for all Customer Lookup integration(s). 5424: Sample code 5425: Sample code for building a Customer Lookup integration can be found here. 5426: Architecture, Setup, Authentication, Sample Requests and More 5427: A detailed overview of Lookup Adaptor architecture, requests, resposnes and more can be found here. 5428: Versioning 5429: As we evolve the Gladly API over time, changes will be either added to the current version of the API (i.e. backwards compatible changes), 5430: or result in a new version that you will need to integrate with afresh (i.e. non-backwards compatible changes). 5431: URL Path Versioning 5432: The various versions of the Gladly API will be differentiated via global versioning, with the relevant version number reflected within the path parameter of the URL: 5433: https://organization.gladly.com/api/v{major-version-number}/{resource path} 5434: Backwards Compatible Changes 5435: For the most part, changes to the API will be backwards compatible, such as adding resources, additional fields to response objects, 5436: new value types for enums, or expanding a validation constraint to be more accepting. 5437: Ensure your client can gracefully handle or ignore unfamiliar fields and values so it continues to operate smoothly over the lifespan of an API version. 5438: Non-Backwards Compatible Changes 5439: Versions will be upleveled when a non-backwards compatible change occurs. This ensures that adequate resources are available for all customers. 5504: Concurrency Limit 5505: Concurrency limits are applied on the number of simultaneous requests to the endpoint. For example, a few long-lasting requests to an API endpoint simultaneously might exceed the concurrent rate limit for that endpoint. 5506: Default Rate Limit 5507: Organizations that send many requests in quick succession may see error responses that show up as status code 429. 5508: Individual APIs may have their own API Rate Limit and will be documented as such. 154: Zendesk MCP Server
155: A Model Context Protocol server for Zendesk.
156: This server provides a comprehensive integration with Zendesk. It offers:
157: Tools for retrieving and managing Zendesk tickets and comments
158: Specialized prompts for ticket analysis and response drafting
159: Full access to the Zendesk Help Center articles as knowledge base
160: Setup
161: build: uv venv && uv pip install -e . or uv build in short.
162: configure authentication: see Authentication below.
163: configure in Claude desktop:
164: {
165: "mcpServers": {
166: "zendesk": {
167: "command": "uv",
168: "args": [
169: "--directory",
170: "/path/to/zendesk-mcp-server",
171: "run",
172: "zendesk"
173: ]
174: }
175: }
176: }
177: Authentication
178: This server authenticates with OAuth. Each operator authorizes with their own
179: Zendesk login, so API calls carry their identity and Zendesk applies exactly the
180: permissions it applies in the UI — their role, their group restrictions, their
181: ticket access. Comments they post are authored by them.
182: API token authentication still works but is deprecated. See
183: Migrating from an API token.
184: 1. Register a public OAuth client
185: In Admin Center, go to Apps and integrations > APIs > OAuth clients and
186: create a client:
187: Field
188: Value
189: Client kind
190: Public — this server runs on each operator's machine, so there is no secret it could keep. PKCE is used instead.
191: Redirect URLs
192: http://localhost:4567/callback
193: Allowed scopes
194: tickets:read tickets:write ticket_attachments:read users:read hc:read
195: Setting Allowed scopes is optional but recommended: it caps what any token
196: from this client can ever request, even if the code changes.
197: Note the client's Identifier — that is the ZENDESK_CLIENT_ID below.
198: If Zendesk rejects http://localhost:4567/callback, register https://localhost
199: instead and use zendesk-auth --manual in step 3.
200: 2. Configure the environment
201: Copy .env.example to .env and set:
202: ZENDESK_SUBDOMAIN=acme # for https://acme.zendesk.com
203: ZENDESK_CLIENT_ID=your-client-identifier
204: Keep .env out of version control.
205: Two optional settings, both of which must agree with the OAuth client:
206: Variable
207: Default
208: When to change it
209: ZENDESK_OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI
210: http://localhost:4567/callback
211: Port 4567 is in use, or the client is registered with a different redirect URL. Must match a redirect URL on the client exactly.
212: ZENDESK_TOKEN_FILE
213: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/zendesk-mcp/tokens.json
214: Storing tokens elsewhere, for example a Docker volume.
215: 3. Authorize this machine, once
216: uv run zendesk-auth
217: This opens a browser, asks the operator to approve access, and stores the
218: resulting tokens locally. From then on the server renews access on its own; the
219: operator never repeats this unless the tokens are revoked or left unused past the
220: refresh token's lifetime (90 days as requested by this server).
221: If the browser cannot reach this machine — a remote shell, or an OAuth client
222: registered with https://localhost — use the paste-based flow instead:
223: uv run zendesk-auth --manual
224: Tokens are written to $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/zendesk-mcp/tokens.json
225: (~/.config/zendesk-mcp/tokens.json by default), created 0600 inside a 0700
226: directory. Override the location with ZENDESK_TOKEN_FILE. The file holds live
227: credentials: treat it like a password and never commit it.
228: How token renewal works
229: Zendesk access tokens are short-lived — 30 minutes by default, 48 hours at most —
230: so the server refreshes them for you:
231: before expiry, when the stored token is within 60 seconds of expiring, and
232: on rejection, when Zendesk answers 401 with {"error": "invalid_token"},
233: in which case the request is retried once with a fresh token.
234: Only invalid_token triggers a retry. A 401 or 403 from insufficient scope or
235: from the operator's own Zendesk permissions is passed through unchanged, so
236: permission problems stay visible instead of looking like auth flakiness.
237: Each refresh rotates the refresh token and invalidates the previous one
238: immediately, so the new pair is written to disk before it is used. Writes are
239: atomic and guarded by a lock file, which matters if you run the server from more
240: than one MCP client at the same time.
241: When the refresh token itself is expired or revoked, tools fail with a message
242: telling the operator to re-run zendesk-auth.
243: Choosing scopes
244: The default scopes cover every tool this server exposes:
245: Scope
246: Needed for
247: tickets:read
248: get_ticket, get_tickets, get_ticket_comments
249: tickets:write
250: create_ticket, update_ticket, create_ticket_comment
251: ticket_attachments:read
252: get_ticket_attachment
253: users:read
254: requester and assignee details on tickets
255: hc:read
256: the zendesk://knowledge-base resource
257: Narrow them with ZENDESK_OAUTH_SCOPES if you do not need every tool — for
258: read-only access, tickets:read users:read hc:read.
259: Scopes are a ceiling, not a grant: a token can never do more than the
260: authorizing operator is allowed to do. Note that Zendesk accepts unrecognised
261: scope names when issuing a token but then rejects every request with 403, so
262: zendesk-auth prints the scope Zendesk actually granted for comparison.
263: Migrating from an API token
264: Zendesk is retiring API tokens on this schedule:
265: Date
266: Change
267: 2026-07-28
268: Tokens unused for 30 days are deactivated automatically; new accounts cannot create tokens.
269: 2026-10-27
270: No account can create new API tokens.
271: 2027-04-30
272: All API tokens stop working permanently.
273: Until then ZENDESK_EMAIL + ZENDESK_API_KEY continue to work, and the server
274: logs a deprecation warning the first time it authenticates. Set
275: ZENDESK_CLIENT_ID and OAuth takes precedence, so you can migrate without
276: removing the old variables.
277: Beyond the deadline, there is a reason to move sooner: a Zendesk API token is
278: account-level and unscoped. Whoever holds it gets the full access of the user it
279: is paired with, which for most installations is an admin. That is what per-operator
280: OAuth fixes.
281: Why not the client credentials flow? It is simpler — no browser step, no
282: refresh tokens — but its tokens are attributed to the Zendesk user who created
283: the OAuth client. Every operator would act as that one user, usually an admin,
284: and audit logs and comment authorship would all point at them. Since the goal
285: is for operators to have exactly their own Zendesk permissions, the
286: authorization code flow is the only one that fits.
287: Docker
288: You can containerize the server if you prefer an isolated runtime:
289: Copy .env.example to .env and fill in your Zendesk configuration. Keep this file outside version control.
290: Build the image:
291: docker build -t zendesk-mcp-server .
292: Authorize on the host, not in the container. zendesk-auth needs a
293: browser and a local callback port, so run it once outside Docker:
294: uv run zendesk-auth
295: Run the server, passing the environment file and mounting the token store:
296: docker run --rm \
297: --env-file /path/to/.env \
298: --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
299: -e ZENDESK_TOKEN_FILE=/tokens/tokens.json \
300: -v "$HOME/.config/zendesk-mcp:/tokens" \
301: zendesk-mcp-server
302: The mount must be writable: the server rewrites the file every time it
303: rotates the refresh token, and a read-only mount will strand it on an expired
304: token. --user makes the container run as you, so it can read the 0600
305: token file created on the host.
306: Add -i when wiring the container to MCP clients over STDIN/STDOUT (Claude Code uses this mode). For daemonized runs, add -d --name zendesk-mcp.
307: The image installs dependencies from requirements.lock and drops privileges to a non-root user. With API token authentication no volume is needed, since configuration comes entirely from environment variables.
308: Claude MCP Integration
309: To use the Dockerized server from Claude Code/Desktop, add an entry to Claude Code's settings.json similar to:
310: {
311: "mcpServers": {
312: "zendesk": {
313: "command": "/usr/local/bin/docker",
314: "args": [
315: "run",
316: "--rm",
317: "-i",
318: "--env-file",
319: "/path/to/zendesk-mcp-server/.env",
320: "zendesk-mcp-server"
321: ]
322: }
323: }
324: }
325: Adjust the paths to match your environment. After saving the file, restart Claude for the new MCP server to be detected.
326: Development
327: Run the test suite:
328: uv pip install -e '.[test]'
329: pytest
330: The tests use mocked HTTP and never contact Zendesk. They cover the API-token and
331: OAuth paths, PKCE derivation, token storage and rotation, and each of the four
332: ways this server calls Zendesk.
333: Resources
334: zendesk://knowledge-base, get access to the whole help center articles.
335: Prompts
336: analyze-ticket
337: Analyze a Zendesk ticket and provide a detailed analysis of the ticket.
338: draft-ticket-response
339: Draft a response to a Zendesk ticket.
340: Tools
341: get_tickets
342: Fetch the latest tickets with pagination support
343: Input:
344: page (integer, optional): Page number (defaults to 1)
345: per_page (integer, optional): Number of tickets per page, max 100 (defaults to 25)
346: sort_by (string, optional): Field to sort by - created_at, updated_at, priority, or status (defaults to created_at)
347: sort_order (string, optional): Sort order - asc or desc (defaults to desc)
348: Output: Returns a list of tickets with essential fields including id, subject, status, priority, description, timestamps, and assignee information, along with pagination metadata
349: get_ticket
350: Retrieve a Zendesk ticket by its ID
351: Input:
352: ticket_id (integer): The ID of the ticket to retrieve
353: get_ticket_comments
354: Retrieve all comments for a Zendesk ticket by its ID
355: Input:
356: ticket_id (integer): The ID of the ticket to get comments for
357: create_ticket_comment
358: Create a new comment on an existing Zendesk ticket
359: Input:
360: ticket_id (integer): The ID of the ticket to comment on
361: comment (string): The comment text/content to add
362: public (boolean, optional): Whether the comment should be public (defaults to true)
363: create_ticket
364: Create a new Zendesk ticket
365: Input:
366: subject (string): Ticket subject
367: description (string): Ticket description
368: requester_id (integer, optional)
369: assignee_id (integer, optional)
370: priority (string, optional): one of low, normal, high, urgent
371: type (string, optional): one of problem, incident, question, task
372: tags (array[string], optional)
373: custom_fields (array[object], optional)
374: update_ticket
375: Update fields on an existing Zendesk ticket (e.g., status, priority, assignee)
376: Input:
377: ticket_id (integer): The ID of the ticket to update
378: subject (string, optional)
379: status (string, optional): one of new, open, pending, on-hold, solved, closed
380: priority (string, optional): one of low, normal, high, urgent
381: type (string, optional)
382: assignee_id (integer, optional)
383: requester_id (integer, optional)
384: tags (array[string], optional)
385: custom_fields (array[object], optional)
386: due_at (string, optional): ISO8601 datetime

This guide will walk you through the process. 50: Setting up OAuth 51: Provide the initial information 52: Redirect URLs 53: Permissions 54: People & conversation data 55: Workspace data 56: Get the authorization code 57: Trade your authorization code for an Access Token 58: Use your token 59: Example Ruby Code 60: Trade your authorization code for an access token 61: After you complete these steps, you'll be able to use your access token to execute the actions authorized by an Intercom customer. 62: Public vs. Private app authentication 63: If you are building a private app that only needs to access the data from your paid Intercom workspace, you can use Access Tokens and do not need to set up OAuth. See the authentication guide for more details. 64: Provide the initial information 65: Each development workspace automatically gives you the option to use OAuth. To start, tick the Use OAuth option on your Authentication page in the Developer Hub. 66: You'll now have two sections to fill out: 67: Redirect URLs 68: This is the URL which we POST to when your user has authorized your app to access their information. In other words, it's the URL that Intercom will use to send the authorization code for your user. 69: ❗️ Redirect URLs must use HTTPS 70: The redirect will need to communicate over a TLS/SSL connection, so the URL will need to be over HTTPS. 71: Multiple Redirect URLs 72: You can provide multiple URLs by selecting the Add redirect URL option after specifying your initial one. The first will always be the default. 73: After approval, you can choose which URL to use when you're initiating the OAuth flow via the redirect_uri parameter. This means you can include testing as well as production URLs here. 74: Permissions 75: Permissions let you specify exactly how your application needs to access an Intercom user's account. 76: You should only specify the scopes you definitely need for your use case. It's best practice as these will go up for review when you submit your app for review. 77: 🚧 Scopes automatically being selected 78: If your app utilizes Canvas Kit, certain permissions are required by default due to the data your app will have access to. The following scopes will be automatically selected and cannot be deselected: 79: Read and list users and companies 80: Read conversations 81: Read admins 82: Gather App data 83: The following permissions can be selected via checkboxes on your Authorization page: 84: People & conversation data 85: Standard scopesDescription 86: Read and list users and companiesList and view all segments, users, companies, and tags 87: Read and write usersList all users, execute bulk actions, and add or remove users from companies 88: Write users and companiesList companies; create, update and delete users, companies, and tags 89: Read one user and one companyList and view a single user and company 90: Read tagsList all tags 91: Write tagsCreate, update, use and delete tags 92: Read conversationsView conversations 93: Write conversationsReply to, mark as read and close conversations 94: Read eventsList all events belonging to a user 95: Write eventsAbility to submit events (i.e. user activity) 96: Read countsCount users and companies with specified criteria 97: Write data attributesCreate and update custom data attributes 98: Export message dataExport engagement data for messages 99: Export content dataExport engagement data for content 100: Read content dataCreate and update custom data attributes 101: Read ticketsView tickets 102: Write ticketsCreate tickets 103: Read and write custom object instancesCreate, read, update and delete custom object instances 104: Read status of jobsRead status of jobs enqueued via the API 105: Workspace data 106: Extended scopesDescription 107: Read adminsList and view all admins 108: Read one adminView a single admin 109: Update adminsUpdate away mode for admins 110: Read admin activity logsList and view all admins and their activity 111: Read data when entered into the appGather data via Intercom Apps 112: Read and List news items and newsfeedsList and view all News items and Newsfeeds 113: Read and Write news items and newsfeedsRead, Update and Create news items and newsfeeds 114: Read and List articlesList and view all articles 115: Read and Write ArticlesRead, create, update and delete Help Center articles, collections and sections, internal articles and folders 116: Create and update articlesRead, create, update and publish Help Center articles, collections and sections. Cannot delete them. 117: Create phone call redirectsCreate phone call redirects 118: Read and list news items and newsfeedsList and view all News items and Newsfeeds 119: Read and write news items and newsfeedsRead, update and create news items and newsfeeds 120: Read and write AI contentCreate and update AI content 121: Read data connectorsAccess data connectors, execution results and execution webhooks 122: Read and write data connectorsConfigure data connectors and read execution results and execution webhooks 123: Selecting webhook topics 124: Webhook topics are related to corresponding permission scopes. For example, if you need to setup a webhook to trigger when a user/lead is created then you will need to select the "Read and write users" permission scopes. You will then be able to setup the webhook topics for your app which will fire for each workspace it is installed on. Checkout our docs on setting up webhooks for more detailed information on how to enable webhooks for your app. 125: Get the authorization code 126: You'll first need your client_id and client_secret. These can be found on the Basic Information page for your app in the Developer Hub. 127: To get the Authorization Code, you will need to redirect your user to the following URL: 128: https://app.intercom.com/oauth?client_id=___&state=___ 129: 📘 Match the authorization host to the customer's region 130: Intercom hosts workspaces in three regions, and each region has its own authorization host. For the smoothest experience, redirect each customer to the host matching their workspace's region. If you use the default US host for an EU or AU customer, they'll simply be asked to check their credentials and select the correct region on the sign-in page (a dropdown) before continuing — so matching the region up front just removes that extra step. One exception: if the customer signs in with Google, the wrong regional host fails rather than prompting, so matching the region is required in that case. 131: RegionAuthorization Code endpoint 132: UShttps://app.intercom.com/oauth?client_id=___&state=___ 133: EUhttps://app.eu.intercom.com/oauth?client_id=___&state=___ 134: Australiahttps://app.au.intercom.com/oauth?client_id=___&state=___ 135: client_id: Your app's Client ID (see above) 136: state: A random session specific string which we will return in the callback to allow you to identify the session and mitigate CSRF attacks 137: Your user will be presented with the permissions that your app is requesting. Once the user approves this request, they are redirected back via the Redirect URLs which you provided earlier. 138: The request to your Redirect URL will have 2 URL parameters: code and state. For example: 139: https://yourapp.com/callback?code=___&state=___ 140: code: This is the Authorization Code you will use to retrieve an Access Token 141: state: This should be the same as the state string you passed to the Authorization Code endpoint above 142: Trade your authorization code for an Access Token 143: We can now exchange the code for the Access Token with a POST request to: 144: https://api.intercom.io/auth/eagle/token 145: with the following parameters in the body: 146: code: The Authorization Code received above 147: client_id: Your app's Client ID from the Developer Hub (see above) 148: client_secret: Your app's Client secret from the Developer Hub (see above) 149: A successful request will receive a response with the following parameters in the body of the response: 150: token_type: Always 'Bearer' 151: token: The Access Token 152: access_token: A duplicate of the Access Token above 153: { 154: "token_type": "Bearer", 155: "token": "dG9rOjBiM...", 156: "access_token": "dG9rOjBiM..." 157: } 158: Confirm code value 159: The code value in the redirect URL may contain a = at the end which needs to be included. 160: Please double check the code value provided in the token exchange POST request if you get a 401 response with error message Unauthorized Code. 161: Use your token 162: Now that we have the authorized token, we can use this to execute some action on behalf of our user. 163: For example, to retrieve the admin and app information associated with the Access Token: 164: curl --request GET \ 165: --url 'https://api.intercom.io/me' \ 166: --header 'accept: application/json' \ 167: --header 'authorization: Bearer ' 168: // npm install api --save 169: const sdk = require('api')('@intercom-api-reference/v2.8#132bo2vleh7syud'); 170: sdk.auth(''); 171: sdk.identifyAdmin({'intercom-version': '2.8'}) 172: .then(({ data }) => console.log(data)) 173: .catch(err => console.error(err)); 174: import requests 175: url = "https://api.intercom.io/me" 176: headers = { 177: "accept": "application/json", 178: "authorization": "Bearer " 179: } 180: response = requests.get(url, headers=headers) 181: print(response.text) 182: require 'uri' 183: require 'net/http' 184: require 'openssl' 185: url = URI("https://api.intercom.io/me") 186: http = Net::HTTP.new(url.host, url.port) 187: http.use_ssl = true 188: request = Net::HTTP::Get.new(url) 189: request["accept"] = 'application/json' 190: request["Intercom-Version"] = '2.8' 191: request["authorization"] = 'Bearer ' 192: response = http.request(request) 193: puts response.read_body 194: // composer require guzzlehttp/guzzle 195: request('GET', 'https://api.intercom.io/me', [ 199: 'headers' => [ 200: 'Intercom-Version' => '2.8', 201: 'accept' => 'application/json', 202: 'authorization' => 'Bearer ', 203: ], 204: ]); 205: echo $response->getBody(); 206: An example, successful response would be: 207: { 208: "type": "admin", 209: "id": "2633609", 210: "email": "hermione.granger@awesomecorp.io", 211: "name": "Hermione Granger", 212: "email_verified": true, 213: "app": { 214: "type": "app", 215: "id_code": "drzzt019", 216: "name": "Hogwarts workspace", 217: "created_at": 1661876617, 218: "secure": true, 219: "identity_verification": true, 220: "timezone": "Europe/Edinburgh", 221: "region": "US" 222: }, 223: "avatar": { 224: "type": "avatar", 225: "image_url": "https://static.intercomassets.com/avatars/56395503/square_128/5449623-166556.jpg" 226: }, 227: "has_inbox_seat": true 228: } 229: Find out more about how to use the token through this link. 230: Use OmniAuth instead 231: We have added support for Intercom to number of OAuth libraries. It makes the setup process much easier, so it is a good way to setup OAuth for your app: 232: For Rails apps, use Intercom strategy for OmniAuth. 233: For Node.js apps, use Intercom Strategy for Passport. 234: For PHP apps, use Intercom Provider for PHP League's OAuth 2.0. 235: For GO apps, use GOTH library. To prevent user impersonation, check that user.RawData["email_verified"] is set to true in the response. 236: Example Ruby Code 237: Intercom provides some Ruby sample code that you can use to allow the user to authorize MyApp's request via a "Connect with Intercom" button. 238: Firstly, you will need to generate a Self Signed Certificate and a Private Key if you don't have SSL setup on your site. 6: # Authentication
7: The Core API uses Bearer tokens to authenticate its user.
8: You MUST send the token for each request in the Authorization header. The token MUST be preceded by `Bearer`. See the `Authorization` header in the example request below.
9: ```curl
10: curl --request GET \
11: --url https://api2.frontapp.com/conversations/cnv_123/drafts
12: --header 'Authorization: Bearer [REQUEST_TOKEN]'
13: ```
14: # OAuth v Front API Tokens
15: **There are two ways to get a Bearer token — through API tokens in your settings or through an OAuth implementation**.
16: In general, Front recommends implementing OAuth when feasible, which has the additional benefit of building within our [application framework](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/create-and-manage-apps). The app framework makes it easy for customers to install your integration and makes it easy for you to update the integration with new Front features as they are added to the framework.
17: However, if you’re just building an integration for your own Front instance or a single Front customer, or just want to test our API endpoints as you brainstorm what to build, you can [generate an API token](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/create-and-revoke-api-tokens) to get up and running more quickly.
18: For Partners looking to launch a public integration to all Front customers, if your integration can support OAuth you’ll want to check out our [OAuth guide](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/oauth). We require that public integrations use OAuth unless there is a reason they cannot. OAuth integrations are part of our application framework and can be easily installed by customers using the Front App Store, without requiring that customers manually configure an API token for your integration.
19: > 📘 OAuth is required for public integrations available to all Front customers unless you obtain an exception from us. OAuth makes it much easier for customers to install your integration through our App Store.
20: ## Token scopes
21: ### Features
22: The following features specify what functionality your token can be used for:
23: * **Access resources** allows you to manage Core API resources such as conversations, contacts, inboxes, etc.
24: * **Auto-provisioning** allows you to manage provisioning resources using our SCIM implementation, which you have to contact our team to learn more about (not generally available to the public).
25: * **Application triggers** allows you to [process events and payloads](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/application-triggers) from external services (not currently available for OAuth tokens).
26: * **MCP server** allows you to connect Front data exposed via MCP server to clients like Claude, ChatGPT, and others (not available for API tokens).
27: ### Namespaces
28: The following namespaces specify the scope of tokens:
29: * **Global resources** are resources available across the company. These are resources created at the company level such as company-level rules, company-level tags, or resources that only exist at the company level, such as teams or accounts. Global resources exclude resources that belong to to specific workspaces, which are separately configured as shared resources.
30: * **Shared resources** are resources that belong to specific workspaces, such as shared inboxes or workspace tags. You can select **All shared workspaces** to manage resources across all your workspaces.
31: * **Private resources** are resources that belong to individual teammates, such as personal inboxes or signatures. The teammate will have to enable API access in their settings for the token to manage their resources.
32: ### Permissions
33: If you selected to access resources, you can granularly specify what access the token has to each resources (read, write, delete, and send).
34: <Callout icon="👍" theme="okay">
35: Tips for using permissions
36: * Refer to the API endpoint topics in the [Core API reference documentation](https://dev.frontapp.com/reference/introduction) to learn which permissions are required for each endpoint.
37: * Front recommends limiting the permissions for each token to prevent misuse or security issues.
38: * The following permissions exist:
39: * **Read** for retrieving resource information.
40: * **Write** for creating and updating resources.
41: * **Delete** for removing API resources.
42: * **Send** for creating and sending messages in Front, such as you would do with endpoints like [Create message](https://dev.frontapp.com/reference/create-message), which start new conversations or reply to active conversations. This is different from endpoints that [import historical messages](https://dev.frontapp.com/reference/import-inbox-message), which only require the Write permission.
43: </Callout>

6: # API tokens
7: API tokens allow you to test the Front [Core API](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/core-api-overview) or implement integrations or scripts that make programmatic updates to Front via the API. Once you have an API token, you can use it to [authenticate](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/authentication) Core API requests.
8: API tokens apply at a company level rather than being tied to a specific user, so anyone at your company with admin privileges will see the token you create.
9: <Callout icon="📘" theme="info">
10: ### You must be an admin to create or manage API tokens.
11: </Callout>
12: ## OAuth access versus API tokens
13: Front requires that partners implement OAuth instead of API tokens when building Core API integrations that make updates on behalf of a Front customer or their account, unless you obtain an exception from us. OAuth makes it easier for users to enable and use your integration by allowing users to simply authorize the app with an existing account. To learn more about this topic, refer to [Authentication](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/authentication).
14: To learn how to configure OAuth, refer to the [Create, manage, and publish apps](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/create-and-manage-apps) topic.
15: ## Create an API token
16: 1. Go to **Settings > Developers**.
17: 2. Go to the **API Tokens** tab.
18: 3. Click **Create API token**.
19: 4. Specify an **API token name**.
20: <Callout icon="👍" theme="okay">
21: ### Use an extremely descriptive name
22: Once you create a token and implement it, you may forget about it. Using a very detailed and specific token name will help you identify where the token is being used after it is created.
23: </Callout>
24: 5. Choose the features, namespaces, and permissions the token should have.
25: ### Features
26: The following features specify what functionality your token can be used for:
27: * **Access resources** allows you to manage Core API resources such as conversations, contacts, inboxes, etc.
28: * **Auto-provisioning** allows you to manage provisioning resources using our SCIM implementation, which you have to contact our team to learn more about (not generally available to the public).
29: * **Application triggers** allows you to [process events and payloads](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/application-triggers) from external services (not currently available for OAuth tokens).
30: * **MCP server** allows you to connect Front data exposed via MCP server to clients like Claude, ChatGPT, and others (not available for API tokens).
31: ### Namespaces
32: The following namespaces specify the scope of tokens:
33: * **Global resources** are resources available across the company. These are resources created at the company level such as company-level rules, company-level tags, or resources that only exist at the company level, such as teams or accounts. Global resources exclude resources that belong to to specific workspaces, which are separately configured as shared resources.
34: * **Shared resources** are resources that belong to specific workspaces, such as shared inboxes or workspace tags. You can select **All shared workspaces** to manage resources across all your workspaces.
35: * **Private resources** are resources that belong to individual teammates, such as personal inboxes or signatures. The teammate will have to enable API access in their settings for the token to manage their resources.
36: ### Permissions
37: If you selected to access resources, you can granularly specify what access the token has to each resources (read, write, delete, and send).
38: <Callout icon="👍" theme="okay">
39: Tips for using permissions
40: * Refer to the API endpoint topics in the [Core API reference documentation](https://dev.frontapp.com/reference/introduction) to learn which permissions are required for each endpoint.
41: * Front recommends limiting the permissions for each token to prevent misuse or security issues.
42: * The following permissions exist:
43: * **Read** for retrieving resource information.
44: * **Write** for creating and updating resources.
45: * **Delete** for removing API resources.
46: * **Send** for creating and sending messages in Front, such as you would do with endpoints like [Create message](https://dev.frontapp.com/reference/create-message), which start new conversations or reply to active conversations. This is different from endpoints that [import historical messages](https://dev.frontapp.com/reference/import-inbox-message), which only require the Write permission.
47: </Callout>
48: 6. Click **Create**.
49: <Callout icon="far fa-circle-info" theme="info">
50: ### Make sure to copy your API test token.
51: For security reasons, you cannot view it after creation. If you lose a token, you can create a new one and replace the value in your integrations.
52: </Callout>
53: ## View API token details
54: After creating an API token, you can view its details to obtain useful information, such as who created the token and when, plus what scopes, features, and permissions are accessible to the token. Note that you cannot view the API token value itself. You must copy this value during creation and retain it for your records.
55: 1. Go to **Settings > Developers**.
56: 2. Go to the **API Tokens** tab.
57: 3. Click an API token to open its details page.
58: 4. Note useful fields about the token, such as who created it and what scopes, features, and permissions it has, to learn more about how the token is used.
59: ## Delete an API token.
60: You can delete any API token by completing the following steps. Note that deleting a token will immediately prevent any applications using the token from making requests to the Core API, so ensure the token is no longer needed because this operation cannot be undone.
61: 1. Go to **Settings > Developers**.
62: 2. Go to the **API Tokens** tab.
63: 3. Click an API token to open its details page.
64: 4. Click **Delete**.
65: ## View API token usage
66: After you create an API token, you can access the API Analytics tab to view its usage. This dashboard allows you to see your token usage over time. For details, refer to our Help Center article:
67: * [API usage analytics dashboard](https://help.front.com/en/articles/2438#api_usage_analytics_dashboard)

1: --- 2: updatedAt: 2026-11-12T15:54:00.000Z 3: agentTools: 4: projectIndex: https://dev.frontapp.com/llms.txt 5: --- 6: # MCP Server 7: ## Connect AI assistants to Front via the MCP server 8: Front's MCP server (`mcp.frontapp.com/mcp`) lets AI agents act on Front conversation data using a single OAuth-authenticated endpoint. Agents authenticate as a specific Front user, with permissions matching that user's role (user-scoped authorization). The MCP server is separate from the [Admin MCP server](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/admin-mcp-server), which manages Front configurations such as rules, setting up teammates, managing AI features, etc. 9: This article covers how to connect the MCP server to any MCP-compatible client to Front using an OAuth app you create yourself in the Front developer settings. For the user-facing overview, official directory listings (Claude, and others coming), and use case inspirations for Front teammates, see the general [Help Center article on the MCP server](https://help.front.com/en/articles/4883136). 10: > **Looking for examples before you build?** 11: > 12: > The [MCP space in the Front Community](https://community.front.com/mcp-server-88) has workflow walkthroughs, sample prompts, and more. You can also start up discussions about the MCP server with fellow users and our team. 13: ## Overview 14: | | | 15: | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 16: | **Endpoint** | `https://mcp.frontapp.com/mcp` | 17: | **Transport** | Streamable HTTP | 18: | **MCP spec version** | 2025-11-25 | 19: | **Auth** | OAuth 2.1 + PKCE compatibility

**Note:** Front does not support Dynamic Client Registration. Your AI assistant must support a ***confidential connection that sends an OAuth client ID and secret***. Some popular AI assistants are currently [not compatible](#incompatibility-list). | 20: | **Identity model** | Per-user tokens. Every tool call attributes to a specific Front teammate | 21: | **Who can connect** | Any teammate | 22: | **Scopes** | `read`, `write`, `send` | 23: The identity model is the part most worth internalizing: the agent's effective permissions are exactly the authorizing teammate's permissions. If the teammate can't see an inbox, the agent can't either. 24: ### Incompatibility list 25: Some AI assistants do not support confidential connections. These clients cannot connect to the Front MCP server: 26: * Any client that requires Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) 27: ## Use cases 28: A few patterns this surface unlocks: 29: * **Custom agent harnesses.** Wire Front into Claude Code, Cursor, or an in-house orchestrator alongside your other tools (GitHub, Notion, Jira, Slack, Linear, your CRM) for cross-system workflows: customer reports a bug, agent reproduces it, identifies the suspect PR, and posts an internal comment with the diagnosis. 30: * **Multi-tenant partner integrations.** Publish an OAuth app that any Front admin can install. Each end user authorizes individually. 31: * **Triage and routing agents.** Scheduled or event-driven agents that search the inbox, classify by topic, assign to the right teammate, and draft a first-pass reply for human review. 32: * **Conversation insights and enrichment.** Pull conversation data into your own pipelines for analysis, KB extraction, or feedback ingestion. The conversation timeline includes messages, comments, tags, assignment history, and more in a single stream. 33: ## Set up the MCP server connection 34: 35: ### Connect Claude and ChatGPT/Codex from the official directory 36: If you're using Claude or ChatGPT, we recommend you connect the Front MCP server from the official directories:
37: * [Claude official directory](https://claude.ai/directory/connectors/front) 38: * [ChatGPT official directory](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugin_asdk_app_6aaab462482c819183764e2f6a72e8e9) 39:
If you install Claude or ChatGPT from the official directories, you do not need to complete either step in this section (**Set up the Front developer app with the Front MCP feature** or **Connect your AI assistant)**. If you are not using Claude or ChatGPT, follow the steps in this section to set up the MCP server as a custom connector. 40: To connect via an official directory: 41: - A Front admin (or any user authorized to install integrations from the Front App Store) must connect via the directory links above. 42: - Then, any user in your company can use the directory links to connect their own accounts. 43: 44: Connecting an AI assistant to Front's MCP server has two general steps: create a Front developer app with the Front MCP feature, and then connect your AI client using the app's credentials. 45: 46: After you complete these two steps, your teammates will be able to find the Front MCP server in your AI assistant and connect to it without having to create a developer app or configure the connection details on the AI client side. 47: 48: ### 1. Set up the Front developer app with the Front MCP feature 49: 50: ### These instructions are completed in your Front settings (Settings > Company > Developer) 51: 52: 53: ### If you want to authorize the MCP server on behalf of an AI agent, skip setting up a Front developer app and instead use the [OAuth credentials associated with the AI agent](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/ai-agents#ai-engine). 54: 55: 1. [Create a developer app](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/create-and-manage-apps) and give it an appropriate name (e.g. "Claude MCP Connector"). 56: 2. Click **Add feature** in the **Features** tab and select **Front MCP**. 57: 3. Note the **Client ID** and **Client secret**. 58: 4. Add a **redirect URL** that corresponds to the AI assistant you're sending data to. For example, as of this writing, the Claude documentation instructs you to use `https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback` for most versions of Claude. If you're using Claude Code or similar CLI, you should enter `http://localhost/callback`. This URL will allow you to connect to a randomly generated local port. 59: 5. Under **Resource permissions**, select the resources available to the MCP server. 60: 61: Request the narrowest set that covers your use case. A read-only research agent only needs `read`. A drafting copilot needs `read` + `write` but not `send`. Only request `send` if your agent will actually send messages. 62: 63: 64: Remember that despite the permissions selected in the OAuth client, agents connecting to the MCP server will be further limited by the subset of data and permissions that the user who connects the agent has access to. 65: 66: 67: If you change the resource permissions after the initial setup, you must disconnect and re-authorize your connection with your AI assistant ("Connect your AI Assistant" steps) before the new permissions take effect. 68: 69: 6. Save the app. 70:
71: ### 2. Connect your AI assistant 72: 73: ### These instructions are completed in your AI assistant, not Front 74: 75: Once the app is configured, connect from your MCP client so that you and your team can view the Front MCP server. Once it is set up for your company, individual teammates can find the MCP server in the list of connectors and authorize it for their individual accounts, but they will not need to configure the technical details involving the server URL and credentials, as explained in this section. 76: The exact configuration syntax for initial configuration varies by AI client, but every client will need: 77: * The MCP server URL: `https://mcp.frontapp.com/mcp` 78: * Your app's `client_id` and `client_secret` 79: * The OAuth scopes the app should request. Either leave this blank or supply `feature:mcp` if you need to input a value 80: * If your AI assistant requests information about our OAuth URLs, use the following values:
81: | URL | Value | 82: | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | 83: | Authorization | `https://app.frontapp.com/oauth/authorize` | 84: | Token & refresh URL | `https://app.frontapp.com/oauth/token` | 85: 86: **Use the UI or command line to connect the MCP server** 87: We recommend using your AI assistant's UI menus to connect the Front MCP server, or terminal commands for CLI assistants. Configuring JSON files is not recommended for most users because varying local paths and environment settings can cause issues. We've provided two recommended examples for Claude below, plus a general JSON shape if you have to modify your AI assistant's configuration file directly. 88: If you have issues connecting the MCP server, please reach out to your AI assistant's support team and share this documentation with them so they can recommend the correct steps. 89: 90: #### Example for Claude (Web and Desktop) 91: 1. Open **Settings** and navigate to the **Connectors** tab (or the **Customize** page). 92: 2. Click **+** and then **Add custom connector**. 93: 3. Enter the server URL: 94: 4. Click **Advanced** settings and enter your OAuth Client ID and Client Secret. 95: 5. Click **Add** and complete the OAuth authentication flow. 96: 97: You may have to close out Claude and re-open it before it sees the new MCP server and has you authorize permissions. 98: 99: #### Example for Claude Code 100: 1. In Front, make sure your developer app contains the `http://localhost/callback` redirect URL. 101: 2. In your terminal, run the following command and enter your client secret when prompted: 102: 103: Including `MCP_CLIENT_SECRET` is optional. If you don't include it, Claude should prompt you for it after. If it fails to do so, then include it inline. 104: 105: 106: You can name the MCP server something other than `front`. If you connect to more than one Front company, give each connection a unique name, such as `front-`. 107: 108: ```Text Terminal 109: MCP_CLIENT_SECRET= claude mcp add --transport http --client-id --client-secret front https://mcp.frontapp.com/mcp 110: ``` 111: 3. Exit Claude and re-open it in your terminal so that it pulls the latest list of servers. 112: 4. Run **/mcp** to see a list of MCP servers. 113: 5. Select the server you added and choose to **Authenticate** it. 114: 6. Authorize in your browser. 115: #### Example for generic MCP server config (confirm with your client's docs on exactly how you structure and pass these properties) - Not recommended for most users 116: ```json 117: { 118: "mcpServers": { 119: "front": { 120: "url": "https://mcp.frontapp.com/mcp", 121: "transport": "streamable-http", 122: "oauth": { 123: "client_id": "", 124: "client_secret": "", 125: "scopes": ["read", "write", "send"] 126: } 127: } 128: } 129: } 130: ``` 131: ### Tips for authorization 132: 133: **Match your client's requested scopes to your OAuth app.** By default, many AI assistants (including Claude) will request every scope the MCP server supports. If those scopes exceed what you enabled on the Front developer app, the authorization flow may return an error. 134: If you encounter this error, configure your client to only request the scopes your app is set up for. In Claude, for example, this is set in the client's JSON config. See Claude's [docs on restricting OAuth scopes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#restrict-oauth-scopes) for the exact syntax. Other clients have similar settings; check their documentation if you hit an authorization error. 135: 136: When the client first connects, each user will be redirected to Front to log in and consent to the requested scopes. The resulting token is bound to that specific Front user and they can only act on data their Front role allows. 137: 138: **A note on enterprise deployment:** If your AI assistant is centrally managed (e.g. Claude Enterprise, ChatGPT Enterprise), your IT team may need to allow the connection or distribute the app credentials. Each end user still completes the OAuth consent flow individually. This is how Front guarantees that every tool call has a real, attributable user behind it. 139: 140: ### Getting access to new tools 141: When Front adds a tool that needs a permission your connection doesn't have yet, the tool appears in your AI assistant, but calling it returns a `missing required scopes` error. That's because a connection keeps the permissions that were approved when it was first authorized; it doesn't pick up new ones on its own. 142: What you need to do depends on how you connected. 143: 144: **Connected from the Claude or ChatGPT directory** 145: Front keeps the directory apps up to date, so there's nothing to change in Front. Each user disconnects Front in their AI assistant, connects it again, and approves the new permission on the consent screen. 146: 147: 148: **Connected with your own developer app** 149: 1. A Front admin opens your developer app (**Settings > Company > Developer**), opens its **Front MCP** feature, and enables the new permission under **Resource permissions**. The error message names the permission the tool needs. 150: 2. Each user disconnects Front in their AI assistant and connects it again. 151: Until both steps are done, the new tool keeps returning the error. Other tools keep working. 152: 153: ## Rate limits 154: The Front MCP server meters usage in tool calls per minute. Every tool costs the same, regardless of which one it is or how much data it returns. MCP server limits are independent of Core API limits. Tool calls never draw down your API rate limit, and API requests never draw down your MCP limit. 155: ### Limits by plan 156: 157: ### The limits are minimums rather than absolute ceilings 158: Capacity refills continuously instead of resetting on a fixed schedule, so unused capacity accumulates. If your agent has been idle or running below its limit, it can briefly exceed the numbers in the table before settling back. 159: 160: | Plan | Tools call per minute | 161: | ------------ | --------------------- | 162: | Starter | 100 | 163: | Professional | 200 | 164: | Enterprise | 300 | 165: **Limits are keyed on the teammate connecting to the MCP server. Connecting additional MCP clients under the same teammate authorization neither increases nor divides the limit.** 166: Capacity refills continuously rather than resetting on a fixed schedule, so short bursts above the stated rate are expected as long as your sustained usage stays below it. 167: ### Limits by developer apps 168: Unpublished apps in your company share a single pool, so adding more apps divides the available capacity rather than multiplying it. An app published in our App Store gets its own pool per install. 169: ### How to handle a limit 170: When you hit an MCP server rate limit, the server returns the rejection as a tool result rather than an HTTP error. The message tells your AI assistant how long to wait and, where one exists, points to a cheaper alternative tool. 171: The message also tells your assistant which limit it hit. 172: * If it ran out of budget, your assistant needs to wait for capacity to refill. 173: * If it hit a safety cap, your assistant needs to slow its request rate. 174: Every response carries your limit, remaining capacity, reset timing, and what the request cost. Wait the stated time before retrying. Earlier retries will simply be rejected again. 175: 176: If you need a rate limit increase, you can change your plan or purchase an add-on. For more details on plans and add-ons, visit our [Pricing](https://front.com/pricing) page. 177: 178: ### AI agents 179: AI agents have their own separate limits. See [AI agents \[Beta\]](doc:ai-agents#rate-limits) for details. 180: ## Tool reference 181: 182: The MCP server currently exposes the following tools. To get the most updated list, ask your AI agent to refresh the tool list, or reconnect. 183: All write tools that mutate state in user-visible ways carry `destructiveHint: true`, which prompts MCP clients to request per-call user confirmation. 184: 185: *** 186: ## Conversations 187: | Tool | Type | Description | Flags | 188: | ---------------------------- | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 189: | `search_conversations` | Read | Full-text and filter search across conversations | `query` — full-text search string (optional if at least one filter is provided)
`scope` — `my_conversations` (default), `my_workspace`, or `all_inboxes`; **must set to **`all_inboxes`** for unassigned conversations to appear**
`filters.inboxId` — restrict to inbox `inb_xxx`
`filters.teammateId` — restrict to assigned teammate `tea_xxx`
`filters.teamId` — restrict to team `tim_xxx`
`filters.tags` — array of tag IDs `tag_xxx` (matches all)
`filters.status` — one of `open`, `archived`, `trashed`, `spam`
`filters.after` / `filters.before` — date range `YYYY-MM-DD`
`cursor` — pagination cursor from previous call | 190: | `read_conversation` | Read | Full timeline of a conversation, its contents, and its header information: subject, message content, internal comments, tag/assignment changes, status transitions, rule actions, and other metadata | `conversationId` *(required)* — public conversation ID `cnv_xxx`
`limit` — max timeline entries to return (default 50, max 200)
`cursor` — pagination cursor for timeline entries | 191: | `create_draft` | Write | Creates a draft reply on an existing conversation, or a new outbound conversation. Does not send. | `body` *(required)* — draft body text
`conversationId` — public conversation ID `cnv_xxx` for a reply draft; omit to create a new outbound draft (requires `channelId`)
`channelId` — channel ID `cha_xxx`; required for new outbound drafts, optional override for reply drafts
`bodyFormat` — `html` (default), `markdown`, or `plain`
`inReplyToMessageId` — pin to specific message; defaults to latest
`replyAll` — reply to all original recipients (default `true`)
`shared` — share with teammates (default `false`)
`to` — recipients for new outbound drafts (channel handles)
`subject` — subject line for new outbound email drafts
`cc` / `bcc` — CC/BCC recipients for new outbound email drafts | 192: | `update_draft` | Write | Updates the body, subject, or recipients of an existing draft. Uses version token for conflict detection. | `draftId` *(required)* — public draft message ID `msg_xxx` from `list_drafts` or `read_message`
`version` *(required)* — opaque version token from `read_message.draft_version`; fails if draft changed since read
`body` — new draft body; omit to leave unchanged
`bodyFormat` — `html` (default), `markdown`, or `plain`
`subject` — new subject for email drafts; omit to leave unchanged
`to` / `cc` / `bcc` — replace recipient lists; pass `[]` to clear
`channelId` — override the sending channel `cha_xxx`
`takeOver` — if `true`, claim authorship from another teammate before editing | 193: | `delete_draft` | Write | Discards an unsent draft owned by the authenticated teammate. Owner-only. | `draftId` *(required)* — public draft message ID `msg_xxx` from `list_drafts` or `read_message`
`version` *(required)* — opaque version token from `read_message.draft_version`; fails if draft changed since read | 194: | `send_message` | Send
(destructive) | Sends a draft message created via `create_draft`. The draft must be in compose state, owned by the authenticated teammate, and have at least one recipient. | `draftId` *(required)* — draft ID `msg_xxx` as returned by `create_draft` | 195: | `update_conversation_status` | Write (destructive) | Archives or reopens a conversation. Can also set a ticket status. If the requester is the assignee, the change is global; otherwise only their view is affected. | `conversationId` *(required)* — public conversation ID `cnv_xxx`
`status` — `open` or `archived` (provide either this or `statusId`, not both)
`statusId` — ticket-status tag `sts_xxx` from `list_statuses`; sets ticket status and updates open/archived state to match | 196: | `assign_conversation` | Write | Assigns a conversation to a teammate, or unassigns it | `conversationId` *(required)* — public conversation ID `cnv_xxx`
`assigneeId` *(required)* — teammate ID `tea_xxx` to assign, or `null` to unassign | 197: | `move_conversation` | Write | Moves a conversation to another inbox. Replaces the conversation's current inbox association — this is not additive. | `conversationId` *(required)* — public conversation ID `cnv_xxx` to move
`inboxId` *(required)* — destination inbox ID `inb_xxx`, from `list_inboxes` | 198: *** 199: ## Messages 200: | Tool | Type | Description | Flags | 201: | ---------------- | ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | 202: | `read_message` | Read | Fetches a single message by ID with full content. Returns body (quoted replies stripped), recipients, attachments, author, draft status, and delivery error if applicable. Use this to get the full message body when `read_conversation` truncates content. | `messageId` *(required)* — message ID `msg_xxx` | 203: | `get_attachment` | Read | Gets a single attachment on a message or comment. Returns metadata (filename, content type, size) plus a short-lived download URL. Attachment IDs come from `read_message`. | `attachmentId` *(required)* — public attachment link ID `fil_xxx`, as returned by `read_message` | 204: *** 205: ## Message templates 206: | Tool | Type | Description | Flags | 207: | -------------------------- | ---- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 208: | `search_message_templates` | Read | Searches the message templates (saved replies) the authenticated user can access: their personal templates plus those of every workspace they belong to. Results show each template's name and body opening, not the full body. Pass `message_template_ids` to read templates in full, including the HTML body. | `query` — keywords; a template matches when its name, subject, or body opening contains every word. Only applied when the user has more than 50 templates; otherwise every template is returned, sorted by name
`message_template_ids` — array of message template IDs `rsp_xxx` to read in full, including the HTML subject and body; ignores `query`
`limit` — max results (default 50, max 50)
`offset` — pagination offset (default 0) | 209: *** 210: ## Comments 211: | Tool | Type | Description | Flags | 212: | ------------- | ----- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 213: | `add_comment` | Write | Posts an internal comment on a conversation. Not visible to customers. Supports `@mentions` auto-resolved to teammate names. | `conversationId` *(required)* — public conversation ID `cnv_xxx`
`body` *(required)* — comment body text; `@mentions` resolved automatically | 214: *** 215: ## Tasks 216: Task IDs are conversation IDs. `read_conversation` reads task content, `search_conversations` finds tasks (using `filters.type: "task"`), and only `update_task` — not `update_conversation_status` — manages task state. 217: | Tool | Type | Description | Flags | 218: | ------------- | ----- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | 219: | `create_task` | Write | Creates a task. Returns the created task, whose ID is a conversation ID — the conversation tools read it, and the task tools manage it. | `subject` *(required)* — task title
`assigneeId` — teammate the task is assigned to (`tea_xxx`); omit to create unassigned
`comment` — internal comment to post on the task as the first entry
`description` — task details; supports `@mentions` by alias or email
`dueAt` — ISO-8601 timestamp the task is due; must be in the future
`inboxId` — inbox to create the task in (`inb_xxx`)
`sourceConversationId` — conversation the task is created from (`cnv_xxx`); links the task to that conversation
`tagIds` — array of tag IDs (`tag_xxx`) to apply
`teammateIds` — teammates whose task lists the task also appears in (`tea_xxx`)
`customFields` — object of custom field values keyed by field name | 220: | `update_task` | Write | Updates a task. Every task state change goes through this tool rather than `update_conversation_status`. A task ID is a conversation ID. | `taskId` *(required)* — task ID (`cnv_xxx`), as returned by `create_task` or `search_conversations`
`subject` — new task title
`description` — new task details, or `null` to clear; supports `@mentions`
`dueAt` — ISO-8601 timestamp, or `null` to clear
`status` — `resolved` archives the task; `open` reopens it and untrashes a trashed one
`statusId` — ticket status to set (`sts_xxx`); requires ticketing enabled
`snoozeUntil` — ISO-8601 timestamp to archive now and reopen then
`accountIds` — accounts to associate (`acc_xxx`); empty array clears them
`customFields` — object of custom field values to set | 221: *** 222: ## Tags 223: | Tool | Type | Description | Flags | 224: | ------------------ | ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 225: | `list_tags` | Read | Lists all tags in the workspace, including hierarchy | `name_query` — filter by tag name keywords
`inbox_ids` — filter to tags that apply to specific inboxes `inb_xxx`
`all_inboxes` — filter to tags that apply to all inboxes (`true`/`false`)
`is_visible_in_conversation_lists` — filter by list visibility
`parent_tag_id` — filter by parent tag `tag_xxx` for hierarchical tags
`limit` — max results (default 50, max 100)
`offset` — pagination offset | 226: | `tag_conversation` | Write | Adds or removes tags on a conversation. Idempotent — safe to call multiple times. | `conversationId` *(required)* — public conversation ID `cnv_xxx`
`addTags` — array of tag IDs `tag_xxx` to add
`removeTags` — array of tag IDs `tag_xxx` to remove | 227: *** 228: ## Contacts & Accounts 229: | Tool | Type | Description | Flags | 230: | ----------------- | ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 231: | `search_contacts` | Read | Searches contacts by name, email, or handle | `query` *(required)* — search string (name, email, or handle)
`cursor` — pagination cursor from previous call | 232: | `read_contact` | Read | Returns a full contact record including handles and linked accounts | `contactId` *(required)* — public contact card ID `crd_xxx` | 233: | `search_accounts` | Read | Searches accounts (companies) by name | `name_query` — filter by account name keywords
`limit` — max results (default 10, max 25)
`offset` — pagination offset | 234: | `read_account` | Read | Returns the full account (company) record | `account_id` *(required)* — numeric account ID or public account ID `acc_xxx` | 235: *** 236: ## Organization 237: | Tool | Type | Description | Flags | 238: | ----------------- | ---- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 239: | `get_my_identity` | Read | Returns the calling agent's own identity: public ID, name, alias, and whether the caller is human. Takes no arguments. | *(no parameters)* | 240: | `list_inboxes` | Read | Lists inboxes accessible to the authenticated user | `name_query` — filter by inbox name keywords
`access_mode` — `everyone` or `restricted`
`ai_enabled` — filter to AI-enabled inboxes (`true`/`false`)
`ticketing_enabled` — filter to ticketing-enabled inboxes (`true`/`false`)
`business_hours_enabled` — filter by business hours status
`global_rules_enabled` — filter by company rules status
`teammate_ids` — filter to inboxes accessible by specific teammates
`circle_ids` — filter to inboxes accessible by specific teammate groups
`limit` — max results (default 25, max 50)
`offset` — pagination offset | 241: | `list_channels` | Read | Lists channels accessible to the authenticated user. Use to discover channel IDs before calling tools that require one. | `name_query` — filter by channel display name or address keywords
`inbox_ids` — filter to channels belonging to specific inboxes `inb_xxx`
`types` — filter by channel type (e.g. `email`, `chat`, `sms`, `gmail`, `twilio`, etc.)
`account_statuses` — filter by channel account status (`ok`, `quarantined`, `degraded`, `offline`, `deleted`)
`limit` — max results (default 25, max 50)
`offset` — pagination offset | 242: | `list_teammates` | Read | Lists all teammates and their roles in the workspace | `name_query` — search by name or email keywords
`statuses` — filter by account status: `active`, `pending`, `pending_email`, `blocked` (defaults to active statuses)
`limit` — max results (default 10, max 25)
`offset` — pagination offset | 243: | `list_teams` | Read | Lists all teams in the workspace | `name_query` — filter by team name or alias keywords
`limit` — max results (default 10, max 25)
`offset` — pagination offset | 244: | `list_statuses` | Read | Lists the company's ticket statuses. Returns empty when ticketing is not enabled. | `name_query` — filter by status name keywords
`limit` — max results (default 50, max 100)
`offset` — pagination offset | 245: | `list_drafts` | Read | Lists in-flight draft messages authored by the authenticated teammate | `limit` — max drafts to return (default 50, max 200) | 246: ## Troubleshooting 247: ### `401 Unauthorized` on every request 248: The token is invalid, expired, or has been revoked. Common causes: 249: * The user revoked the app's access in Front's connected apps settings. 250: * A company admin uninstalled the OAuth app entirely. 251: * The access token expired and the refresh flow didn't fire. Re-authenticate to mint a new token. 252: ### `missing required scopes` on a tool 253: Your connection doesn't have a permission this tool needs. This usually happens after Front adds a tool. See [Getting access to new tools](#getting-access-to-new-tools). 254: ### A tool stops working after a user's Front access changes 255: A tool can also fail if the authenticated Front user lost access to the relevant inbox, team, or resource between authorization and the tool call. Permissions are enforced at call time against the user's current Front role. 256: ### `429 Too Many Requests` 257: If you're seeing rate-limit errors during normal operation, the most common cause is a polling loop that's tighter than it needs to be. Approval-by-polling loops should generally poll on the order of seconds-to-minutes, not sub-second. For more details, please see the [rate limits](#rate-limits) section. 258: ## Feedback & community discussions 259: To share feedback about tools you'd like to see in the MCP server, please [add an idea](https://community.front.com/ideas) in our community or vote on an existing one.

To discuss MCP server use cases and workflows, please create a post in or subscribe to our [discussion space](https://community.front.com/mcp-server-88). 260:
