1: --- 2: updatedAt: 2026-11-18T17:49:57.000Z 3: agentTools: 4: projectIndex: https://dev.frontapp.com/llms.txt 5: --- 6: # Admin MCP Server 7: ## Connect AI assistants to Front via the Admin MCP server 8: Front's Admin MCP server (`mcp.frontapp.com/admin-mcp`) lets AI agents manage your Front configuration through a single OAuth-authenticated endpoint. Agents can set up AI teammates, author knowledge, build rules, and manage inboxes, tags, templates, teammates, and more. Agents authenticate as a specific Front admin, and can only reach what that admin can manage. The Admin MCP server is separate from the [Front MCP server](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/mcp-server), which works with conversation data on behalf of any teammate. 9: This article covers how to connect any MCP-compatible client to the Admin MCP server using an OAuth app you create yourself in the Front developer settings. For the user-facing overview and use case inspiration for Front admins, see the general Help Center article on the Admin MCP server. 10: 11: ### The Admin MCP server is in open beta 12: The Admin MCP server is free on all plans during the beta. Tool names and parameters may change before general availability. 13: 14: > **Looking for examples before you build?** 15: > 16: > The [MCP space in the Front Community](https://community.front.com/mcp-server-88) has workflow walkthroughs, sample prompts, and more. You can also start up discussions about the Admin MCP server with fellow users and our team. 17: ## Overview 18: | | | 19: | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 20: | **Endpoint** | `https://mcp.frontapp.com/admin-mcp` | 21: | **Transport** | Streamable HTTP (stateless) | 22: | **MCP spec version** | 2025-11-25 | 23: | **Auth** | OAuth 2.1 + PKCE compatibility

**Note:** Front does not support Dynamic Client Registration. Your AI assistant must support a ***confidential connection that sends an OAuth client ID and secret***. Some popular AI assistants are currently [not compatible](#incompatibility-list). | 24: | **Identity model** | Per-user tokens. Every tool call attributes to a specific Front admin | 25: | **Who can connect** | Company admins and workspace admins | 26: | **Scopes** | `read`, `write` | 27: The connected agent can only manage what the authorizing admin can manage. Company admins can work across the whole company, while workspace admins can only change the workspaces they administer and don't see tools for company-level resources such as AI teammates, knowledge bases, or custom fields. Changes made through the Admin MCP server show in your audit log under the admin who authorized the connection. 28: ### Incompatibility list 29: Some AI assistants do not support confidential connections. These clients cannot connect to the Front Admin MCP server: 30: * Any client that requires Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) 31: ## Use cases 32: A few patterns this surface unlocks: 33: * **Set up an Autopilot AI teammate end to end.** Have your AI assistant read an inbox's resolved conversations to learn what to automate, then create the AI teammate, write its instructions, tone, and playbooks, connect a knowledge source, and build the rule that routes conversations to it. 34: * **Tune AI teammates after launch.** Pull improvement opportunities and Replies Hub data, figure out whether a failure is a knowledge gap or a guidance problem, then edit the article, playbook, or instructions that caused it. Simulation sets and success criteria let you track whether a fix worked. 35: * **Author and publish knowledge.** Create knowledge bases, categories, and articles, edit them in bulk, and publish them so AI teammates can answer from them. 36: * **Build and maintain workspace configuration.** Create or update rules (including branching rules and SLA or CSAT recipes), inboxes, tags, message templates, views, custom fields, task templates, shifts, and teammate groups by describing what you need instead of clicking through settings. 37: * **Connect AI teammates to your other systems.** Build custom application connectors, test their requests against the third-party API, and attach them to playbooks. 38: ## Set up the Admin MCP server connection 39: Connecting an AI assistant to Front's Admin MCP server has two general steps: create a Front developer app with the Front Admin MCP feature, and then connect your AI client using the app's credentials. 40: 41: After you complete these two steps, other admins at your company will be able to find the Front Admin MCP server in your AI assistant and connect to it without having to create a developer app or configure the connection details on the AI client side. 42: 43: 44: ### Connect Claude from the official directory 45: If you're using Claude, we recommend you connect the Front Admin MCP server from the [Claude official directory](https://claude.ai/directory/front-admin). 46: If you connect from the directory, you do not need to complete either step in this section (**Set up the Front developer app with the Front Admin MCP feature** or **Connect your AI assistant**). If you are not using Claude, follow the steps in this section to set up the Admin MCP server as a custom connector. 47: To connect via the official directory: 48: - A Front admin (or any user authorized to install integrations from the Front App Store) must connect via the directory link above. 49: - Then, any other admin in your company can use the directory link to connect their own account. 50: 51: ### 1. Set up the Front developer app with the Front Admin MCP feature 52: 53: ### These instructions are completed in your Front settings (Settings > Company > Developer) 54: 55: 56: You need a dedicated developer app for the Admin MCP server. An app can't use both the Front MCP server and the Admin MCP server, so don't reuse an app you set up for the Front MCP server. 57: 58: 1. [Create a developer app](https://dev.frontapp.com/docs/create-and-manage-apps) and give it an appropriate name (e.g. "ChatGPT Admin MCP Connector"). 59: 2. Click **Add feature** in the **Features** tab and select **Front Admin MCP**. 60: 61: If **Front Admin MCP** isn't in the list, refresh the page. 62: 63: 3. Note the **Client ID** and **Client secret**. 64: 4. Add a **redirect URL** that corresponds to the AI assistant you're sending data to. For ChatGPT, use the callback URL ChatGPT shows when you add the connector (see the example below). CLI assistants often use a local callback such as `http://localhost/callback`, which lets them connect on a randomly generated local port. Check your assistant's documentation for the exact value. 65: 5. Under **Resource permissions**, select the resources available to the Admin MCP server and whether the agent can `read` or `write` each one. Besides the resources you may know from the Front MCP server, the Admin MCP feature includes `ai_agents`, `ai_resources` (playbooks, tones, and knowledge sources), `applications`, `macros`, and `task_templates`. 66: 67: Request the narrowest set that covers your use case. An agent that only audits or reports on your configuration needs `read`. Only grant `write` on the resources your agent will actually change. 68: 69: 70: Remember that despite the permissions selected in the OAuth client, agents connecting to the Admin MCP server will be further limited by the subset of data and permissions that the admin who connects the agent has access to. 71: 72: 73: If you change the resource permissions after the initial setup, you must disconnect and re-authorize your connection with your AI assistant ("Connect your AI Assistant" steps) before the new permissions take effect. 74: 75: 6. Save the app. 76:
77: ### 2. Connect your AI assistant 78: 79: ### These instructions are completed in your AI assistant, not Front 80: 81: Once the app is configured, connect from your MCP client so that you and your team can view the Front Admin MCP server. Once it is set up for your company, individual admins can find the server in the list of connectors and authorize it for their own accounts, without configuring the server URL and credentials described in this section. 82: The exact configuration syntax for initial configuration varies by AI client, but every client will need: 83: * The Admin MCP server URL: `https://mcp.frontapp.com/admin-mcp` 84: * Your app's `client_id` and `client_secret` 85: * The OAuth scope the app should request. Either leave this blank or supply `feature:admin_mcp` if you need to input a value 86: * If your AI assistant requests information about our OAuth URLs, use the following values:
87: | URL | Value | 88: | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | 89: | Authorization | `https://app.frontapp.com/oauth/authorize` | 90: | Token & refresh URL | `https://app.frontapp.com/oauth/token` | 91: 92: **Use the UI or command line to connect the Admin MCP server** 93: We recommend using your AI assistant's UI menus to connect the Front Admin MCP server, or terminal commands for CLI assistants. Configuring JSON files is not recommended for most users because varying local paths and environment settings can cause issues. We've provided an example for ChatGPT below, plus a general JSON shape if you have to modify your AI assistant's configuration file directly. 94: If you have issues connecting the Admin MCP server, please reach out to your AI assistant's support team and share this documentation with them so they can recommend the correct steps. 95: 96: #### Example for ChatGPT 97: 1. In ChatGPT settings, turn on developer mode. 98: 2. In **Plugins**, click **+** and enter the server URL: `https://mcp.frontapp.com/admin-mcp` 99: 3. Open the advanced OAuth settings and enter your OAuth Client ID and Client Secret. 100: 4. Copy the callback URL ChatGPT shows and add it as a redirect URL in your Front developer app. 101: 5. Complete the OAuth authentication flow. 102: #### Example for generic MCP server config (confirm with your client's docs on exactly how you structure and pass these properties) - Not recommended for most users 103: ```json 104: { 105: "mcpServers": { 106: "front-admin": { 107: "url": "https://mcp.frontapp.com/admin-mcp", 108: "transport": "streamable-http", 109: "oauth": { 110: "client_id": "", 111: "client_secret": "", 112: "scopes": ["read", "write"] 113: } 114: } 115: } 116: } 117: ``` 118: ### Tips for authorization 119: 120: **Match your client's requested scopes to your OAuth app.** By default, many AI assistants will request every scope the Admin MCP server supports. If those scopes exceed what you enabled on the Front developer app, the authorization flow may return an error. 121: If you encounter this error, configure your client to only request the scopes your app is set up for. Check your client's documentation for the exact syntax. 122: 123: When the client first connects, each admin will be redirected to Front to log in and consent. The resulting token is bound to that specific Front admin, and they can only manage what their Front role allows. AI teammates can't authorize the Admin MCP server. 124: 125: **A note on enterprise deployment:** If your AI assistant is centrally managed (e.g. Claude Enterprise, ChatGPT Enterprise), your IT team may need to allow the connection or distribute the app credentials. Each admin still completes the OAuth consent flow individually. This is how Front guarantees that every tool call has a real, attributable admin behind it. 126: 127: ### Which tools you'll see 128: Not every admin sees every tool. Workspace admins don't see tools for company-level resources, and some tools only appear when your plan or account includes the matching feature. For example, shift tools need the Shifts feature, simulation tools need Autopilot, and connector-building tools need custom application connectors. 129: ### Getting access to new tools 130: When Front adds a tool that needs a permission your connection doesn't have yet, the tool appears in your AI assistant, but calling it returns a `missing required scopes` error. That's because a connection keeps the permissions that were approved when it was first authorized; it doesn't pick up new ones on its own. 131: 132: 1. A Front admin opens your developer app (**Settings > Company > Developer**), opens its **Front Admin MCP** feature, and enables the new permission under **Resource permissions**. The error message names the permission the tool needs. 133: 2. Each admin disconnects Front in their AI assistant and connects it again. 134: Until both steps are done, the new tool keeps returning the error. Other tools keep working. 135: 136: ## Rate limits 137: The Admin MCP server allows 200 tool calls per minute per company, on every plan. Every admin, AI assistant, and developer app at your company shares this limit, and every tool call counts the same regardless of which tool it is. 138: 139: We'll revisit this limit before general availability based on usage during the beta. 140: 141: ### How to handle a limit 142: When your company goes over the limit, the call fails with an MCP error that says how long to wait: 143: ```Text 144: Admin MCP is limited to 200 tool calls per minute per company. Retry after Xs. 145: ``` 146: Wait the stated time before retrying. Earlier retries will simply be rejected again. 147: ## Tool reference 148: 149: The Admin MCP server currently exposes the following tools. Each tool's full input schema is available to your AI assistant through the server. To get the most updated list, ask your AI agent to refresh the tool list, or reconnect. 150: The **Access** column shows who can use each tool. Workspace-scoped tools are available to workspace admins, but only for the workspaces they administer. Doesn't create or authorize them. | 304: | `get_expression_reference` | Read | Global admin | Explains the `{{ }}` expressions some tools accept, such as the references in app requests. Tools that take expressions name the scope to pass. | 305: | `test_app_request` | Test | Global admin | Tests an app request, including drafts, by calling the third-party API. This can create, update, or delete data in that system. Sensitive values in the response are redacted. | 306: ## Troubleshooting 307: ### `401 Unauthorized` on every request 308: The token is invalid, expired, or has been revoked. Common causes: 309: * The admin revoked the app's access in Front's connected apps settings. 310: * A company admin uninstalled the OAuth app entirely. 311: * The access token expired and the refresh flow didn't fire. Re-authenticate to mint a new token. 312: ### `missing required scopes` on a tool 313: Your connection doesn't have a permission this tool needs. This usually happens after Front adds a tool. See [Getting access to new tools](#getting-access-to-new-tools). 314: ### `This token cannot access the Admin MCP Server` 315: The connection is using a developer app set up for the Front MCP server. Create a separate developer app with the **Front Admin MCP** feature and connect with its credentials. 316: ### `The Admin MCP Server requires an admin requester` 317: Only company admins and workspace admins can use the Admin MCP server. Have an admin authorize the connection instead. 318: ### A tool is missing or refuses a workspace 319: Workspace admins only see workspace-level tools and can only change workspaces they administer. Some tools also depend on your plan or features enabled for your company. See [Which tools you'll see](#which-tools-youll-see). 320: ### A tool stops working after an admin's Front access changes 321: Permissions are enforced at call time against the admin's current Front role. If the admin lost admin rights or access to a workspace after authorizing, tools that need that access will fail. 322: ### `Admin MCP is limited to 200 tool calls per minute per company` 323: Your company went over its shared rate limit. Wait the number of seconds in the error before retrying. If this happens during normal use, look for a polling loop that's tighter than it needs to be, or several agents running at once, since everyone at your company shares the limit. For more details, see the [rate limits](#rate-limits) section. 324: ## Feedback & community discussions 325: To share feedback about tools you'd like to see in the Admin MCP server, please [add an idea](https://community.front.com/ideas) in our community or vote on an existing one. You can also ask your AI assistant to send feedback directly with the `send_feedback` tool.

To discuss Admin MCP server use cases and workflows, please create a post in or subscribe to our [discussion space](https://community.front.com/mcp-server-88). 326:
327: ***

1: > For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/llms.txt). Markdown versions of documentation pages are available by appending `.md` to page URLs; this page is available as [Markdown](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/developer/api/authentication.md).
2: # Authentication
3: How to authenticate with Pylon's API
4: The Pylon API uses [Bearer](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750#section-2.1) authentication. This means you’ll need to pass your API token in the header of your request:
5: ```
6: Authorization: Bearer <token>
7: ```
8: {% hint style="info" %}
9: Generate an API token in the [Pylon dashboard](https://app.usepylon.com/settings/api-tokens).
10: {% endhint %}
11: ### API regions
12: Pylon’s API is available in two regions. Use the base URL that matches where your Pylon tenant is hosted:
13: * US region: <https://api.usepylon.com>
14: * EU region: <https://api.eu.usepylon.com>
15: Both regions use the same API endpoints and authentication. Configure your integration to use the region where your Pylon tenant is hosted.
16: You can tell a token's region from its prefix:
17: | Prefix | Region |
18: | --------------- | ------ |
19: | `pylon_api_eu_` | EU |
20: | `pylon_api_` | US |
21: Tokens created before prefixes were introduced have no prefix. Sending a token to the other region's API returns `401` with the `wrong_region_token` error code, and the message names the correct URL.
22: Once you've created a token, call the [`/me`](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/developer/api/api-reference/me.md) endpoint to retrieve details about your organization and confirm your token works.
23: ## Create an API token
24: Only Admins can create and manage API tokens.
25: 1. Go to **Settings > Integrations & dev > API**. On the **Tokens** tab, click **Create API Token**.
26: 2. Enter a **Name**.
27: 3. Choose who the token acts as:
28: * Leave **Act as user or bot (optional)** empty to give the token its own identity. Pick a **Role** to control what it can access, and optionally upload an icon.
29: * Or select a teammate or bot. The token uses that user's current role and permissions.
30: 4. Optionally, add an **IP allowlist** (see below).
31: 5. Click **Create** and copy the token. Pylon shows it only once.
32: Tokens don't expire, and their access is controlled only by the role. There are no separate scopes.
33: ### Roles
34: A token with its own identity uses the role you pick when you create it. You can change the role later with **Edit**. Older tokens that have no role act as Admin.
35: A token that acts as a user or bot has no role of its own. It always uses that user's current role, so changing the user's role changes what the token can do.
36: See [Roles and user management](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/platform/roles-and-user-management.md) for what each role allows.
37: ### Who actions are attributed to
38: * **Token with its own identity:** actions show up under the token's name and icon.
39: * **Token that acts as a user or bot:** actions are attributed to that user or bot.
40: ### Bots
41: Bots are identities for automation, so API activity is attributed to the bot instead of to a teammate. Bots can't sign in to Pylon.
42: To create one, go to **Settings > Workspace > Users**, open the **Bots** tab, and click **New Bot**. Give it a name, an avatar, and a role. Then select the bot under **Act as user or bot** when you create a token.
43: ### IP allowlist
44: Add IP addresses (for example `203.0.113.10`) or CIDR blocks (for example `203.0.113.0/24`) to restrict where the token can be used. You can add up to 20 entries. If the list is empty, the token works from any IP.
45: Pylon checks the public IP address your requests come from, so add the public egress IPs or ranges of the servers that call the API. Private addresses such as `10.0.0.0/8` or `192.168.0.0/16` never match.
46: A request from an address that isn't on the list returns `401` with the `invalid_api_token` error code.
47: ## Manage tokens
48: The **Tokens** tab shows each token's **Acts as**, **Token preview**, **Role**, **Created by**, **Last used**, and **Created** values. From the **…** menu on a token you can:
49: * **Edit:** change the name, role, or IP allowlist.
50: * **Duplicate Token:** create a new token with the same settings.
51: * **Rotate:** generate a new token value. The current token stops working immediately.
52: * **Delete:** permanently revoke the token. Calls using it stop working immediately.
53: * **View Activity:** open the token's request logs.
54: ## Review API request logs
55: Only Admins can view request logs. Go to **Settings > Integrations & dev > API** and open the **Logs** tab, or choose **View Activity** from a token's **…** menu to see only that token's requests.
56: Filter by token, or choose **All tokens**, and by a date range of up to 90 days. The range defaults to the last 7 days. Each request shows when it was made, the token, who it acted as, the method, endpoint, response status, source IP, user agent, and request ID. Requests made with a token that was since deleted still appear.
57: Requests rejected for authentication or rate limits aren't logged, and older requests may not show a token.
58: ### When tokens are revoked automatically
59: When a user is deactivated, Pylon deletes:
60: * every API token that user created, and
61: * every API token that acts as that user.
62: Before you deactivate someone who created tokens your integrations rely on, create replacement tokens from another Admin's account.
63: An Admin who has created Admin-role tokens can't be moved to a different role until those tokens are deleted.
64: ---
65: # Agent Instructions
66: This documentation is published with GitBook. GitBook is the documentation platform designed so that both humans and AI agents can read, navigate, and reason over technical content effectively. Learn more at gitbook.com.
67: ## Querying This Documentation
68: If you need additional information that is not directly available in this page, you can query the documentation by asking a question.
69: Perform an HTTP GET request on the following URL with the `ask` and `goal` query parameters:
70: ```
71: GET https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/developer/api/authentication.md?ask=<question>&goal=<user_goal>
72: ```
73: `ask` is the immediate question: it should be specific, self-contained, and written in natural language.
74: `goal` is what the user is ultimately trying to achieve, the reason they need the answer. Sharing it helps GitBook give you a better, more relevant answer. A goal is most helpful when it describes the outcome the user wants rather than restating the question. For example, with `ask=how do I create an API token`, a goal like `automate deployments from our CI pipeline` lets GitBook tailor the answer to that use case.
75: The response will contain a direct answer to the question and relevant excerpts and sources from the documentation.
76: Use this mechanism when the answer is not explicitly present in the current page, you need clarification or additional context, or you want to retrieve related documentation sections.

1: > For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/llms.txt). Markdown versions of documentation pages are available by appending `.md` to page URLs; this page is available as [Markdown](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/integrations/pylon-mcp.md).
2: # Pylon MCP
3: Expose Pylon data to AI tools and assistants via Model Context Protocol.
4: ## Pylon MCP Server
5: The Pylon MCP Server exposes Pylon data to AI tools that support the Model Context Protocol (e.g. Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor). AI tools authenticate with OAuth or an API token and can read and update issues, accounts, contacts, knowledge base articles, tasks and projects, triggers, and more within the authenticated identity's permissions.
6: * **Server URL (US):** `https://mcp.usepylon.com`
7: * **Server URL (EU):** `https://mcp.eu.usepylon.com`
8: * **Auth:** OAuth 2.0 or an API token. Actions are performed as the signed-in user or the token's identity, with that identity's current role and permissions.
9: * **Transport:** Streamable HTTP (stateless; no server-side sessions).
10: ### Setup in Pylon
11: Open **Settings > AI Controls > MCP Server** in Pylon. Copy your workspace's regional MCP URL from **Installation** and use it in your AI tool. For client-specific instructions, see [connecting to the Pylon MCP Server](https://support.usepylon.com/articles/2407390554-connecting-to-the-pylon-mcp-server?lang=en).
12: ### Authentication
13: Both methods use the same regional MCP URL. Choose the method your client supports.
14: #### OAuth
15: Use OAuth with AI tools that offer an interactive connection flow. Add the regional MCP URL to your client, then sign in to Pylon when prompted. MCP requests run as the user who authorizes the connection.
16: #### API token
17: Use an existing API token for headless workers, scripts, or MCP clients that support custom authorization headers. You don't need a separate MCP token or an interactive sign-in.
18: 1. Create or choose an [API token](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/developer/api/authentication.md#create-an-api-token).
19: 2. Configure your client with your workspace's regional MCP URL.
20: 3. Include this header on every MCP request:
21: ```http
22: Authorization: Bearer <API_TOKEN>
23: ```
24: Replace `<API_TOKEN>` with the token value. Use `https://mcp.usepylon.com` for US workspaces and `https://mcp.eu.usepylon.com` for EU workspaces; the token must belong to the same region.
25: A token with its own identity uses the role assigned to that identity. A token linked to a teammate or bot uses that user's current role and permissions. The identity must have **MCP Access**, and each tool still requires the permissions for its operation. Any IP allowlist configured on the token also applies to MCP requests.
26: Some clients only support OAuth connections. Use their OAuth flow if they don't let you configure an authorization header.
27: ### What you can do with MCP today
28: The authenticated user or token identity needs the **MCP Access** [permission](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/platform/roles-and-user-management#member-permissions-2) to connect. The standard Member and Admin roles include this permission. Each tool also requires the permissions for its operation. Access follows the same scoping as the Pylon dashboard — the MCP cannot return data that the authenticated user cannot already see, or perform writes that the authenticated user cannot already write in the UI.
29: Some tools also require a plan feature, noted in their section. Rate limits apply per tool, elaborated below.
30: Use the tool names below when configuring your AI client. Your client discovers the input schema for each tool through MCP; available tools depend on your workspace, plan, and permissions.
31: For a tool whose input schema includes `arguments`, put its required and optional fields inside that object. For example:
32: ```json
33: {
34: "name": "get_account_relationships",
35: "arguments": {
36: "arguments": {
37: "account_id": "<ACCOUNT_ID>"
38: }
39: }
40: }
41: ```
42: Use the schema returned by your client for the exact fields. Writes apply immediately; confirm the intended change before calling them. If the outcome of a write is unknown, check the record before retrying.
43: Write tools reject arguments they don't recognize instead of ignoring them; the error names the unknown arguments and lists the valid ones. A different casing of a field name, such as `customerPortalTitle` for `customer_portal_title`, is accepted, and tools with a `state` field also accept `status`. Supply each field only once: sending a field under both its name and an alias returns an error.

On large pages, `max_messages_per_issue` keeps only each issue's latest messages (`messages_truncated` is set when older ones were dropped), and `max_message_chars` cuts each message body to that many characters (`body_truncated` is set). Set `include_total` to also get the exact number of matching issues you can read across all pages; it costs an extra query, so use it when sizing work rather than on every page. Images hosted in Pylon (PNG, JPEG, GIF, and WebP) are returned as image content, up to 5 images per call, 5 MB each and 10 MB in total, and images that can't be attached are noted in the response. 78: For UTF-8 text attachments hosted by Pylon, `get_message_attachment` returns the text in a content block and reports the read status in `read`. 79: * `complete`: no more text remains.
80: * `partial`: pass `read.next_cursor` as `cursor` with the same `issue`, `message_id`, and `attachment_index` to read the next page. Access is checked on every call. If the file changes, restart without a cursor.
81: * `unsupported`: use the download link for other formats, external files, non-UTF-8 content, or oversized files.
82: * `unavailable`: the download failed. Retry or use the download link.

Neither field can be set to an empty value, so `update_issue` can't remove an issue's account or clear its requester.

246: #### **Triggers**
247: New triggers are created disabled so you can review them in Pylon before turning them on.
248: Use `validate_trigger` before saving. `save_trigger` supports custom trigger groups and flat branches with compatible actions, delays, and conditions, including recurring schedule kickoffs. Configure default or special groups, phone/IVR triggers, nested branches, and background-agent investigations in Pylon instead. Updating a trigger replaces its editable configuration while preserving its group and enabled state.
249: To change only which records a trigger acts on, use `update_trigger_conditions`. Pass `branch_conditions`, mapping top-level branch IDs from `get_trigger` to new filters from `build_filter`; only those branches' conditions are replaced. Kickoffs, actions, branch and step IDs, group, title, description, and enabled state are kept, so this also works on triggers in default or special groups and on triggers with background-agent actions. To add an exclusion, combine it with the branch's complete existing filter, including any OR group. Updating conditions doesn't run the trigger.
250: To build a recurring schedule, call `describe_trigger_kickoff` with `kickoff_type` `recurring_schedule` and the `object_type` the schedule runs on (for example `issue` or `account`). It returns the schedule fields and the actions that object supports; `get_trigger_examples` includes a weekday schedule example. Every enabled branch of a scheduled trigger needs a filter that selects which records it acts on. `build_filter` can't build meeting filters, so reuse an existing meeting filter from `get_trigger` or set it up in Pylon. To change an existing schedule, start from its `get_trigger` configuration. If a schedule uses recurrence settings that `save_trigger` can't represent, the update is rejected and the trigger is left unchanged; edit it in Pylon instead.

301: #### **Audit Logs**
302: Requires Admin permission. Full audit log history is available on the Enterprise plan; otherwise, searches cover only the last 30 days. A search starting earlier than that limit returns an error.
303: | **Tool** | **Read / Write** | **Description** |
304: | ---------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
305: | **`list_audit_log_actions`** | Read | Discover exact supported action names, regardless of recorded events |
306: | **`search_audit_logs`** | Read | Search recorded actions and changes in your organization by object, action, and time |
307: Each search needs `actions`, 1 to 10 exact action names from `list_audit_log_actions`, and a `happened_after` time. `happened_before` defaults to now, and a search can span at most 7 days, so search longer periods one 7-day window at a time. Both accept RFC3339 timestamps, such as `2026-10-01T00:00:00Z`. Optionally, use `object_id` to find changes to an issue or account. Resolve a ticket number to its ID with `get_issue` first. Filters combine with AND; within `actions`, an entry can match any supplied action. Actor IDs are returned, but actor filtering is not supported. Each call also needs an `intent`, a short reason for the search of up to 200 characters.
308: Results include `audit_logs`, the current page's `count`, and `has_next_page`. The default `limit` is 25 and the maximum is 100. Continue with the returned `cursor` and unchanged filters, passing the returned `happened_before`. Set `include_metadata` to `true` for action-specific details; metadata is omitted by default. When history is restricted, `history_limited_to_days` is `30`.
309: **Find action names**
310: Call `list_audit_log_actions` for the authoritative catalog of action names supported by audit-log search. It includes names regardless of whether matching events exist in your workspace and excludes hidden actions. It requires the same Admin permission as `search_audit_logs`.
311: Use optional `query` for a case-insensitive substring match on names. Results are alphabetical; `limit` defaults to 50 and has a maximum of 100. Continue with the returned `cursor` and unchanged `query` while `has_next_page` is true to read the full catalog. The `count` is the number of names on the current page.
312: The `actions` filter takes exact strings from this catalog or a returned entry's `action` field. Copy those values rather than guessing from a UI label: some stored action names differ from the labels shown in Pylon.
313: Common exact action names include:
314: | Change | Exact action name |
315: | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
316: | One issue custom field changed | `Issue Custom Field Updated` |
317: | Multiple issue custom fields changed | `Issue Custom Fields Updated` |
318: | Issue assigned | `Success Issue Assigned` |
319: | Issue closed | `Success Ticket Closed` |
320: | Issue tags changed | `Issue Tags Changed` |
321: | Account owner changed | `Account Owner Changed` |
322: | Account created | `Account Created` |
323: | Macro edited | `Macro Updated` |
324: For example, call `list_audit_log_actions` to discover custom-field action names:
325: ```json
326: {
327: "query": "Custom Field",
328: "limit": 50
329: }
330: ```
331: Then copy returned names into `search_audit_logs.actions`:
332: ```json
333: {
334: "actions": ["Issue Custom Field Updated", "Issue Custom Fields Updated"],
335: "include_metadata": true,
336: "limit": 25
337: }
338: ```
339: These are examples, not a complete catalog. Use `list_audit_log_actions` for the full catalog. A listed action may have no recorded events in your workspace; search results remain subject to your history access. In `search_audit_logs`, `action_contains` searches action names only, not attributes, field values, or metadata.
340: Audit logs show recorded events, not a complete explanation of every automation or field change.

376: #### **REST API**
377: AI tools can run operations from the [Pylon REST API](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/developer/api) directly. Each REST API operation has its own tool: either a dedicated tool such as `update_account`, or a tool named after the operation, such as `create_ticket_form`. A tool named after an operation takes the operation's path, query, and body parameters in `arguments`. Each call runs as the authenticated user, so the operation's own permission checks apply, just as they do in the Pylon dashboard. If no tool does what you need, use the [Pylon CLI](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/developer/api/cli) instead.
378: `search_api_operations`, `get_api_operation`, `call_api_read`, and `call_api_write` no longer appear in tool lists, but integrations that already call them by name keep working.
379: Writes apply immediately and can be visible to customers. Some updates replace a whole list, such as an account's tags, so read the current value first and send the full list. Writes have no idempotency key: if a write's outcome is unknown, read the record before retrying.
380: Pass `select`, a [JMESPath](https://jmespath.org) expression, to return only the fields you need, such as `data[].{id: id, name: name}`. Read responses over 200 KB return an error; narrow them with `select` or request fewer results. If a write's response is over 200 KB, the write still succeeds and returns a short note instead of the response, so don't retry it.
381: Each operation uses its REST API [rate limit](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/developer/api/rate-limits). When an operation is throttled, the error says how many seconds to wait.
382: Some REST API operations aren't available through MCP, so they have no tool. Some operations are available only through MCP: `api.usepylon.com` rejects them, they aren't in the [API reference](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/developer/api), and the Pylon CLI and SDKs don't support them. They're experimental and can change or be removed without notice.

492: ### **Combined tools**
493: Some tools were combined to keep the list short for AI tools. Use the replacement names below for new integrations and migrate scripts that use old names. Old names marked *(removed)* no longer work. The others remain callable but are hidden from tool discovery.
494: | **Old tool** | **Use instead** |
495: | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
496: | `create_task` | `save_task` without `task_id` |
497: | `update_task` | `save_task` with `task_id` |
498: | `create_contact` *(removed)* | `save_contact` without `contact_id` |
499: | `update_contact` | `save_contact` with `contact_id` |
500: | `create_feature_request`, `update_feature_request` *(removed)* | `save_feature_request` without or with `feature_request_id` |
501: | `create_project` *(removed)* | `save_project` without `project_id` |
502: | `update_project` | `save_project` with `project_id` |
503: | `create_milestone` *(removed)* | `save_milestone` without `milestone_id` |
504: | `update_milestone` *(removed)* | `save_milestone` with `milestone_id` |
505: | `create_account_note` *(removed)* | `save_account_note` without `note_id` |
506: | `update_account_note` *(removed)* | `save_account_note` with `note_id` |
507: | `get_notebook_content` *(removed)* | `get_account_notes` for a Notes block |
508: | `create_trigger` *(removed)*, `update_trigger` | `save_trigger` |
509: | `list_trigger_kickoffs`, `list_trigger_actions` *(removed)* | `describe_trigger_kickoff`, `describe_trigger_action` with no type |
510: | `get_issue_filter_attributes`, `get_account_filter_attributes` | `get_filter_attributes` with `object_type` |
511: | `get_contact_filter_attributes`, `get_task_filter_attributes`, `get_project_filter_attributes`, `get_opportunity_filter_attributes`, `get_feature_request_filter_attributes` *(removed)* | `get_filter_attributes` with `object_type` |
512: | `get_tasks`, `get_projects` | `search_tasks`, `search_projects` |
513: | `create_project_from_template` *(removed)* | `save_project` with `project_template_id` (omit `project_id`) |
514: | `get_article_by_identifier` *(removed)* | `get_article` with `identifier` |
515: | `create_draft_article`, `create_draft_article_version` *(removed)* | `save_draft_article` |
516: | `list_teams` | `search_teams` |
517: | `get_tag` | `list_tags` with `value` |
518: ### Tool errors
519: Classified failures from native and REST-backed tools return `isError: true` and one text block containing JSON:
520: ```json
521: {"error":{"code":"invalid_arguments","message":"tags_apply_mode requires tags.","fields":["tags_apply_mode","tags"],"tool":"update_account","request_id":"<request ID>"}}
522: ```
523: Use `error.code` to handle a classified failure. When available, `error` also includes the tool name (`tool`), request identifier (`request_id`), API operation (`operation_id`), HTTP `status`, affected `fields`, or `retry_after_seconds`. Unclassified tool failures and SDK validation errors may still return plain text. JSON-RPC errors, including native tool throttling, use their existing format.
524: ### **Rate limits**
525: Rate limits are applied per tool and per organization to keep the MCP server healthy under bursty AI traffic. Tool throttling returns a JSON-RPC error with code **`-32000`**. Its message identifies the tool and tells you how many seconds to wait before retrying. Wait for that delay before retrying the call.
526: ---
527: # Agent Instructions
528: This documentation is published with GitBook. GitBook is the documentation platform designed so that both humans and AI agents can read, navigate, and reason over technical content effectively. Learn more at gitbook.com.
529: ## Querying This Documentation
530: If you need additional information that is not directly available in this page, you can query the documentation by asking a question.
531: Perform an HTTP GET request on the following URL with the `ask` and `goal` query parameters:
532: ```
533: GET https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/integrations/pylon-mcp.md?ask=<question>&goal=<user_goal>
534: ```
535: `ask` is the immediate question: it should be specific, self-contained, and written in natural language.
536: `goal` is what the user is ultimately trying to achieve, the reason they need the answer. Sharing it helps GitBook give you a better, more relevant answer. A goal is most helpful when it describes the outcome the user wants rather than restating the question. For example, with `ask=how do I create an API token`, a goal like `automate deployments from our CI pipeline` lets GitBook tailor the answer to that use case.
537: The response will contain a direct answer to the question and relevant excerpts and sources from the documentation.
538: Use this mechanism when the answer is not explicitly present in the current page, you need clarification or additional context, or you want to retrieve related documentation sections.

16: MCP Integration for agents
17: LiveAgent exposes a built-in MCP server (Model Context Protocol) that lets you connect external AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, Cursor, claude.ai, FlowHunt, or any other MCP-compatible client, directly with your LiveAgent account. Once connected, your own AI tools/agents can read ticket data and perform actions on your behalf, using your agent identity and permissions.
18: There are two ways to authenticate your MCP client - OAuth 2.1 (recommended), where the AI tool discovers the authorization server automatically and redirects you to a consent screen, or Bearer token, where you generate an MCP access token in your profile and paste it into the AI tool's configuration manually.
19: In this article

28: Finding MCP Integration in your profile
29: Click your avatar in the top-right corner of the LiveAgent panel and select Edit profile.
30: In the left-hand menu, navigate to the MCP Integration section.
31: This screen shows your connection details and access tokens. Use these values to configure any MCP-compatible client:
32: SettingValue
33: MCP server URLhttps://<your-liveagent-domain>/api/mcp
34: Transport protocolStreamable HTTP
35: AuthenticationOAuth 2.1 (Authorization Code + PKCE) or Bearer token
36: Connecting with OAuth
37: OAuth authentication lets AI tools connect to your LiveAgent MCP server without you having to generate, copy, and paste a token. The tool handles the entire authentication flow automatically using standard OAuth 2.1 with PKCE.
38: How it works
39: In your AI tool (for example Claude app), add a new MCP server/connector/plugin using your LiveAgent MCP server URL.
40: The AI tool calls that URL, receives a discovery hint, and fetches LiveAgent's OAuth server metadata automatically.
41: You are redirected to the LiveAgent login page (if not already logged in) and then to a consent screen asking you to approve the connection.
42: After you approve, the tool receives an access token and is ready to use.
43: Note: Your consent decision is remembered. If you remove and reconnect the same tool later, the consent screen is skipped and completes silently.
44: Managing authorized apps
45: The MCP Integration screen in your profile lists all OAuth clients you have approved under Authorized apps. You can revoke any authorized app. The tool will lose access immediately and will need to go through the OAuth flow again to reconnect.
46: Tip: Administrators or users with a custom role with the permission to manage agents can view and revoke authorized apps for other agents in the account.
47: Connecting with a bearer token
48: If your AI tool does not support OAuth authentication, you can use a bearer token to connect it. Bearer tokens are MCP access tokens you generate in your profile and paste directly into your MCP client. Bearer tokens are also used by scripts that require manual configuration.
49: Generating an access token
50: On the MCP Integration screen in your profile and click Generate token.
51: Copy the access token.
52: Paste the access token into your MCP client as the Bearer token value.
53: Important: Store the access token securely as soon as you generate it. If you lose it, you will need to revoke the existing token and generate a new one.
54: You can generate up to 10 active access tokens per account. Having multiple tokens is useful if you connect the same account to more than one tool or device.
55: Managing access tokens
56: The access token list on the MCP Integration screen shows each token's masked identifier and expiration date. Each can be revoked independently without affecting the others. Upon revoking a token, the corresponding MCP client/AI tool will lose access immediately.
57: Note: Access tokens expire automatically after two years from the date they were generated, regardless of how frequently they are used. Plan to rotate access tokens before they expire to avoid interruption.
58: Permissions and available tools
59: Regardless of whether you connect via OAuth or bearer token, your AI tool has access to the full set of LiveAgent MCP tools. See the MCP tools reference for the complete list of tools and their detailed description.
60: All actions are performed under your agent identity and are subject to your role's permissions, exactly as if you had performed them in the LiveAgent panel. They appear in the ticket's activity history under your name.
61: Note: Unlike LiveAgent AI agents, which restrict the tool set per AI agent configuration, personal MCP integration gives access to all tools. Your role's permissions still apply - actions your role is not permitted to perform will be rejected.
62: Note: Actions performed through an MCP connection count toward a common AI budget shared by all users, which limits the number of tool calls. See the AI budgets article for details on how AI budgets work.

1: # Plain Docs: Developer
2: ## Developer
3: ### GraphQL API
4: - [Introduction](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/introduction.md): An overview of Plain's GraphQL API and the data model behind it.
5: - [Authentication](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/authentication.md): Create a machine user and an API key, and scope it with fine-grained permissions.
6: - [OAuth](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/oauth.md): Call the API as a user in your workspace after they sign in to your OAuth app.
7: - [Schema](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/schema.md): Download the GraphQL schema for code generation, or read it in the API explorer.
8: - [Pagination](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/pagination.md): Every collection in the API follows the Relay cursor pagination spec.
9: - [Error handling](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/error-handling.md): GraphQL queries and mutations require different error handling.
10: - [Error codes](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/error-codes.md): Look up what an error code from the Plain API means and how to handle it.
11: - [AI feedback](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/ai-feedback.md): List the feedback your team has left on Customer Agent replies and other Plain AI features.
12: - [Notes](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/notes.md): Notes are internal comments on a thread. They appear in the timeline but never reach the customer.
13: - [Building your own ticket importer](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/custom-ticket-importer.md): Write your own importer to bring support history into Plain from a tool with no built-in importer.
14: - [Attachments](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/attachments.md): How to upload attachments programmatically for messages and events in Plain.
15: - [API explorer](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/api-explorer.md)
16: - [GraphQL SDK](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/sdk.md): A typed SDK for Plain's GraphQL API, auto-generated from the schema.
17: #### Customers
18: - [Customers](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/customers.md): Customers are created automatically when someone contacts you, and you can also upsert them yourself.
19: - [Fetch customers](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/customers/get.md): Fetch customers by ID, email, or external ID, or as a paginated collection.
20: - [Upserting customers](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/customers/upsert.md): Learn how to create and update customers programmatically.
21: - [Delete customers](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/customers/delete.md): Permanently delete a customer and their threads with the deleteCustomer mutation.
22: - [Mark customer as spam](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/customers/spam.md): Flag a customer as spam to hide their threads and keep them out of your metrics.
23: - [Customer groups](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/customers/customer-groups.md): Segment customers into named groups you define, separate from accounts.
24: #### Accounts
25: - [Accounts](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/accounts.md): Accounts are how you group the customers you support into the organizations that they belong to.
26: - [Upserting accounts](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/accounts/upsert.md): Create or update an account, keyed on the external ID it has in your own product.
27: - [Get accounts](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/accounts/get.md): Fetch accounts by ID or external ID, or as a paginated collection.
28: - [Delete an account](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/accounts/delete.md): Delete an account, unlinking its customers and removing its account fields.
29: - [Account fields](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/accounts/account-fields.md): Attach custom fields to an account, such as plan, MRR, or account owner.
30: - [Add customers to accounts](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/accounts/add-customers.md): Add a customer to one or more accounts in a single call.
31: - [Remove customers from accounts](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/accounts/remove-customers.md): Remove a customer from one or more accounts in a single call.
32: - [Set customer accounts](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/accounts/set-customer-accounts.md): Replace all of a customer's accounts at once, rather than adding or removing individually.
33: #### Threads
34: - [Threads](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads.md): Threads are the core of Plain's data model. Every customer conversation becomes one.
35: - [Fetch threads](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/get.md): Fetch threads by ID or external ID, list them with filters, or search their contents.
36: - [Create threads](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/create.md): Create a thread from the API, for contact forms or proactive outreach.
37: - [Importing threads](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/import.md): Import historical threads and their messages, preserving original timestamps.
38: - [Update thread attributes](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/update.md): Change individual thread attributes such as title, priority, customer, or account.
39: - [Delete a thread](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/delete.md): Permanently delete a thread and all its associated data from Plain.
40: - [Assignment](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/assignment.md): Assign a thread to a user or a machine user, add co-assignees, or unassign it.
41: - [Escalating threads](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/escalation.md): Move a thread up an escalation path, or set which path it follows.
42: - [Changing status](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/status-changes.md): Move a thread between Todo, Snoozed, and Done, and read what each status means.
43: - [Thread fields](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/thread-fields.md): Extend the thread model with your own typed fields, defined by a schema.
44: - [Autoresponders](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/threads/autoresponders.md): Build an autoresponder that decides what to send, rather than using a fixed workspace reply.
45: #### Tiers
46: - [Tiers & SLAs](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tiers.md): Tiers group accounts so you can attach different SLA targets to each.
47: - [Get tiers](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tiers/get.md): Fetch tiers by ID or as a paginated collection, with their SLA configuration.
48: - [Update account tier](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tiers/update-account-tier.md): Set the tier for an account explicitly, rather than inheriting it.
49: - [Add accounts to tiers](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tiers/add-members.md): Add accounts to a tier in a single mutation.
50: - [Remove accounts from tiers](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tiers/remove-members.md): Remove accounts from the tiers they belong to.
51: - [Service level agreements](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tiers/service-level-agreements.md): Set first response, next response, and resolution time SLA targets per tier and per priority.
52: #### SLA policies
53: - [SLA policies](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/sla-policies.md): SLA policies are named sets of SLA targets that you create once and apply to threads with a workflow or the API.
54: - [Get SLA policies](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/sla-policies/get.md): List the SLA policies in your workspace or fetch one by ID.
55: - [Manage SLA policies](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/sla-policies/manage.md): Create, update, and delete SLA policies and their targets.
56: - [Apply SLA policies](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/sla-policies/apply-to-thread.md): Set or remove the SLA policy on a thread.
57: #### Business hours
58: - [Business hours](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/business-hours.md): Read business hours schedules and manage the overrides that change their hours on specific dates.
59: - [Manage business hours overrides](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/business-hours/overrides.md): List, create, update, and delete overrides that replace a schedule's weekly hours for holidays and one-off closures.
60: #### Reporting
61: - [Reporting](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/reporting.md): Query Plain Insights metrics from the API, with filters, group-by, percentiles, and the thread IDs behind each number.
62: - [Reporting metrics reference](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/reporting/metrics.md): Every metric name the Reporting API accepts, what it measures, its unit, and which queries support it.
63: - [Filter and group reporting queries](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/reporting/filters.md): Narrow Reporting API queries with filters and AND, OR, and NOT, and split results by a dimension with groupBy and topN.
64: - [Get a time series metric](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/reporting/time-series.md): Fetch a metric as one value per hour, day, week, or longer bucket with threadTimeSeriesMetric.
65: - [Get a single value metric](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/reporting/single-value.md): Fetch one value for a whole date range, overall or per group, with threadSingleValueMetric.
66: - [Get a heatmap](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/reporting/heatmap.md): Fetch thread counts by day of week and hour of day, in UTC, with threadHeatmapMetric.
67: #### Events
68: - [Events](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/events.md): Log important events to have the full picture of what happened in Plain.
69: - [Create a customer event](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/events/create-customer-event.md): Add a custom event to every thread belonging to a customer.
70: - [Create a thread event](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/events/create-thread-event.md): Add a custom event to a single thread's timeline.
71: #### Labels
72: - [Labels](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/labels.md): Labels categorize threads. Each one references a label type that defines its name, icon, and color.
73: - [Add labels](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/labels/add.md): Add one or more labels to a thread by label type ID.
74: - [Remove labels](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/labels/remove.md): Remove labels from a thread by label ID.
75: - [Manage label types](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/labels/label-types.md): Create, update, archive, and fetch the label types available in your workspace.
76: #### Messaging
77: - [Messaging](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/messaging.md): Send and reply to customer messages over email and chat from the API.
78: - [Reply to threads](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/messaging/reply-to-thread.md): Reply on a thread over whichever channel it already uses.
79: - [Send new emails](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/messaging/send-email.md): Start a new outbound email to a customer, creating a thread for it.
80: - [Reply to emails](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/messaging/reply-email.md): Reply to a specific inbound email with the replyToEmail mutation.
81: - [Suggested replies](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/messaging/suggested-replies.md): Add a suggested reply to a thread for a user to review, edit, and send.
82: #### Snippets
83: - [Snippets](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/snippets.md): Snippets are reusable pieces of text that users insert into a reply with a few keystrokes.
84: - [Fetch snippets](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/snippets/get.md): Fetch snippets by ID or as a paginated collection.
85: - [Create a snippet](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/snippets/create.md): Create a snippet, with a name to find it by and optional dynamic variables.
86: - [Update a snippet](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/snippets/update.md): Change a snippet's name, text, or group using field-level wrapper inputs.
87: - [Delete a snippet](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/snippets/delete.md): Soft-delete a snippet, hiding it from the picker while keeping reply history intact.
88: #### Tasks
89: - [Tasks](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tasks.md): Tasks are internal reminders and follow-ups, tracked alongside threads rather than on them.
90: - [Fetch tasks](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tasks/get.md): Fetch tasks by ID, by their short reference, or as a paginated collection.
91: - [Create a task](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tasks/create.md): Create a task with a title, and optionally a description, priority, assignee, and due date.
92: - [Update a task](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tasks/update.md): Change individual fields on a task, including who and what it is linked to.
93: - [Delete a task](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/tasks/delete.md): Soft-delete a task, removing it from the active list but keeping it queryable by ID.
94: #### Knowledge gaps
95: - [Knowledge gaps](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/knowledge-gaps.md): Knowledge gaps are questions customers keep asking that your knowledge sources do not answer, detected by the Customer Agent and tracked as tasks.
96: - [Fetch knowledge gaps](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/knowledge-gaps/get.md): List the knowledge gaps in your workspace or fetch one by ID.
97: - [Record a knowledge gap signal](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/knowledge-gaps/create-signal.md): Tell Plain a thread revealed a question your knowledge sources do not answer, so it can group it into a knowledge gap.
98: #### Webhook targets
99: - [Webhook targets](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/webhook-targets.md): A webhook target is an HTTP endpoint Plain delivers events to, subscribed to the events you choose.
100: - [Fetch webhook targets](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/webhook-targets/get.md): Fetch webhook targets by ID or as a paginated collection.
101: - [Create a webhook target](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/webhook-targets/create.md): Register an HTTP endpoint to receive webhook events, and choose which events it gets.
102: - [Update a webhook target](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/webhook-targets/update.md): Change a target's URL, pause it, or move it to a newer schema version.
103: - [Delete a webhook target](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/webhook-targets/delete.md): Delete a webhook target and stop all deliveries to that endpoint.
104: - [Inspect delivery attempts](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/webhook-targets/delivery-attempts.md): Inspect each delivery attempt to a webhook target, including failures and retries.
105: #### Discussions
106: - [Discussions](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/discussions.md): A discussion is an internal Slack thread, email chain, agent session, or workflow task.
107: - [Fetch discussions](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/discussions/get.md): Fetch a discussion by ID or a filtered list, including messages and permissions.
108: - [Start a discussion](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/discussions/create.md): Open a Slack or email side-conversation attached to an existing thread.
109: - [Send a discussion message](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/discussions/send-message.md): Post a new message into an existing discussion, in its original channel.
110: #### Help center
111: - [Help Center](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/help-center.md): Publish and manage Help Center articles, groups, and navigation through the API.
112: - [Fetch help centers and articles](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/help-center/get.md): Fetch help centers, and fetch articles by slug or ID.
113: - [Manage articles](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/help-center/manage-articles.md): Create, update, publish, and delete individual Help Center articles.
114: - [Manage article groups](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/help-center/manage-article-groups.md): Create, update, and delete the nested groups that organize Help Center articles.
115: - [Manage the navigation](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/help-center/navigation.md): Set the order of groups and articles in your Help Center navigation.
116: - [Access & authentication](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/help-center/authentication.md): Control who can read your Help Center, from fully public to signed-in customers only.
117: ### Building Agents
118: - [Set up an agent](https://www.plain.com/docs/agents.md): Create a machine user for your agent, give it an API key, and start receiving events from Plain.
119: - [Interacting in discussions](https://www.plain.com/docs/agents/discussions.md): Let users talk to your agent in Ask Agent, receive their messages as webhooks, and reply through the API.
120: - [Working on threads](https://www.plain.com/docs/agents/threads.md): Listen for thread events, check whether your agent is assigned, and read, reply to, and hand off threads through the API.
121: - [Tool calls](https://www.plain.com/docs/agents/tool-calls.md): Show users which tools your agent ran, and in discussions, wait for approval or ask a question before carrying on.
122: - [Suggesting replies](https://www.plain.com/docs/agents/suggested-replies.md): Draft a reply on a thread for a user to review, edit, and send, instead of replying to the customer directly.
123: - [Working with notes](https://www.plain.com/docs/agents/notes.md): Get a webhook when a user mentions your agent in a note on a thread, and reply with a note of your own.
124: - [Using knowledge](https://www.plain.com/docs/agents/searching-knowledge.md): Search Help Center articles and indexed documents from your agent and put the results in its prompt.
125: - [Example agents](https://www.plain.com/docs/agents/examples.md): Working agents built on the Plain API that you can run locally and copy from.
126: ### Agent integrations
127: - [Agent integrations](https://www.plain.com/docs/integrations.md): Connect Plain to your editor or a local assistant.
128: - [MCP server](https://www.plain.com/docs/integrations/mcp-server.md): Connect Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client to your Plain workspace over the Model Context Protocol.
129: - [Agent skill](https://www.plain.com/docs/integrations/agent-skill.md): Connect Plain to AI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Amp, and OpenCode using the Plain Support Skill.
130: - [Cursor](https://www.plain.com/docs/integrations/cursor.md): Ask Cursor about your product's code from inside a Plain thread.
131: ### Webhooks
132: - [Webhooks](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks.md): Get notified when something happens in your workspace, and react to it in your own systems.
133: - [Webhook versions](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/versions.md): Every webhook target is pinned to a schema version. This page lists each version and what changed.
134: - [Webhooks SDK](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/sdk.md): Webhook parsing and signature verification for Plain webhooks.
135: #### Webhook events
136: - [Thread created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-created.md): Fired when a new thread is created in your workspace, whatever channel it arrived on.
137: - [Thread status transitioned](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-status-transitioned.md): Fired when a thread moves between Todo, Snoozed, Done, or Ignored.
138: - [Thread assignment transitioned](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-assignment-transitioned.md): Fired when a thread's assignee changes or the thread is unassigned.
139: - [Thread labels changed](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-labels-changed.md): Fired when labels are added to or removed from a thread.
140: - [Thread priority changed](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-priority-changed.md): Fired when the priority of a thread changes.
141: - [Note created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-note-created.md): Fired when an internal note is added to a thread.
142: - [Note mention created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-note-mention-created.md): Fired when a note on a thread mentions a machine user.
143: - [Email received](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-email-received.md): Fired when an inbound email arrives in your workspace.
144: - [Email sent](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-email-sent.md): Fired when an email is sent from your workspace.
145: - [Slack message received](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-slack-message-received.md): Fired when a Slack message arrives in a connected channel.
146: - [Slack message sent](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-slack-message-sent.md): Fired when a Slack message is sent from your workspace.
147: - [Slack message updated](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-slack-message-updated.md): Fired when a Slack message on a thread is edited, deleted or reacted to.
148: - [Discord message received](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-discord-message-received.md): Fired when a customer sends a Discord message on a thread.
149: - [Discord message sent](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-discord-message-sent.md): Fired when a Discord message is sent on a thread.
150: - [Discord message updated](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-discord-message-updated.md): Fired when a Discord message on a thread is edited or deleted.
151: - [Microsoft Teams message received](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-ms-teams-message-received.md): Fired when a customer sends a Microsoft Teams message on a thread.
152: - [Microsoft Teams message sent](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-ms-teams-message-sent.md): Fired when a Microsoft Teams message is sent on a thread.
153: - [Chat sent](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-chat-sent.md): Fired when a chat message is sent to a customer on a thread.
154: - [Chat received](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-chat-received.md): Fired when a customer sends a chat message, with the payload schema and an example.
155: - [Thread field created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-field-created.md): Fired when a thread field is set on a thread for the first time.
156: - [Thread field updated](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-field-updated.md): Fired when the value of a thread field changes.
157: - [Thread field deleted](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-field-deleted.md): Fired when a thread field is removed from a thread.
158: - [Thread SLA status transitioned](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-service-level-agreement-status-transitioned.md): Fired when the status of an SLA attached to a thread changes, including breaches.
159: - [Thread account updated](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-account-updated.md): Fired when the account a thread belongs to is changed, added or removed.
160: - [Thread locked](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/thread-locked.md): Fired when a thread is locked and can no longer receive new customer messages.
161: - [Discussion created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/discussion-created.md): Fired when a discussion is started on a thread.
162: - [Discussion message created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/discussion-message-created.md): Fired when a message is posted in a discussion.
163: - [Tool call approval requested](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/discussion-tool-call-approval-requested.md): Fired when your agent asks a user to approve one of its tool calls.
164: - [Tool call approval resolved](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/discussion-tool-call-approval-resolved.md): Fired when a user approves or denies a tool call made by your agent.
165: - [Question resolved](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/discussion-question-resolved.md): Fired when a user answers or dismisses a question card your agent asked.
166: - [Discussion turn stop requested](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/discussion-turn-stop-requested.md): Fired when someone requests that an agent stop its current turn.
167: - [Task created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/task-created.md): Fired when a new task is created in your workspace.
168: - [Task updated](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/task-updated.md): Fired when a task's title, description, priority, account, or assignment changes.
169: - [Task status transitioned](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/task-status-transitioned.md): Fired when a task's status changes, for example moving to done or canceled.
170: - [Task deleted](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/task-deleted.md): Fired when a task in your workspace is deleted.
171: - [Account created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/account-created.md): Fired when an account is created in your workspace.
172: - [Account updated](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/account-updated.md): Fired when the details of an account in your workspace change.
173: - [Account deleted](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/account-deleted.md): Fired when an account in your workspace is deleted.
174: - [Account membership changed](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/account-membership-changed.md): Fired when a customer is added to or removed from an account.
175: - [Account field created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/account-field-created.md): Fired when a field is set on an account for the first time.
176: - [Account field updated](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/account-field-updated.md): Fired when the value of a field on an account changes.
177: - [Account field deleted](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/account-field-deleted.md): Fired when a field is removed from an account.
178: - [Customer created](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/customer-created.md): Fired when a new customer is created in your workspace. Includes the payload schema and an example.
179: - [Customer updated](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/customer-updated.md): Fired when a customer is updated, including which changes trigger it.
180: - [Customer deleted](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/customer-deleted.md): Fired when a customer is deleted from your workspace. Includes the payload schema and an example.
181: - [Customer changed](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/customer-changed.md): Fired when a customer is created or updated, with the previous state on updates.
182: - [Customer group membership changed](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/customer-group-membership-changed.md): Fired when a customer is added to or removed from a customer group.
183: - [Customer group changed](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/customer-group-changed.md): Fired when a customer group is created, updated or deleted.
184: - [Timeline entry changed](https://www.plain.com/docs/webhooks/timeline-entry-changed.md): Fired when a timeline entry is added, updated or removed.
185: ### Channels
186: - [Headless portal](https://www.plain.com/docs/headless-portal.md): Build a support portal inside your own product using the Plain API, so customers read and reply to their threads without leaving your UI.
187: - [Custom channels](https://www.plain.com/docs/custom-channels.md): Bring messages from any channel Plain does not support yet into Plain as threads.
188: ### Customer Cards
189: - [Customer cards](https://www.plain.com/docs/customer-cards.md): Live context straight from your own systems when helping customers.
190: - [Create a customer card](https://www.plain.com/docs/customer-cards/create-a-customer-card.md): Define the details of the customer card.
191: - [Protocol](https://www.plain.com/docs/customer-cards/protocol.md): Learn how we request customer cards from your API and how to respond to these requests.
192: - [Playground](https://www.plain.com/docs/customer-cards/playground.md)
193: - [Examples](https://www.plain.com/docs/customer-cards/examples.md)
194: ### UI Components
195: - [UI components](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components.md): Describe UI declaratively when creating threads, events, and customer cards.
196: - [Badge](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/badge.md): Useful for statuses or when you need to attract attention to something.
197: - [Container](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/container.md): Useful when you need to create a bit of structure.
198: - [CopyButton](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/copy-button.md): Useful if you have any IDs or other details you want to copy for use in messages or outside of Plain.
199: - [Divider](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/divider.md): Useful when you need a bit of structure.
200: - [LinkButton](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/link-button.md): Links out to an external tool, such as your own admin panel or payment provider.
201: - [WorkflowButton](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/workflow-button.md): Lets users trigger a workflow directly from a customer card.
202: - [PlainText](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/plain-text.md): Useful when you want to show any text that should not have any formatting (is not Markdown). If you want markdown please use [Text](/ui-components/text).
203: - [Row](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/row.md): Useful when you need to show two things next to each-other.
204: - [Spacer](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/spacer.md): Adds vertical space between components, in one of five fixed sizes.
205: - [Text](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/text.md): Renders a line of text, with optional size, color, and formatting.
206: - [UI components SDK](https://www.plain.com/docs/ui-components/sdk.md): Helper functions for building Plain UI components with full type safety.
207: ### Security
208: - [Request signing](https://www.plain.com/docs/request-signing.md): Verify that a webhook or customer card request came from Plain using its HMAC signature.
209: - [mTLS](https://www.plain.com/docs/mtls.md): Plain presents a client certificate on outbound requests, so you can verify they came from Plain.
210: - [Allowlist the IP addresses Plain sends requests from](https://www.plain.com/docs/ip-addresses.md): The fixed IP addresses Plain sends webhooks, customer card requests, and workflow HTTP requests from.
211: ### Changelog
212: - [API and webhook updates](https://www.plain.com/docs/changelog.md): Updates to Plain's API, and new webhook schema versions.
