1: --- 2: updatedAt: 2025-09-16T01:15:05.000Z 3: agentTools: 4: projectIndex: https://developers.gorgias.com/llms.txt 5: --- 6: # OAuth2 authentication for creating apps with Gorgias 7: ## Introduction 8: In order to be able to have an approved public app with Gorgias, it is required that the app is using OAuth2 for authentication. 9: You can obtain the OAuth2 token by following these steps and requirements: 10:
    11:
  1. Creating an app on the partners’ account
    2. 12:
  2. Obtaining the client_id and client_secret
    3. 13:
  3. Redirect authorization
    4. 14:
  4. Post request to obtain the access token (has a 24 hours expiration time)
    5. 15:
  5. Refresh token used to obtain the next token (does not have expiration time)
    6. 16:
17: ## Partners account and retrieving client\_id and client\_secret 18: Once the application is created you will be able to retrieve the client\_id and client\_secret parameters. \*note that the client\_id and client\_secret are application-bound parameters, and if you are to create more than one application, you would have different parameter values per application. 19: 20: partners page screenshot for the client\_id and client\_secret 21: 22: ## Authorization redirection 23: Once the application is approved it will appear on the applications page in the helpdesk, and on that page, the connect app button will be available. The Gorgias users will click on the button to initiate the app installation and they will be redirected to the app URL which was specified on the app submission form in the partners’ account. After you have received that request, the app should send an authorization redirect to the following URL: https\://`{subdomain}`.gorgias.com/oauth/authorize 24: The app authorization is received through redirects. 25: Each Gorgias account has its own endpoint, which is defined by the subdomain. On these endpoints are sent all API requests, including the authorization requests. 26: The parameters which are required to be sent in this redirect are: 27:
    28:
  • response_type=code
    • 29:
  • client_id=`{your_app_client_id}`
    • 30:
  • redirect_uri=(app’s backend endpoint where to redirect once the app is authorized in order to obtain the tokes)
    • 31:
  • scope={scopes}
    • 32:
33: Additional parameters: 34:
    35:
  • state=(random string, protecting against CSRF attacks)
    • 36:
  • nonce=(random string, binds it with the token, so we identify the original request that issued it)
    • 37:
38: You can send multiple scopes in the requests, depending on the requirements of your app. 39: > 📘 Example for the redirect URL: 40: > 41: > https\://`{subdomain}`.gorgias.com/oauth/authorize?response\_type=code\&client\_id=6218fa8cfexxxxxxc5929712\&state=randomString1234Test\&scope=customers%3Aread%20tickets%3Aread%20integrations%3Aread\&redirect\_uri=`{apps_redirect_uri}` 42: 43: Authorization page screenshot 44: 45: ## Post request to obtain the access token 46: When the user accepts the authorization for the app, they will be redirected to the redirect\_uri that was set in the previous redirect. In this redirect, the code parameter will be sent as well as the state parameter you provided. The code parameter would be required for the POST request in order to obtain the access token. 47: ```http 48: curl -u : POST https://`{subdomain}`.gorgias.com/oauth/token 49: Content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded 50: grant_type:authorization_code 51: redirect_uri:(the same redirect URL you used during the authorization step) 52: code=`{received_in_redirect}` 53: ``` 54: After this request, you will receive a JSON response containing the access\_token as well as the refresh token. Bear in mind that this access token you receive has a 24 hours expiration time. 55:

access_token JSON response example

56: ```json 57: { 58: "access_token":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6", 59: "expires_in":86400, 60: "id_token":"..v7Hl0iULirBC5UpxeoHpPFuEMLcZKz6IrR8xrLFIcLdT6LB-20u1UPei2ZlpO4ZoyojIglJNKYc1oPYHk1FExa9CKSJGw-dsQVumqNXP7Xk4AwN9PYYIOhyJHA37eRqsbGiLWzMDS4QknZ-OPnrgMFUSSDF1bhyQRqrXiVLOGmESOMJNUd5xKiaQ3a9t7tWdu3IB7Y8sx9UwYC8VOqZSzE3Zihn0Ydg6_xQ9u9ocLKK7bIar7r3aYADUVwBkAzB7J59QN0RZxVnEAtDQZFqViEK0gImWaWpDOMQBPRNpkm3VFZCQYY50qJAA9Pb53XRdvkCyC6R06vYiawgkNUjd4g", 61: "refresh_token":"Bn8nh9P76uDYZb6wADnV93CyuiqaKaaI00mXQpWFWjfbBR06", 62: "scope":"openid email profile offline write:all", 63: "token_type":"Bearer" 64: } 65: ``` 66: ## Refresh token used to obtain the next token 67: With the refresh\_token parameter you have received in the first POST request to obtain the access\_token, you can send another request, to obtain another access\_token. 68: ```http 69: Refresh token request 70: POST https://`{subdomain}`.gorgias.com/oauth/token 71: Content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded 72: grant_type:refresh_token 73: refresh_token:(refresh token you received in the response for obtaining the access_token) 74: ``` 75:

The JSON response containing the new access token will look like this:

76: ```json 77: { 78: "access_token":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCIsImtpZCI6IjB6NWZwe", 79: "expires_in":86400, 80: "scope":"openid email profile offline write:all", 81: "token_type":"Bearer" 82: } 83: ``` 84: > 🚧 85: > 86: > In case the application is deactivated on the helpdesk, in order to obtain the access token again, the entire process for obtaining an access token needs to be repeated. 87: ## Testing the OAuth2 flow before application is submitted 88: In order to test the OAuth2 flow before the application is submitted, you can access it through the partner portal, and on my apps page you can choose the preview option when selecting the additional options of the application, or you can use the following URL to start the installation process: https\://`{subdomain}`.gorgias.com/app/settings/integrations/app/`{your_app_client_id}`\ 89: You can use your sandbox subdomain and your app client id values in order to generate the testing URL. 90: 91: app preview selection 92:

6: # 5. Submit app for review
7: Congratulations! You've built your app and it will soon become available to thousands of Gorgias customers.\
8: There are only a couple of final steps that separate you from this moment.
9: * You need to get back to your [Draft App form](https://developers.gorgias.com/docs/2-create-a-draft-app-submission-form) and complete all the fields that you haven't completed yet. If you're unsure about some fields and not ready to submit your app yet, you can always click on **Save** and come back to this page later.
10: * Add screenshots ([guide](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1qj-KRqAatZ5m7WTUKf7LLRWvcm2836Ud_wzCxElm0S4/edit?usp=sharing)) to the app form, they will appear on the listing and make your app more compelling for merchants.
11: * Once done, click on **Submit Application**.
12: * Our tech partnership team will review your app to make sure it works properly and is aligned with our expectations.
13: * Once we complete the review we will reach out to you to let you know about the result. If it is approved, it will appear in both the in-product App Store and the [public App Store page](https://www.gorgias.com/apps). If it is not approved, we will let you know what needs to be fixed/changed for your app to be approved.

139: An MCP server for interacting with the Gorgias helpdesk API. This server provides tools and resources for managing tickets, customers, and other Gorgias functionality.
140: ## Setup
141: 1. Clone this repository
142: 2. Install dependencies:
143: ```
144: npm install
145: ```
146: 3. Create a `.env` file based on `.env.example` with your Gorgias credentials:
147: ```
148: GORGIAS_DOMAIN=your-domain.gorgias.com
149: GORGIAS_USERNAME=your-username
150: GORGIAS_API_KEY=your-api-key
151: ```
152: Or for OAuth apps:
153: ```
154: GORGIAS_DOMAIN=your-domain.gorgias.com
155: GORGIAS_ACCESS_TOKEN=your-oauth-access-token
156: ```
157: ## Running the Server
158: Start the server:
159: ```
160: npm run dev
161: ```
162: ## Testing with MCP Inspector
163: Test the server with the MCP Inspector:
164: ```
165: npm run inspect
166: ```
167: This will open a web interface where you can test all the available tools and resources.
168: ## Available Tools
169: ### Tickets
170: - `list_tickets`: List tickets from Gorgias helpdesk
171: - `get_ticket`: Get a specific ticket by ID
172: - `create_ticket`: Create a new ticket in Gorgias
173: - `add_message_to_ticket`: Add a message to an existing ticket
174: ### Customers
175: - `list_customers`: List customers from Gorgias
176: - `get_customer`: Get a specific customer by ID
177: ## Available Resources
178: - `gorgias://tickets`: List all tickets
179: - `gorgias://ticket/{id}`: Get a specific ticket by ID
180: ## Authentication
181: This server supports two authentication methods:
182: 1. API Key authentication (username/API key)
183: 2. OAuth token authentication
184: Configure your preferred method in the `.env` file.

1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://www.plain.com/docs/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # Introduction
5: > An overview of Plain's GraphQL API and the data model behind it.
6: Plain itself is built on this same GraphQL API. This means that there are **no limitations** in what can be done via the API vs the UI.
7: These docs cover the most used operations. For anything not documented here, read the [schema](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/schema.md) or [get in touch](mailto:help@plain.com).
8: > [!NOTE]
9: >
10: > If you're looking to access our GraphQL API from an Agent, try our [MCP Server](https://www.plain.com/docs/integrations/mcp-server.md) instead.
11: <Snippet file="graphql/sdk-note.mdx" />
12: ## Key details
13: Our API is compatible with all common GraphQL clients with the following details:
14: * **API URL:** `https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1`
15: * **Allowed method**: POST
16: * **Required headers:**
17: * `Content-Type: application/json`
18: * `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN` where the token is your API key. See [authentication](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/authentication.md) for more details.
19: * **JSON body:**
20: * `query`: the GraphQL query string
21: * `variables`: a JSON object of variables used in the GraphQL query
22: * `operationName`: the name of your GraphQL operation (used for tracking only; it does not affect the call or its result)
23: If you'd like to use the **GraphQL schema to generate types** for your client code you can fetch the schema
24: from: `https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1/schema.graphql`
25: ## Your first API call
26: In this example, we're going to get a customer in your workspace by their email address. You can find a customer's email on the right-hand side when looking at one of their threads in Plain.
27: You will need an API key with the `customer:read` permission. See [authentication](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/authentication.md) for details on how to get an API key
28: You'll need to set two shell variables:
29: * `PLAIN_TOKEN`: The API key
30: * `PLAIN_CUSTOMER_EMAIL`: The email of the customer you want to fetch
31: ```bash theme={null}
32: PLAIN_TOKEN=XXX
33: PLAIN_CUSTOMER_EMAIL=XXX
34: curl -X POST https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1 \
35: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
36: -H "Authorization: Bearer $PLAIN_TOKEN" \
37: -d '{"query":"query customerByEmail($email: String!) { customerByEmail(email: $email) { id fullName updatedAt { iso8601 } } }","variables":{"email":"'"$PLAIN_CUSTOMER_EMAIL"'"},"operationName":"customerByEmail"}'
38: ```
39: This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

4: # Authentication
5: > Create a machine user and an API key, and scope it with fine-grained permissions.
6: A machine user can have several API keys, so you can rotate them without downtime. Each API key carries its own fine-grained permissions.
7: To call the API as a user in your workspace, use an [OAuth app](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/oauth.md).
8: **1. Create a machine user**
9: Go to **Settings → Machine users & agents** and click **Add machine user**. Pick **API User** and click **Continue**. Pick **Agent** instead if you're building an [agent](https://www.plain.com/docs/agents.md).
10: A machine user has two fields:
11: * **Name:** visible only to you and could indicate the usage e.g. "Autoresponder"
12: * **Public name:** This is the name visible to customers (if the machine user interacts with customers) e.g. "Mr Robot"
13: **2. Create an API Key**
14: Click "Add API key" and select the permissions you need. When making API calls, if you have insufficient permissions, the error should tell you which permissions you need.
15: The relevant documentation will tell you which permissions are required for each feature.
16: Once you've made an API key you should copy it and put it somewhere safe, as you will not be able to see it again once you navigate away.
17: **3. Go build things 🚀**
18: Now that you have an API key, pass it on any API call as a header:
19: ```plaintext theme={null}
20: Authorization: Bearer plainApiKey_xxx
21: ```
22: This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://www.plain.com/docs/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # OAuth
5: > Call the API as a user in your workspace after they sign in to your OAuth app.
6: An OAuth app lets users in your workspace sign in to your app with their Plain account. Your app then calls the API as that user, with the permissions their role already has, and Plain records those actions as that user. To call the API as an integration rather than as a user, create a [machine user](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/authentication.md) instead.
7: ## Choose an OAuth app type
8: The OAuth app type determines how your app authenticates when it exchanges an authorization code for an access token. Pick the type before you create the app, because you can't change it afterwards:
9: * **Client-side**: your app exchanges the code in a browser or a mobile or desktop app, where a secret wouldn't stay secret. The app has no client secret and must use Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE).
10: * **Server-side**: your app exchanges the code from your backend, where you can keep a secret. Plain creates a client secret for the app and shows it once.
11: PKCE proves that the token request comes from the app that started the sign-in. Your app generates a random code verifier, sends its SHA-256 hash as the code challenge when the user signs in, then sends the verifier itself with the authorization code.
12: To switch types, create a new OAuth app and move your integration to it.
13: ## Create an OAuth app
14: Creating an OAuth app gives you a client ID, which identifies your app to Plain and isn't secret. A server-side app also gets a client secret.
15: **1. Open the form**
16: Go to **Settings → OAuth applications** and click **Add OAuth app**.
17: **2. Fill in the form**
18: The form has these fields:
19: * **App name**: The name users see when they sign in.
20: * **Description**: Optional.
21: * **OAuth app type**: **Client-side** or **Server-side**. The form selects **Client-side** by default.
22: * **Redirect URLs**: Where Plain sends a user after they sign in. Put each URL on its own line.
23: * **Allowed origins**: Shown only for a client-side app. See [Allowed origins for a client-side app](#allowed-origins-for-a-client-side-app).
24: Each redirect URL and allowed origin must use HTTPS, or HTTP on `localhost`.
25: **3. Create the app**
26: Click **Create OAuth app**. For a client-side app, Plain opens the app's settings page, which shows the client ID.
27: For a server-side app, Plain first shows the client ID and client secret. Click **Done** to open the app's settings page.
28: > [!WARNING]
29: >
30: > Copy the client secret before you click **Done**. You can't see it again. If you lose it, create a new server-side app.
31: The list in **Settings → OAuth applications** shows each app's type, and so does the **Credentials** card on the app's settings page.
32: ### Allowed origins for a client-side app
33: An allowed origin is a website that may call Plain's sign-in endpoints, such as the token endpoint, from the browser. A client-side app needs at least one, because it exchanges the code from the browser, and the browser blocks the call from any other origin.
34: Write each origin on its own line as a scheme and host, with an optional port and no path, such as `https://app.example.com` or `http://localhost:3000`. A server-side app exchanges the code from your backend, so the create form doesn't ask for allowed origins.
35: ## Get an access token
36: Your app gets an access token with the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow: it sends the user to sign in, receives a code at a redirect URL, and exchanges that code for tokens. The authorization server is `https://signin.auth.plain.com`, and its [OpenID configuration](https://signin.auth.plain.com/.well-known/openid-configuration) lists the endpoints.
37: **1. Send the user to sign in**
38: Redirect the user to the authorize endpoint with these query parameters:
39: * **`client_id`**: Your app's client ID.
40: * **`redirect_uri`**: One of the app's redirect URLs.
41: * **`response_type`**: `code`.
42: * **`scope`**: `openid`, plus `offline_access` if you want a refresh token.
43: * **`state`** and **`nonce`**: Random values you generate for this sign-in. Check that the `state` Plain returns matches the one you sent.
44: * **`code_challenge`** and **`code_challenge_method`**: The PKCE code challenge, with method `S256`. A client-side app must send these. A server-side app can skip PKCE, but we recommend it.
45: This builds the URL in TypeScript:
46: ```ts theme={null}
47: const params = new URLSearchParams({
48: client_id: 'your_client_id',
49: redirect_uri: 'your_redirect_url',
50: response_type: 'code',
51: scope: 'openid offline_access',
52: state: 'your_state',
53: nonce: 'your_nonce',
54: code_challenge: 'your_code_challenge',
55: code_challenge_method: 'S256',
56: });
57: const authorizeUrl =
58: `https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/authorize?${params}`;
59: ```
60: A user in more than one workspace chooses which workspace to sign in to. The app only works in the workspace you created it in.
61: **2. Exchange the code for tokens**
62: After the user signs in, Plain redirects to `redirect_uri` with a `code`. Exchange it at the token endpoint, `https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token`.
63: For a server-side app, send the client secret from your backend. This request also sends the code verifier, because it used PKCE:
64: ```bash theme={null}
65: curl -X POST https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token \
66: -d client_id=your_client_id \
67: -d client_secret=your_client_secret \
68: -d grant_type=authorization_code \
69: -d code=your_authorization_code \
70: -d redirect_uri=your_redirect_url \
71: -d code_verifier=your_code_verifier
72: ```
73: For a client-side app, send the code verifier and no client secret. The page's origin must be one of the app's allowed origins:
74: ```ts theme={null}
75: const tokenUrl = 'https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token';
76: const response = await fetch(tokenUrl, {
77: method: 'POST',
78: body: new URLSearchParams({
79: client_id: 'your_client_id',
80: grant_type: 'authorization_code',
81: code: 'your_authorization_code',
82: redirect_uri: 'your_redirect_url',
83: code_verifier: 'your_code_verifier',
84: }),
85: });
86: ```
87: The response includes these fields:
88: * **`access_token`**: The token you send to the API.
89: * **`expires_in`**: How many seconds the access token lasts.
90: * **`refresh_token`**: Included when the sign-in requested `offline_access`.
91: **3. Refresh the access token**
92: Before the access token expires, send the refresh token to the token endpoint with `grant_type=refresh_token` and the client ID. A server-side app also sends its client secret:
93: ```bash theme={null}
94: curl -X POST https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token \
95: -d client_id=your_client_id \
96: -d client_secret=your_client_secret \
97: -d grant_type=refresh_token \
98: -d refresh_token=your_refresh_token
99: ```
100: Store the refresh token from each response and use it for the next refresh.
101: ## Call the API
102: The API URL and request body are the same as for an API key; see [Key details](https://www.plain.com/docs/graphql/introduction.md#key-details). Send the access token in the same header an API key uses:
103: ```plaintext theme={null}
104: Authorization: Bearer your_access_token
105: ```
106: Each query and mutation runs as the signed-in user, with their current role. Changing their role changes what the app can do, and removing them from the workspace stops the app working for them. If they lack a permission, the error names it.
107: GraphQL subscriptions don't accept OAuth app tokens. The API rejects a token from a disabled or deleted app, or from another workspace, with HTTP status `401` and the error code `UNAUTHENTICATED`. The error doesn't say which of these applies.
108: ## Disable or delete an OAuth app
109: Disabling an OAuth app stops it without losing its settings. On the app's settings page, turn off **Enabled** in the **Status** card and click **Save changes**. Users can't sign in to the app, and the API rejects every request from it, including tokens issued before you disabled it, until you enable it again.
110: To delete the app, use the **Delete** card on its settings page.
111: > [!WARNING]
112: >
113: > Deleting an OAuth app ends its access immediately. You can't undo a delete.
114: This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://www.plain.com/docs/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # MCP server
5: > Connect Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client to your Plain workspace over the Model Context Protocol.
6: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI tools connect to external platforms. The Plain MCP server at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp` lets tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor work with your support data directly.
7: You authenticate with your existing Plain account, so the MCP server has the same permissions as your user. No API keys needed.
8: ![MCP server in Plain](https://mintcdn.com/plain/esnLSCL6AbjPxXFS/public/images/mcp-server-1.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=esnLSCL6AbjPxXFS\&q=85\&s=39ebccf73a1794538e5573a64ade642d)
9: ## Setup
10: ### ChatGPT
11: In ChatGPT, add the official Plain plugin:
12: 1. Open the [Plain plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugin_asdk_app_6aec88addd3c8191bc0daa4b3fff3a4c) and add it
13: 2. Sign in with your Plain account and choose your workspace
14: 3. In a chat, type **@** and pick **Plain**
15: ### Cursor
16: You can add the Plain MCP to Cursor via your Cursor config at `~/.cursor/mcp.json`
17: ```json theme={null}
18: {
19: "mcpServers": {
20: "plain": {
21: "type": "remote",
22: "url": "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp"
23: }
24: }
25: }
26: ```
27: Go to **Cursor Settings** → **Tools & MCP** and click **Connect** next to Plain to authenticate.
28: ### Claude.ai
29: 1. Go to "Customize" → "Connectors"
30: 2. Click the ➕ icon, then choose "Add custom connector"
31: 3. Add a custom connector named "Plain" with the Remote MCP server URL `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp`
32: 4. Click the "Connect" button next to the newly created Plain connector to authenticate.
33: ![Claude.ai in Plain](https://mintcdn.com/plain/esnLSCL6AbjPxXFS/public/images/mcp-server-3.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=esnLSCL6AbjPxXFS\&q=85\&s=37b8d1a0b1d71c8740d7aea06b7c4d4d)
34: If you're on a Claude Team plan, you may need to reach out to your administrator to add this custom connector for you.
35: ### Claude Code
36: Adding the Plain MCP to claude-code can be done via the `mcp-remote` helper package which involves adding the following to your `~/.claude.json` configuration.
37: ```json theme={null}
38: "mcpServers": {
39: "plain": {
40: "command": "npx",
41: "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp"],
42: "enabled": true
43: }
44: }
45: ```
46: Unfortunately Claude Code does not support refreshing OAuth tokens yet. A workaround until that is implemented is to use the `mcp-remote` npm package.
47: Next time you start Claude Code, it will launch a browser window asking you to authenticate with your Plain account and select the workspace you'd like to connect. Run the `/mcp` command and select the `plain` MCP to see more details.
48: ### **FX**
49: [**fx**](https://fx.sh/ "https://fx.sh") is a terminal AI coding agent from Vercel Labs. Add the Plain MCP via the CLI:
50: ```text theme={null}
51: fx mcp add --transport http plain https://mcp.plain.com/mcp
52: ```
53: Or add it manually to `~/.fx/mcp.json`:
54: ```text theme={null}
55: {
56: "mcp": {
57: "plain": {
58: "type": "http",
59: "url": "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp",
60: "enabled": true
61: }
62: }
63: }
64: ```
65: fx will prompt you to complete the OAuth flow with your Plain account on the next session start.
66: ### Other MCP clients
67: MCP clients that run locally (not in the browser) can connect to Plain if they support remote HTTP servers. Point it at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp` and complete the OAuth flow when prompted.
68: ## Authentication
69: Plain MCP uses OAuth to allow your MCP server connection to share the same context as your normal web app user. No additional managing of permissions required. This means replies to threads will appear as though they come from your user.
70: ### Required OAuth scopes
71: The Plain MCP server requires every OAuth token to include the `openid` and `offline_access` scopes. If your authorization request omits these, the server returns `403 Forbidden` , even when OAuth completes successfully and returns tokens.
72: Set `scope` to `openid offline_access` (space-separated) in your authorization request. If you are using `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, some versions discover required scopes automatically via the [Protected Resource Metadata endpoint](https://mcp.plain.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp). If yours does not, set them explicitly in your client configuration.
73: After you sign in, your client receives an access token and a refresh token; automatic refresh depends on your client.
74: ## Available tools
75: Once connected, your AI client can do almost anything you can do in Plain, across nearly 400 tools.
76: Tools cover:
77: * Threads and replies
78: * Customers and accounts
79: * Labels, thread fields, and tasks
80: * The Help Center and knowledge sources
81: * Workflows and broadcasts
82: * Tiers, service level agreements (SLAs), and business hours
83: * Snippets and saved views
84: * Discussions with the Sidekick Agent
85: ### Good to know
86: * Your AI client can ask you to confirm actions such as sending a reply or deleting data.
87: * Your Plain role and permissions apply to every tool.
88: * Some changes stay in the Plain app: API keys, billing, roles, invites, webhooks, and custom domains.
89: * The tool list can change. Reconnect the server if a tool is missing.
90: ## Interactive views in your chat
91: Some AI clients can show parts of Plain right inside the chat, so you can review and change what your AI client set up without opening Plain. These views are built on [MCP Apps](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/apps/overview), an official extension to MCP. They act as your user, with your role and permissions, like every other tool.
92: Your AI client opens a view by calling one of the tools below. AI clients call these tools when they're relevant, for example after creating a workflow or when a specific thread comes up. You can also ask for one directly: "Show me my labels."
93: ### Thread
94: `showThread` shows a [thread](https://www.plain.com/docs/product/platform/threads/what-is-a-thread.md) as Plain's thread page. You can read the thread's messages, reply, add notes, and change the thread's status, assignee, priority, labels and fields. The view doesn't update live; it refreshes every 15s while it's on screen.
95: ![The Thread view in a Claude chat, showing a test thread's timeline and reply bar](https://mintcdn.com/plain/GOsEKYocdnM2CjQv/public/images/mcp-server-4.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=GOsEKYocdnM2CjQv\&q=85\&s=c285c33b2675d6ec2fcab5600528dc23)
96: ### Workflow editor
97: `showWorkflow` opens a [workflow](https://www.plain.com/docs/product/workflows.md) in Plain's workflow editor, so you can review and change a workflow your AI client built or changed.
98: ![The workflow editor view in a Claude chat, showing the AI labels triage workflow](https://mintcdn.com/plain/GOsEKYocdnM2CjQv/public/images/mcp-server-5.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=GOsEKYocdnM2CjQv\&q=85\&s=fec41c9dab5df0eb85e52d6d01007168)
99: ### Labels
100: `showLabels` shows your workspace's [labels](https://www.plain.com/docs/product/platform/labels.md), which you can create and edit in place. Your AI client can pass labels it recommends as suggestions, and you create the ones you want by clicking them. The call itself creates nothing.
101: ![The Labels view in a Claude chat, with three suggested labels above the workspace's active labels](https://mintcdn.com/plain/GOsEKYocdnM2CjQv/public/images/mcp-server-6.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=GOsEKYocdnM2CjQv\&q=85\&s=bbcda9d6e9bc949773e89c40f79c2d42)
102: ### Which clients show views
103: Views appear in clients that support the MCP Apps extension, for example Claude.ai, Claude Desktop and ChatGPT. For the current list, see the [MCP extension support matrix](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/client-matrix).
104: In clients without MCP Apps support, the view tools aren't listed. Every other tool works as usual and returns text, so there's nothing to set up.
105: ## Use case examples
106: ### Triage your queue
107: > "Show me my assigned threads. Summarize the top 5 by urgency and suggest which ones I should handle first."
108: Read your active threads and get a prioritized summary without opening each one.
109: ### Understand a customer's history
110: > "Look up the customer with email [alex@acme.com](mailto:alex@acme.com). Show me their recent threads and summarize the pattern. Are they hitting the same issue repeatedly?"
111: Pull together a customer's full context in seconds instead of clicking through timelines.
112: ### Summarize what's waiting
113: > "Show me all my TODO threads. Group them by label and summarize what each one is about."
114: See what has gone quiet, so you can decide what needs attention.
115: ### Draft a reply with full context
116: > "Show me thread th\_01ABC123. Read the full timeline, then draft a reply that addresses the customer's latest question. Use a helpful but concise tone."
117: The AI reads the full thread history and drafts a reply for you to review before sending.
118: ### Audit your Help Center
119: > "List all articles in my Help Center. Flag any that haven't been updated in the last 90 days."
120: Spot outdated documentation without manually checking each article.
121: ### Fill a knowledge gap
122: > "Show me the knowledge gaps customers hit this week. For the top one, check whether our knowledge sources already cover it, draft a Help Center article, and mark the gap's task done."
123: Turn a question the Customer Agent couldn't answer into an article without leaving your AI client.
124: ### Get a snapshot of an account's health
125: > "Look up the account 'Acme Corp'. Show me their details and all open threads. Are there any patterns or escalation risks?"
126: Prep for an account review by pulling account context and open issues together.
127: ### Cross-reference with other tools
128: The Plain MCP works alongside other MCP servers. If you also have Slack, GitHub, or Linear MCPs connected, you can combine them:
129: > "Find threads about 'payment errors' from the last 7 days, check if there's a related GitHub issue, and post a summary to #incidents in Slack."
130: Each server handles its own domain, and the AI coordinates between them.
131: ## If something isn't working
132: * **Can't authenticate:** Make sure you can log into Plain at [app.plain.com](http://app.plain.com) first. The MCP server uses the same auth.
133: * **403 after OAuth completes:** Your token is missing required scopes. Add `openid offline_access` to the `scope` parameter in your authorization request and complete a fresh OAuth flow. See [Authentication](#authentication) for details.
134: * **Tool not appearing:** Some AI clients cache available tools. Try disconnecting and reconnecting the MCP server.
135: * **View not appearing:** Check that your client supports MCP Apps (see [Which clients show views](#which-clients-show-views)). If it does, disconnect and reconnect the Plain MCP server, then start a new chat.
136: * **Permission errors:** Check that your Plain user has the right role for the action you're trying to take.
137: If it's still not working, collect:
138: * Your workspace ID (visible in **Settings → General**)
139: * The exact error message
140: * Which AI client you're using
141: Then reach out to us via [**help@plain.com**](mailto:help@plain.com) for assistance.
142: This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

evidence.observation: quote: When you first receive a refresh token, it will have an expiration date set six months out. You should note this expiration date. During the six months of validity, the API will return the same refresh token to you when you obtain new tokens. In the last 24 hours of validity, however, the API will return a new refresh token, which will then start a new six month period of validity. Therefore, it is important to request new tokens in the last 24 hours of the refresh token's validity period to continue extending this timeframe without having to restart the entire OAuth process.

evidence_rules:
# Research format and evidence rules

Contract version 1.1, 2026-11-23 (updated in Task 06 from v1.0 based on verified Task 05 pilot findings; sealed v1.0 runs retain their frozen contract snapshots).

### Changelog (v1.0 → v1.1)
- Added `vendor_approval_required` to `credential_eligibility.{testing,production}` to separate platform/vendor API-access review (e.g., Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard application) from commercial/agency `partner_approval_required`.
- Clarified edition-matching for `mcp.discovery`: a community MCP targeting a different product edition (e.g., personal web/cookie scraping vs. Enterprise REST API) must not assert `found` for the Enterprise scope without explicit edition alignment.
- Reinforced per-claim attachment: every material detail in a claim (including `purpose` and MCP tool-list observations) must be anchored inside that claim's own attached evidence array and locator line range.

## Files and migration

- `data/apps.json` is the 100-app identity roster, in assignment order. Its provenance identifies the original conversation and user turn. Original app/hint Markdown is retained verbatim, including link targets and parenthetical hints. Categories and normalized names match the audited roster.
- `legacy_candidate_doc_urls` preserves the scaffold's URL leads with their separate provenance. Neither these URLs nor assignment hints establish auth, access, API or MCP findings. Do not inherit the old OAUTH/APIKEY/GATED/MCP lists, generic descriptions, breadth placeholders or buildability labels.
- `schemas/record.json` is a Draft 2020-12 schema for one app in one immutable run. `examples/unresearched-record.json` is a format example, excluded from research and accuracy totals.
- Initialize substantive claims as `not_researched`, with null values and empty evidence. Keep prior artifacts intact as legacy material; a migration must not relabel their guesses as documentary observations. Existing scripts do not yet consume or enforce this contract.
- Paygent Connect (84) is unresolved. Preserve the original `paygent (NMI-powered)` hint. The legacy paygentglobal.com lead has no established identity match. Resolve vendor/product/edition with primary evidence before attaching that domain's facts; do not substitute a similarly named payment company. The example intentionally leaves this unresolved.

## Claim states and evidence

Each scalar claim has a stable `claim_id`, `status`, `value`, `context`, `evidence`, `supporting_claim_refs` and `rationale`. Context names the edition, API version, account type, region and environment where relevant; say which details remain unknown. IDs remain stable across revisions for the same question. Split materially different scopes into distinct method/entry claims rather than merging them.

| Status | Meaning and counting |
| --- | --- |
| `observed` | Explicitly supported by captured source content; non-null value and evidence required. This means documentary observation, not verified truth or a successful API call. |
| `inferred` | Reasoned conclusion; non-null value, evidence, rationale and supporting claim references required. Report separately from documentary observations. |
| `unknown` | Attempted investigation did not resolve the question. Null value; explain the gap. |
| `disputed` | Conflicting content has not been reconciled. Null value; at least two evidence observations and an explanation required. |
| `not_researched` | No investigation yet. Null value; never count as a finding. |
| `not_applicable` | Evidence explains why the question does not apply to the stated scope. Null value; not a negative result or a correct auth/access claim. |
| `not_found_in_checked_sources` | A bounded search found no supported result. Null value and evidence identifying checked content/search scope required. Use for MCP discovery; never translate to 'no MCP exists'. |

`coverage_status` on auth/protocol/resource collections is workflow metadata: `not_researched`, `partial`, or `checked_sources`. `checked_sources` means only the listed sources were examined, never exhaustive coverage of the vendor. Empty arrays do not prove absence. Record unresolved questions in `notes`; a researched collection can still be incomplete.

For each evidence observation record:

- The actual source URL, source kind, exact heading/anchor, page/line range, or repository path plus commit and line range in `locator`.
- A short captured observation or faithful paraphrase supporting this specific claim. A homepage URL, search-result snippet, or a whole-page citation without a locator is a lead, not substantive evidence.
- `captured_on` (ISO date), capture method, and document date/version when known. Null document metadata means unknown, not current. Capture dates must reflect actual reading, not run creation.
- SHA-256 of the captured content and a relative `snapshot_ref` where feasible. Hash normalized/extracted content only if the snapshot is exactly that content and the extraction method is recorded. If no content snapshot/hash is available, use null and a specific `hash_unavailable_reason`; do not fabricate a digest. A hash proves content identity, not correctness. Never store credentials in snapshots.

For actual operational tests, use `source_kind: execution_receipt` and `capture_method: execution_log`. These require a real local receipt/log in `snapshot_ref` and its SHA-256; `source_url` may be null for a local log. Its locator identifies the run/tool call and relevant log lines; observation states the actual result. This is the only source kind that allows a null source URL. This format permits future receipts; it implements no execution functionality and the Task 02 example has no operational findings.

Prefer vendor developer/auth/pricing/access docs and official repositories. Community repositories support their own implementation claims, not vendor endorsement. Assignment text supports identity/category/hints only. Cite approval and pricing sources for eligibility claims; an API reference alone need not establish a free credential path. If official sources conflict, preserve both observations and their time, version and scope; do not silently pick one. `conflicts` links the affected claim IDs and explains the discrepancy; `disputed` claims may also hold both observations directly.

Evidence is attached per claim. Each auth method, API protocol, resource group and MCP entry has its own claim and evidence. A shared page may be cited repeatedly with the appropriate locator. One citation must not silently support other array members or scopes. When one claim necessarily includes several details (e.g. an auth method plus documented scopes), its evidence must support every detail; otherwise split the claim or omit unestablished optional details. For review, any unsupported material detail makes that whole claim unsupported; do not inflate the denominator by splitting punctuation into claims.

## Field rules

**Identity and purpose.** `identity.id`, `app` and `category` come from the roster; resolve product identity in `identity.resolution` using a cited product/edition description. Category is assignment metadata, not a researched auth claim. `purpose` is a short, single-line, cited description. Do not put placeholder prose in an observed value.

**Auth.** `auth.items` contains a separate claim per method and scope. Preserve OAuth2, API key, Basic and tokens separately; don't choose a single winner. `context` and `details` explain API/edition/actor, OAuth grant or signing scheme; `scopes` lists only documented scopes relevant to the described use. An empty scopes list means no scopes captured, not unrestricted permissions. For CLI/local software, only assert `none` or `not_applicable` when supported for that interface; lack of a REST API does not settle CLI buildability.

**Credentials.** `credential_eligibility.testing` and `.production` each contain independent boolean claims:

- `free_access`, `trial_access`, `sandbox_access`: true means a documented credential/use path is available for this environment; false requires evidence of its absence or inapplicability. Unknown stays null.
- `paid_required`, `admin_approval_required`, `vendor_approval_required`, `partner_approval_required`, `contact_sales_required`: true means this condition is required for the stated path/scope. False needs explicit support for proceeding without it; silence is unknown. Distinguish `vendor_approval_required` (vendor/platform API-access review or application, such as Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard) from `partner_approval_required` (commercial, agency, or technology partnership program gating) and `admin_approval_required` (customer tenant/organization admin role or approval).
- `self_serve`: a documented path allows the intended developer to obtain the relevant credentials without vendor/partner intervention. A paid path may be self-serve; an existing tenant's admin can still be required. State actor/plan/prerequisites in each claim's context. Never derive this by default or from 'Sign up'.

These conditions can coexist. A free sandbox can require admin approval; production may require a paid account and partner approval. For alternative credential paths, the context of each claim must identify exactly which path it describes. Do not collapse conflicting paths to one app-wide boolean: use unknown/disputed with explanatory evidence until a scoped answer is possible. A paid product does not automatically mean API access is gated, and a free trial does not establish production access.

**API surface.** Protocols, public documentation, resource groups and breadth are independent claims. A known REST protocol must survive even when breadth and resource groups are unknown. Record each documented protocol and resource group separately with supporting sections; a source can establish 'contacts' while leaving 'billing' unresearched. `public_documentation` refers to documentation visibility for this API scope, not credential eligibility or public data access. Public documentation does not mean anonymous API access.

`breadth` is an inference supported by resource-group claim IDs: `narrow` = one focused workflow/group; `moderate` = multiple related groups; `broad` = multiple distinct business domains. Explain the classification and captured examples in context/rationale. This is qualitative scope, not a fabricated endpoint inventory or a guarantee of completeness. Leave unknown if not enough resource documentation was read. REST/GraphQL/SDK/CLI can coexist; include other interfaces when relevant to agent-callable tools.

**MCP.** `mcp.discovery` is `observed` with value `found` only when at least one supported entry matching the record's declared product edition/scope is recorded. A community MCP targeting a separate consumer/personal edition (e.g., undocumented web-cookie scraping) does not establish `found` for an Enterprise API scope unless tested and documented for that edition; preserve such community entries only with explicit edition separation or leave Enterprise MCP discovery `not_found_in_checked_sources`/`unknown`. Otherwise use the appropriate null state. Each `mcp.entries` item is its own claim with `official`/`community`, source URL, scope, and repository/server URL where established (null otherwise). A server URL may be a hosted endpoint, while a local stdio server may have only a repository URL. No guessed URL. Vendor endorsement must be supported to call it official. Entries for outgoing MCP clients do not establish an app's callable server; record tool direction/scope. `operational_check` remains `not_researched` unless actual execution logs support the result. Docs, a server listing, or a GitHub README cannot establish successful connection, tool calls, or production readiness. This task runs no operational checks.

**Buildability.** This is an explicit inference for a stated agent workflow: `build_now`, `conditional`, `outreach_required` or `not_buildable_for_stated_scope`. Cite supported identity/auth/access/API/MCP or CLI claims through `supporting_claim_refs`, include relevant source evidence, explain the conclusion, list blockers and next steps. A public API can still require outreach; no MCP alone is not a blocker to building an API wrapper. Unknown identity/access/API details can leave buildability unknown. `build_now` is feasibility from evidence, not an implemented or tested integration. Blocker statements also require support; do not label an app unbuildable because a fetch failed.

## Fetch telemetry is separate

`fetches` records URL, attempt date, status, HTTP status, resolved URL, error and optional content digest. It never supplies claim truth. DNS/HTTP errors, login walls, robots blocks and timeouts do not establish no API, paid access, partner gating or nonexistent MCP. A 200 response does not establish a cited claim. Fetch outcomes can prompt follow-up but cannot promote research states automatically.

## Review, runs and accuracy

1. Every saved run gets a unique `run_id`, creation date and producer identity/type. Persist the run input roster hash, schema/rules versions, tool/model versions and configuration alongside that run in a run manifest. Never reuse a run ID or overwrite original records, evidence snapshots, logs or adjudications. The example's run ID is illustrative only.
2. Corrections create a new run with `parent_run_id` and `correction_refs` naming original run/claim IDs plus reasons. Keep the original value/evidence unchanged in the parent; revised claims reuse the same question ID where scope is unchanged. Record added/removed/split claims explicitly in the correction log. New evidence does not retroactively become first-pass evidence.
3. `review` is pending until actual claim adjudications exist. Completed means the listed adjudications are completed, not that every field/app was reviewed. Capture reviewer ID, `ai` or `human`, date, original run ID, each claim ID, judgment, rationale and review evidence. A tool/browser action or another AI is still AI review; only an actual identified person can sign human review. Producer and reviewer identities must be distinct for independent review; disclose shared model/context. Do not copy pending entries over completed reviews.

   An `unresolved` judgment may have an empty evidence array when no source content could be captured. Its required reason must name the actual fetch attempt (for example `fetches[0]` and its date/URL) or an existing failure-log path and describe why adjudication could not finish. Runtime review must resolve that reference. Do not fabricate a source observation for a DNS/access failure. `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported` and `not_applicable` judgments still require captured evidence; a failure-only review cannot establish any of them. A completed review containing unresolved judgments does not mean those claims have been verified and contributes no accuracy denominator for those judgments.
4. Before full-run verification, freeze a sampling manifest: manifest ID/path, target run, roster SHA-256, selection date, method/algorithm/version, seed, selected IDs, category counts, reviewer assignments and claim rubric. Use a deterministic seeded selection of two apps per category (20 total), without replacement; report all ten categories including Support and Helpdesk. Preserve pilot/targeted reviews separately from this sample. A seed alone does not reproduce an unspecified algorithm. Do not select actual sample IDs in Task 02.
5. Freeze the claim inventory and scoring rubric before review. Unit = each non-null `observed` or `inferred` claim object, identified by `(run_id, app_id, claim_id)`. Count auth methods, protocols, groups and MCP entries separately; nested operational checks are separate claims only if asserted. Score a compound claim correct only if all material details hold for its scope. Report documentary and inference results separately. Category/roster metadata, example fixtures, collection metadata, null states and bare URLs are not scored findings.
6. Each adjudication is `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported`, `unresolved`, or `not_applicable`. Unsupported is a failure to substantiate, not proof of factual falsity. Let C/I/U be completed correct/incorrect/unsupported judgments for asserted claims. Evidence-backed accuracy = C / (C + I + U); print those counts, with unresolved/pending/excluded totals alongside. If the denominator is zero, accuracy is null ('unmeasured'), not 0% or 100%. Exclude null-state claims and not-applicable judgments from this accuracy denominator; report any invalid applicability claims as audit issues. Do not drop incorrect or unsupported results after correction.
7. Report review coverage = completed C/I/U judgments / eligible asserted claims in the frozen sample, with unresolved and pending counts. Separately report research coverage across all 100: counts of observed, inferred and each null state for the six required research areas (purpose, auth, credentials, API, MCP, buildability), plus identity resolution. A collection is not covered just because it exists; distinguish partial protocol knowledge from missing breadth. Report area completion criteria and every denominator. Unknowns do not count as correct findings. No one overall 'accuracy' number should conceal missing research or missing review.
8. First-pass and corrected scores refer to immutable runs, the same sample and the frozen claim questions. Link changed/removed/split/new questions; publish paired results on comparable questions and the changed inventory separately. Do not claim improvement by deleting hard claims, changing denominators or relabeling a failure unknown. A corrected/previously reviewed sample is not an unbiased held-out estimate; disclose reuse. Report no accuracy or improvement until actual adjudication exists. Prepare a human checklist if no person has reviewed yet; do not claim human checks were performed.

## Publication contract (later tasks only)

A hosting config, Site registration, expected URL, local Git directory or ZIP is not proof of publication. Save a repository creation/write receipt, actual repository URL, commit SHA, source/README existence and readback evidence. Save the deployment ID/status, actual live URL, deployed commit or artifact SHA-256, date, and an independent fetch/browser result demonstrating the page is accessible to the intended reviewer. Record real errors/blockers when unsuccessful. No publication is attempted in Task 02.

## Validation and Task 03 handoff

No dependencies were installed. From the workspace root, the available PowerShell validates the example:

```powershell
Test-Json -Path examples/unresearched-record.json -SchemaFile schemas/record.json
$roster = Get-Content -Raw data/apps.json | ConvertFrom-Json
if ($roster.apps.Count -ne 100) { throw 'Expected 100 apps' }
if (($roster.apps.id -join ',') -ne ((1..100) -join ',')) { throw 'IDs/order changed' }
if (@($roster.apps | Group-Object category).Count -ne 10) { throw 'Expected 10 categories' }
if (@($roster.apps | Group-Object category | Where-Object Count -ne 10).Count) { throw 'Expected 10 apps per category' }
```

If `jsonschema` is already installed in another environment, this optional check verifies both the schema and example (do not install it for this task):

```console
python -c "import json,jsonschema; s=json.load(open('schemas/record.json')); jsonschema.Draft202012Validator.check_schema(s); jsonschema.Draft202012Validator(s, format_checker=jsonschema.FormatChecker()).validate(json.load(open('examples/unresearched-record.json'))); print('valid')"
```

Schema validation enforces required fields, value types, explicit states, local evidence minimums for assertions, reference presence for inferences, and pending/completed review shape. It cannot establish source truth, identity, evidence relevance, all reference integrity, actual human activity, or immutable run history. Validators may treat `format` as annotation: Task 03 must explicitly validate URLs/date values.

Runtime/reviewer checks to implement in Task 03 (not implemented here):

- Match IDs/names/categories to the roster; unresolved identity blocks promotion of product-specific claims.
- Ensure unique claim IDs (including nested checks), resolve all support/conflict/adjudication/correction references, reject self/circular support, and ensure buildability/breadth dependencies are supported and scoped consistently. Referenced IDs are claim IDs within this app/run unless explicitly paired with an original run ID.
- Require each asserted method/group/server and every material detail to be supported by its own evidence; inspect the actual cited content. Do not accept assignment hints or legacy leads as product evidence. `breadth` must use `inferred` and reference resource claims; `not_found_in_checked_sources` is restricted to MCP discovery.
- Require no asserted items under `not_researched` collection status; track partial knowledge and source scope. MCP `found` needs at least one supported entry and source-backed origin; operational success needs execution receipts. No nonempty MCP entries under an unknown/negative discovery state.
- Verify valid dates/URLs, content hashes/snapshot paths, document versions, primary/community attribution and conflicts. Keep fetch failures separate and ensure captures correspond to real reads.
- Enforce append-only runs/reviews and snapshot storage, parent/correction linkage, review identity/type, sample reproducibility/category coverage, frozen claim denominators and metric arithmetic. Retain unsupported results.
- Require publication receipts/readback before reporting repo/live-page success.

Coordinator acceptance should cover: honest unknown example passes; multi-auth and REST-only partial knowledge pass; evidence-free observed auth/purpose and unsupported inferred buildability fail; malformed dates/refs are flagged by runtime if the validator does not reject them; completed review with no reviewer/judgments fails. Passing a schema is not evidence that Task 03 or the assignment research is complete.

roster.purpose: Assignment identity inputs and source leads only; no researched app findings.

provenance.method: Original user assignment read via read_thread; hints preserved verbatim as Markdown; normalized app names, IDs, categories and order checked against research_agent.py RAW. No websites fetched.
provenance.legacy_warning: Candidate URLs are unverified source leads, not original assignment hints or evidence. Legacy auth/access/API/MCP/buildability guesses are excluded.

apps.identity_note: Original hint is paygent (NMI-powered). No evidence links this product to paygentglobal.com. Do not endorse that domain, substitute another Paygent product, or attach its docs until primary evidence resolves the identity.
